    Engineering Fundamentals/Motion and Rotation

    Rotation and Linear Speed

    Turn a shaft speed into the speed of what it drives, and back again, using the radius - belts, rollers, wheels, and grinding wheels.

    The radius is what links turning to travelling; Watch out

    The radius is what links turning to travelling

    A roller turns; the belt on it travels. A wheel turns; the vehicle moves. The two speeds are not the same number, and the thing that converts one into the other is the radius.

    v = ωr  ·  a = αr

    Here a is the tangential acceleration, not the rim point’s total acceleration: it also has an inward component ω2r. Belt and vehicle speeds match rim speed only when there is no slipping.

    v
    The straight-line speed of a point on the rim — the speed of the belt, the sheet, the vehicle.
    ω
    Angular velocity, in radians per second. See Angular Motion for the conversion from rpm.
    r
    The radius, in the same length unit you want the answer in. Rollers and wheels are almost always specified by diameter, so halve it first.

    Both of these formulas are only true when the angle is in radians. Feed them rpm and the answer is wrong by a factor of about 9.55; feed them degrees per second and it is wrong by a factor of about 57.3. Convert to rad/s first, every time.

    Two mistakes account for nearly every wrong answer here: using the diameter where the radius belongs, and leaving the speed in rpm. Both are worth a deliberate check before the arithmetic starts.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 27 — Why the radian is the only angle unit that works.

    Worked example: a conveyor drive roller

    Worked example: a conveyor drive roller

    A conveyor belt runs over a drive roller 200 mm in diameter, turning at 45 rpm. What is the belt speed, and how long does a package take to travel 15 m?

    1. Halve the diameter: r = 100 mm = 0.100 m.
    2. Convert the speed: 45 r/min × 0.1047198 rad/s per r/min = 4.712389 rad/s.
    3. Multiply: v = 4.712389 rad/s × 0.100 m = 0.4712 m/s.
    4. Divide the distance by the speed: 15 m ÷ 0.4712389 m/s = 31.83 s.

    0.47 m/s, and about 32 s for 15 m. That assumes the belt does not slip on the roller, which is the assumption a real drive is designed to make true.

    Worked example: a roll-forming feed rate

    Worked example: a roll-forming feed rate

    Forming rolls 150 mm in diameter rotate at 25 rpm. What is the feed rate of the sheet in m/min, and how long does 20 m of sheet take?

    1. r = 75 mm = 0.075 m.
    2. 25 r/min × 0.1047198 rad/s per r/min = 2.617994 rad/s.
    3. v = 2.617994 rad/s × 0.075 m = 0.19635 m/s.
    4. The question asks for metres per minute, so convert the time unit: 0.19635 m/s × 60 s/min = 11.78 m/min.
    5. 20 m ÷ 11.78 m/min = 1.70 min, which is about 1 min 42 s.

    Note what step 4 did and did not do. Changing seconds to minutes in a speed takes one factor of 60. If the quantity had been an acceleration, the same change would take 602 — see Acceleration and Squared Time.

    Worked example: running the conversion backwards

    Worked example: running the conversion backwards

    Sometimes the linear quantity is what you know. The formulas simply rearrange: ω = v/r and α = a/r.

    A wheel, from angular to linear

    A tyre 28 in in diameter turns at 3.5 rad/s. How fast is the vehicle moving, in miles per hour?

    1. r = 14 in × 0.0254 m/in = 0.3556 m.
    2. v = 3.5 rad/s × 0.3556 m = 1.2446 m/s.
    3. 1.2446 m/s ÷ 0.44704 m/s per mph = 2.78 mph.

    A wheel, from linear to angular

    A vehicle accelerates at 5 m/s2 on tyres 78 cm in diameter. What is the angular acceleration of a wheel?

    1. r = 39 cm = 0.39 m.
    2. α = 5 m/s2 ÷ 0.39 m = 12.8 rad/s2.

    Check the unit on the answer, not just the number. Dividing m/s2 by m leaves 1/s2, and because the radian is a ratio of two lengths, rad/s2 is the same thing named for what it describes.

    Rim speed is why wheel size changes the safe rpm; Stop

    Rim speed is why wheel size changes the safe rpm

    A grinding wheel is limited by how fast its rim moves, not by how fast its centre turns. Put a bigger wheel on the same spindle at the same rpm and the rim goes faster, because every point on it travels a longer circle in the same time.

    Take a wheel whose rim speed must stay at or below 35 m/s:

    Same 35 m/s rim-speed limit, two wheel sizes.
    Wheel diameterRadiusω = v/rSame speed in rpm
    200 mm0.100 m350 rad/s3,342 rpm
    250 mm0.125 m280 rad/s2,674 rpm

    The larger wheel has to run slower, by about 670 rpm, to keep the same rim speed. Nothing about the machine changed; only the radius did.

    Do not calculate your way to a grinding-wheel speed. The number that governs is the maximum operating speed marked on the wheel, and OSHA requires that the spindle speed of the machine be checked before a wheel is mounted, to be certain it does not exceed that marking (29 CFR 1910.215(d)(1)). The arithmetic above explains why a bigger wheel is marked slower. It does not authorise a wheel, and it is not a substitute for reading the wheel. See Machine Hazards and Housekeeping.

    Engineering Fundamentals/Force and Power

    Torque

    Turning effort is force times radius - how to calculate it, which unit belongs to it, and why the order of the two words is not decoration.

    Torque is force applied at a radius; Watch out

    Torque is force applied at a radius

    A force pushes. A torque turns. The same force produces more torque the further it acts from the axis of rotation, which is why a longer wrench loosens a tighter nut with the same pull.

    τ = rF  —  torque (τ, tau) equals radius times force.

    r is the radius, measured from the axis of rotation to where the force acts. Pulleys, rollers, and wheels are specified by diameter, so halve the number on the drawing before it goes into this formula.

    Note: when a turning effort is described about an axis rather than about a shaft, it is often called a moment and given the symbol M. It is the same calculation.

    The unit, and the word order that identifies it

    The unit, and the word order that identifies it

    Torque units and rounded conversion factors between them.
    SystemUnitSymbolConversion
    SInewton metreN·m1 N·m = 0.7375621 lbf·ft
    Foot–slug–secondpound-force footlbf·ft1 lbf·ft = 1.355818 N·m

    Case matters, and this one bites. The SI torque unit is N·m with a lower-case m. Written N·M it is not a valid SI torque unit: M is the prefix for 106, but a prefix cannot stand alone as a unit. The same trap catches Kg for kg and S for s. See Measurement Language.

    Here torque is written lbf·ft; energy is written ft·lbf. The same two units, the same numerical factor, written in the opposite order — and NIST prints them that way round on purpose: pound-force foot converts to the newton metre, foot pound-force converts to the joule. They are different physical quantities that happen to share a unit combination. Word order is a convention, not a mathematical distinction; use the quantity and context to tell them apart. SI avoids the ambiguity by giving energy its own name, the joule; a torque is never written in joules. See Work and Energy.

    Worked example: can the motor hold the arm up?

    Worked example: can the motor hold the arm up?

    A robot-arm joint motor produces 15 N·m. The arm segment is 0.35 m long and carries a 25 N load at its end. Will the motor hold the arm horizontal?

    1. The load acts straight down, at right angles to a horizontal arm, at the full 0.35 m: τ = 0.35 m × 25 N = 8.75 N·m.
    2. Compare with what the motor produces: 8.75 N·m < 15 N·m.

    Yes, with 6.25 N·m to spare — for the load alone. The weight of the arm segment itself also produces a torque about the joint, and no mass was given for it, so this answer is a partial one. In a real selection you would add the arm weight acting at its own centre of mass, then keep margin on top of that.

    This is the shape of most torque questions: work out what the load demands, then check it against what the drive can supply, and be explicit about what you have left out.

    Worked example: torque from a tangential force

    Worked example: torque from a tangential force

    A wheel 250 mm in diameter needs 3.5 kN of tangential force to overcome resistance. What torque must the motor supply to the axle?

    1. r = 125 mm = 0.125 m.
    2. 3.5 kN = 3,500 N.
    3. τ = 0.125 m × 3,500 N = 437.5 N·m.

    The same formula, rearranged

    When the torque is what you know and the force is what you want, F = τ/r. That single rearrangement explains a family of everyday machines: a longer wrench, a bigger steering wheel, and a larger pulley all trade radius against force. Double the radius and the same torque delivers half the force — and, at the same rotational speed, the rim travels twice as far, which is why Power and Efficiency comes out unchanged.

    Engineering Fundamentals/Motion and Rotation

    Gear Ratios

    Follow tooth counts through pairs, idlers and compound trains; multiply stage efficiencies and choose gears to meet speed and torque limits.

    Experiment: trade speed for turning effort; Interactive

    Experiment: trade speed for turning effort

    Predict first: a 20-tooth gear turns at 120 rpm clockwise and drives a 40-tooth gear. Will the larger gear turn faster or slower? What changes if you add an idler between them?

    All three examples use the same ideal input: 120 rpm and 2 N·m. Input power is 25.13 W, and ideal output power is also 25.13 W. More output torque comes with less speed.

    With each actual mesh at 96% efficiency, the pair delivers 3.84 N·m and 24.13 W; the idler train delivers 3.6864 N·m and 23.16 W; the compound train delivers 7.3728 N·m and 23.16 W. Their output speeds remain 60, 60 and 30 rpm. This comparison charges a loss at both idler meshes.

    Count the teeth to find the speed

    Count the teeth to find the speed

    The driver supplies motion; the driven gear receives it. For one external gear mesh, each tooth passing on the driver advances the driven gear by one tooth space. A gear with twice as many teeth needs twice as many passing teeth to complete a turn.

    Output speed = input speed × driver teeth ÷ driven teeth. A 20-tooth driver at 120 rpm driving 40 teeth gives 120 × 20 ÷ 40 = 60 rpm. External meshing reverses the direction.

    This lesson uses reduction ratio i = input speed ÷ output speed, with speed magnitudes. A 2:1 reduction means two input turns for one output turn. Ratios above 1 reduce speed; ratios below 1 increase it. At zero speed, use tooth counts to find the ratio; do not divide 0 by 0.

    Notation map: this page's original equations use N for teeth and n for speed. The course uses n for teeth, ω for angular velocity and τ for torque. Thus page N = course n; page speed n is written ω in the additions below. GR and i name the same reduction ratio.

    In course notation, using magnitudes: GR = nout/nin = dout/din = ωin/ωout = τout/τin for an ideal single pair. Here d is pitch diameter; the torque equality assumes no losses. For a compound train, multiply the stage ratios; the first and last tooth counts alone do not give the overall ratio.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 30 — Why tooth counts work, and what the dashed circles mean.

    An idler and a compound shaft do different jobs

    An idler and a compound shaft do different jobs

    One mesh reverses

    A → B turns the output opposite to the input, viewed from the same end of each shaft.

    An idler cancels

    A → I → B reverses twice. I affects its own speed and the spacing, but its tooth count cancels from the end-to-end ratio.

    Compound stages multiply

    A → B, then C → D, with B and C fixed together: i = (NB/NA) × (ND/NC).

    Same shaft means the same angular speed. A large B and a small C fixed to one shaft make the same number of turns in the same direction. Their rim speeds differ because their radii differ. They do not mesh with each other.

    In the compound example, 20 → 40 teeth halves the speed. A second 20 → 40 stage halves it again: 120 → 60 → 30 rpm. The two external meshes make the final output turn in the same direction as the input.

    An idler is not another reduction stage. Drop its tooth count when finding the end-to-end ratio, but count every external mesh for direction: odd means opposite; even means the same, viewed from the same end of the parallel shafts. Do not drop a gear that shares a shaft with a different gear in a compound train.

    More torque costs speed; it does not create power

    More torque costs speed; it does not create power

    Torque is turning effort. In this ideal, lossless train at steady load, output torque magnitude = input torque magnitude × reduction ratio. A 2:1 reduction changes 120 rpm and 2 N·m into 60 rpm and 4 N·m. The 4:1 compound example gives 30 rpm and 8 N·m.

    Rotational power is torque × angular speed: P = T × 2πn/60 when T is in N·m and n is in rpm. Both sides of either example carry 25.13 W ideally. Real friction and other losses leave less output power. Tooth strength, bearings, shafts, lubrication and the motor all limit usable torque.

    At zero speed, mechanical power is zero. A loaded, stationary gear train can still carry torque. The lab shows ideal static torque balance in that case; it does not model motor stall behavior or promise a safe load.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 31 — Primary references and model boundaries.

    Connect the gears to Angular Motion, Rotation and Linear Speed and Torque.

    Stage efficiencies multiply; losses accumulate

    Stage efficiencies multiply; losses accumulate

    Each stage receives only the power that survived the stage before it. Use decimal efficiencies and multiply: ηtotal = η1 × η2 × η3. Never add or average them. See Power and Efficiency for the general meaning of efficiency.

    At 98% per stage, three stages give 0.98³ = 0.941192: about 5.88% total loss, not 6%. Fewer, higher-quality stages often beat many cheap stages for efficiency, provided they can meet the ratio and load requirements.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 32 — Why adding losses is only an approximation.

    Positive drives keep the speed ratio; losses reduce torque

    Positive drives keep the speed ratio; losses reduce torque

    A positive drive keeps input and output linked in a fixed ratio without slipping. Gears, chains and timing belts are positive drives. A slipping flat belt or V-belt is not. Follow Rotation and Linear Speed for the connection from rotation to belt travel.

    At a stated steady input speed and load, use magnitudes:

    ωout = ωin/i
    τout = τin × i × ηtotal
    Pout = ηtotal × Pin

    The teeth still set the speed exactly in this model. Efficiency reduces output torque from its ideal value. It does not reduce output rpm as well. Use matching torque units on both sides: lbf·ft or N·m. The course conversion is 1 rpm ≈ 0.1047 rad/s when angular speed in rad/s is needed.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 33 — Follow both stages of one loaded train.

    Count stages for ratio, meshes for direction and stated losses

    Count stages for ratio, meshes for direction and stated losses

    For a simple train A → I → B, the idler cancels from (NI/NA) × (NB/NI) = NB/NA. The two external meshes still reverse direction twice.

    Follow the loss assumption in the problem. Real meshes lose some power, but a problem may explicitly ignore it. If every actual mesh is 96% efficient, A → I → B has ηtotal = 0.96². If a whole stage including its idler is assigned 96%, use that stage value once. If η = 1.00 is stated, ignore losses. Do not infer the loss count from the reduction-stage count when an idler is present.

    Choose teeth, then check both output limits; Checklist; Practice

    Choose teeth, then check both output limits

    • Record input speed and torque, the output speed ceiling and torque floor, available integer tooth counts, maximum ratio per stage, and the loss assumption.
    • Use the speed ceiling to find i ≥ ωin/ωceiling. With at most R:1 per stage, k reduction stages can provide at most Rk:1.
    • For each candidate stage count k, calculate ηtotal and check the torque bound i ≥ τfloor/(τin × ηtotal). Use the larger of the speed and torque bounds.
    • Choose whole-tooth pairs within the range and per-stage limit. Connect successive pairs by shared shafts. Multiply their actual ratios; do not assume a rounded target is achievable.
    • Calculate output speed and torque, keeping full precision for both limit checks. Check direction by counting external meshes. An added idler may require recalculating losses.

    To choose the faster of feasible designs at the same input speed, compare their actual overall ratios: the smaller one is faster. A feasible design is not automatically the fastest possible design.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 34 — Worked design: a winch with a speed ceiling and torque floor.

    Engineering Fundamentals/Force and Power

    Work and Energy

    Force moving through a distance is work - the joule, the foot pound-force, and why an energy unit reads backwards from a torque unit.

    Work is a force moving something through a distance

    Work is a force moving something through a distance

    Holding a heavy box still is exhausting, and in this sense it is zero work. Work needs a component of force along the displacement; work is negative when that component opposes the movement.

    W = Fs  —  work equals force times displacement for a constant force parallel to the motion.

    Work is one of the ways energy moves from one place to another, so it is measured in energy units and is often written E when what matters is the energy delivered rather than the act of delivering it.

    The two systems, for work and every other form of energy.
    SystemUnitSymbolBuilt from
    SIjouleJ1 J = 1 N·m
    Foot–slug–secondfoot pound-forceft·lbf1 ft·lbf = 1.355818 J

    Worked example: lifting a load

    How much work is required to lift a 2,000 lb load to a height of 10 ft?

    1. The force needed to lift steadily is the load’s weight, 2,000 lbf, and it acts straight up along the 10 ft of travel.
    2. W = 2,000 lbf × 10 ft = 20,000 ft·lbf.
    3. In SI: 20,000 ft·lbf × 1.355818 J per ft·lbf = 27,116 J, or 27.1 kJ.

    Two things this calculation assumes, both worth saying out loud: the load is raised at a steady speed, so no extra force goes into accelerating it, and the 2,000 lb figure is a weight in pound-force, not a mass in pound-mass. On Geometry, Mass, and Force those are separate quantities, and here it is the force that belongs in the formula.

    Work and torque share dimensions - word order is a convention; Watch out

    Work and torque share dimensions - word order is a convention

    Multiply a constant force by displacement along that force and you get work. Multiply a force by a radius and you get torque. Both are a force times a length, so in the foot–pound system both come out as some arrangement of feet and pounds-force.

    Here torque is written lbf·ft. Energy is written ft·lbf. The numerical factor is identical — 1.355818 of either — but word order alone does not establish the physical quantity. Torque describes turning effort; work describes energy transferred through displacement.

    SI removes the ambiguity by naming the energy unit separately. A torque stays N·m; energy becomes the joule. Numerically 1 J = 1 N·m, but a torque is never reported in joules. See Torque.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 35 — Turning a torque into work, and where the radian goes.

    The energy units you will actually meet

    The energy units you will actually meet

    Energy is billed, rated, and specified in a lot of different units. They all convert; the only work is knowing which one a number is in.

    Common energy units, expressed in joules.
    UnitSymbolIn joulesWhere it turns up
    jouleJ1 JThe SI unit. Everything else converts to it.
    foot pound-forceft·lbf1.355818 JU.S. mechanical work and energy.
    watt hourW·h3,600 J (exact)Battery capacity.
    kilowatt hourkW·h3,600,000 J (exact)The line on an electricity bill.
    British thermal unit (IT)BtuIT1,055.056 JHeating, cooling, and fuel ratings.
    horsepower hourhp·h≈ 2,684,520 JEngine and drive energy.
    calorie (IT)calIT4.1868 J (exact)Thermal work and material data.

    A kilowatt hour is a power multiplied by a time, and that is all it is. One kilowatt sustained for one hour. It is not an SI unit — NIST lists it among the units to be converted into SI — but it is exactly 3.6 MJ, and it is the unit an electricity meter counts in.

    “Btu” on its own is ambiguous. NIST lists six different British thermal units, from 1,054.35 J to 1,059.67 J depending on which definition is meant. The spread is about half a percent, which is small until it is multiplied by a fuel bill. Use BtuIT unless a specification names another one.

    Engineering Fundamentals/Force and Power

    Power and Efficiency

    Power is work per unit time - three equivalent ways to calculate it, the horsepower conversions, and what an efficiency figure can and cannot be.

    Power is how fast work gets done

    Power is how fast work gets done

    Two hoists that lift the same load to the same height do the same work. The one that does it in half the time needs twice the power.

    P = W / t  —  average power equals work divided by elapsed time.

    The two power units and the factors between them.
    SystemUnitSymbolDefinition and conversion
    SIwattW1 W = 1 J/s; 1 W = 0.001341022 hp
    Foot–slug–secondhorsepowerhp1 hp = 550 ft·lbf/s; 1 hp = 745.6999 W

    The symbol W does double duty: upright W after a number is the watt, while W standing in a formula for a quantity is usually work. Context separates them: P = W/t uses W for work, while 1 W = 1 J/s uses it for the watt.

    Worked example: powering the lift

    On Work and Energy, lifting 2,000 lbf through 10 ft took 20,000 ft·lbf, or 27.1 kJ. How much power does doing it in 4 s require?

    1. In U.S. units: 20,000 ft·lbf ÷ 4 s = 5,000 ft·lbf/s, and 5,000 ÷ 550 = 9.09 hp.
    2. In SI: 27,116 J ÷ 4 s = 6,779 W, or 6.78 kW.
    3. Cross-check the two: 9.0909 hp × 745.6999 W/hp = 6,779 W. They agree, which is the point of doing both.

    That is the power delivered to the load. A motor sized for this job needs more than that, because no drive is perfectly efficient.

    The same power, three ways to reach it; Watch out

    The same power, three ways to reach it

    Which form you use depends on what you have been given, not on which is more correct. All three produce watts in SI. In P = Fv, force and velocity must be parallel; otherwise use the force component along the velocity.

    Three routes to a power, in each system.
    FormSIFoot–pound
    Work over time
    P = W/t    		 J/s = W (ft·lbf/s) ÷ 550 = hp
    Force times speed
    P = Fv    		 N × (m/s) = W (lbf × ft/s) ÷ 550 = hp
    Torque times angular velocity
    P = τω    		 (N·m) × (rad/s) = W (lbf·ft × rad/s) ÷ 550 = hp

    In the third form the angular velocity must be in rad/s. An rpm figure substituted directly is wrong by a factor of about 9.55. Convert it first — Angular Motion.

    The divisor 550 is not a fudge factor. One horsepower is defined as 550 pound-force feet of work per second, so dividing by 550 is simply converting the unit.

    Two shortcut formulas, and the conditions attached to them

    Two shortcut formulas, and the conditions attached to them

    These two save a lot of arithmetic in practice. Both are unit conversions with an assumption hidden inside.

    From volts and amps

    hp = (volts × amps) ÷ 746

    The 746 is exact: NIST defines a separate unit, horsepower (electric), as 746 W. So the formula is really two steps — find the electrical power in watts, then convert watts to horsepower.

    The hidden condition is in the first step. Volts times amps gives real power in watts for a direct-current circuit or a purely resistive load. For single-phase AC, RMS volts times RMS amps gives apparent power, in volt-amperes; the real power in watts is that multiplied by the power factor, the ratio of real power to apparent power. Use the shortcut on an AC motor without its power factor and the answer comes out high. See Current, Voltage, and Resistance.

    From torque and rpm

    hp = (torque in lbf·in × speed in rpm) ÷ 63,025

    This one is the P = τω row above, with the rpm-to-rad/s conversion and the inch-to-foot conversion already folded into the constant. It only works with the torque in pound-force inches and the speed in rpm; feed it lbf·ft and the answer is twelve times too small.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 37 — Where 63,025 comes from.

    Efficiency is the fraction that makes it through; Watch out

    Efficiency is the fraction that makes it through

    The efficiency of a machine is the ratio of useful output to total input. Its symbol is η (eta), and it can be written with either power or work as long as both sides of the ratio use the same one:

    η = Pout / Pin  ·  η = Wout / Win

    It is a ratio of two like quantities, so the units cancel: efficiency is a plain number, usually quoted as a percentage.

    For a real machine in steady operation, η < 1; the ideal lossless limit is 1. You cannot get more power out than you put in, and some of every input always leaves as heat, noise, or friction rather than as useful output. A calculated efficiency above 1 means an error in the numbers, not a remarkable machine.

    Worked example: an electric hoist motor

    A motor consumes 500 W and applies 1,000 N of force to lift an object at 0.45 m/s. What is the efficiency of the system?

    1. Useful output, using P = Fv: 1,000 N × 0.45 m/s = 450 W.
    2. η = 450 W ÷ 500 W = 0.90, or 90%.

    The missing 50 W has not vanished. It is power lost rather than delivered to the load, typically as heat in the motor and drive.

    Worked example: follow power through two stages

    A hypothetical steady system receives 100 W. Stage 1 is given as 80% efficient, and Stage 2 is given as 90% efficient. Each percentage applies to the power entering that stage.

    1. Stage 1 output: 100 W × 0.80 = 80 W. Stage 1 loss: 100 W − 80 W = 20 W.
    2. Stage 2 receives 80 W, not the original 100 W. Its output is 80 W × 0.90 = 72 W. Its loss is 80 W − 72 W = 8 W.
    3. Overall efficiency: 72 W / 100 W = 0.72, or 72%. Equivalently, 0.80 × 0.90 = 0.72.
    4. Total accounted loss: 20 W + 8 W = 28 W. Check the boundary: 72 W useful + 28 W loss = 100 W input.

    Do not add 20% + 10% and call the system 70% efficient. The 20% loss is measured from 100 W, while the 10% loss is measured from the 80 W that reaches Stage 2. Watts may be added here because 20 W and 8 W are amounts of power accounted across the same overall boundary.

    Work backward when the required output is known: Stage 2 needs 72 W / 0.90 = 80 W at its input, and Stage 1 needs 80 W / 0.80 = 100 W. The same result comes from 72 W / 0.72 = 100 W. Use Gear Ratios to explore the same multiplication idea for stated per-mesh losses.

    These are given, illustrative constant efficiencies at steady operation with no changing stored energy. They are not a motor performance prediction. The accounted losses leave the useful-flow path rather than disappearing; this example does not predict their temperature or physical mechanism.

    Efficiency figures are only comparable when the boundary is the same. A motor efficiency, a drive efficiency, and a system efficiency measured from the wall socket to the load are three different numbers for the same machine, and the largest of them is the one a datasheet prefers to print. Say which one you mean.

    Engineering Fundamentals/Power Transmission

    Belt, Chain and Gear Drives

    Choose a drive by shaft spacing, timing, speed and environment, then check its load rating and maintenance needs.

    Three ways to carry rotation from one shaft to another

    Three ways to carry rotation from one shaft to another

    A drive transfers motion and turning effort from a driver to a driven shaft. Belts and chains bridge a gap. Gears engage directly and fit into a compact housing. Start with the job the drive must do, then choose the parts.

    Gears, chains and timing belts are positive drives: engagement maintains a tooth-count ratio without ordinary frictional slip. Flat and V-belts are friction drives: their grip depends on friction and tension, so slip can change the speed ratio.

    Positive engagement does not mean perfect positioning. Tooth clearance, elastic deflection and chain speed ripple still matter. For ratios, compound trains and losses, use Gear Ratios. For turning effort and power, use Torque and Power and Efficiency.

    Explore which drives fit the job; Interactive

    Explore which drives fit the job

    Choose a shaft arrangement, a timing requirement, a speed range and an environment. Change one requirement at a time and watch which reason changes. “Close” allows a compact gear mesh; “separated” needs a flexible span. These are qualitative screening rules, not a component sizing tool.

    Try this on paper: two separated parallel shafts must stay synchronized in a clean, lubricant-sensitive area. A timing belt is a useful starting candidate: its teeth maintain timing and the belt mesh needs no oil. Flat and V-belts cannot guarantee timing. An ordinary chain needs lubrication; a single gear pair cannot bridge the chosen gap without making the gears much larger.

    Now remove the timing requirement: flat or V-belts become candidates. Bring the shafts close together inside a lubricated housing: gears become candidates. Each change removes a different constraint.

    Compare timing, space and upkeep side by side

    Compare timing, space and upkeep side by side

    Typical tendencies for correctly selected industrial drives; actual ratings come from the chosen product.
    QuestionFlat / V-beltTiming beltRoller chainGear pair
    Center distanceUseful across separated shaftsUseful across separated shafts; check available lengthsUseful across separated shafts; manage slackClose shafts; size and mesh set spacing
    Slip and timingCan slip; unsuitable for fixed timingPositive; matched teeth engagePositive average ratio; clearance and speed ripple remainPositive ratio; backlash matters on reversal
    NoiseUsually quiet; absorbs vibrationOften quiet, but tooth engagement can make noiseLink engagement becomes noisier at speedSpur teeth can whine; helical engagement is smoother
    LubricationBelt contact runs dryBelt contact runs dryOrdinary chain needs lubricant at its jointsMost loaded metal gears need lubrication
    CostOften low initial costMatched toothed parts usually cost more than basic friction beltsInclude sprockets, lubrication and replacementPrecision gears, bearings and housing can raise initial cost
    MaintenanceInspect wear, alignment and tensionInspect teeth, tracking and specified tensionLubricate; measure wear elongation; inspect sprocketsCheck oil/grease, seals, tooth condition and alignment

    Belt contact running dry does not mean the shaft bearings need no lubrication. A sealed gearbox can keep lubricant away from a product; an exposed chain generally cannot. Special materials and lubrication-free products need their own ratings.

    Read the parts in detail: Belt Drives, Chain Drives and Gear Drives and Tooth Geometry.

    Turn a shortlist into a rated drive; Checklist; Practice

    Turn a shortlist into a rated drive

    • Record shaft directions, center distance, available space and adjustment travel.
    • Specify input speed, required output speed, power and torque, including starts and shock loads.
    • Decide whether the job needs synchronized motion, low noise or accurate reversal.
    • Check temperature, abrasive dust, water and chemicals against the material and lubricant ratings.
    • Use the manufacturer's selection procedure to check size, service factor, wrap or tooth engagement, shaft loads and bearings.
    • Plan inspection access, replacement parts, lubrication and the total cost over the drive's life.

    A bigger pitch is not a complete strength rating. Width, material, speed, tooth count and duty also matter. A drive that fits the space can still fail the load check.

    For safe access to a drive, use Machine Hazards and Housekeeping and Equipment Operating Procedure. Screw-driven motion is covered separately in Screw Threads.

    Engineering Fundamentals/Power Transmission

    Belt Drives

    Distinguish friction belts from timing belts, read belt and pulley terminology, and recognize common wear patterns.

    Flat and V-belts grip; timing belts engage teeth

    Flat and V-belts grip; timing belts engage teeth

    Flat belt
    A broad, flat band transmits force through friction against a pulley. Useful for smooth, quiet motion and long spans when the drive is designed for them. Tracking and tension matter.
    V-belt
    A trapezoidal section runs in a matching V-groove. Contact at the sides gives a wedging action that increases grip. The belt should not rely on rubbing the bottom of the groove.
    Timing / synchronous belt
    Teeth on the belt engage matching grooves in the pulleys. Load is carried by this engagement, so the drive keeps its tooth-count ratio without frictional slip in normal operation.

    Timing does not come from extra tension. It comes from matching teeth. An undertensioned or overloaded timing belt can jump teeth or strip them; that is a fault, not its normal way of transmitting power. A notched V-belt remains a friction belt: relief notches for bending do not make it a timing belt.

    Read length, tension and wrap before ordering

    Read length, tension and wrap before ordering

    Pulley / sheave
    The wheel that carries a belt. “Sheave” is commonly used for a grooved belt pulley. A timing pulley has matching tooth grooves.
    Pitch and pitch length
    Timing-belt pitch is the spacing between adjacent tooth centers along the pitch line. Pitch length is the loop length along that reference line, near the tensile cords. It is not the outside circumference. Match pitch and tooth profile to the pulley.
    Tension
    The pulling force along the belt. The difference between the loaded and return spans transmits torque. Installation tension keeps the belt seated; too little encourages slip or tooth jumping, and too much loads belts and bearings.
    Wrap angle
    The angle through which the belt contacts a pulley. Less wrap gives a friction belt less contact and a timing belt fewer teeth in engagement. Check the smaller pulley in particular.

    Catalogs may specify inside, outside, datum, effective or pitch lengths. Use the length convention and measuring method for that belt family; do not substitute a tape measurement of the outside for the catalog value.

    One-stage reminder: nout = nin × Ddriver / Ddriven using matching effective/pitch diameters and assuming no slip. For timing belts, use tooth counts N in place of diameters. Write the reduction as i:1, where i = input speed / output speed. Follow Gear Ratios for the ratio method and Rotation and Linear Speed for belt linear speed.

    Here N means teeth and n means rotational speed. Some class slides use n for teeth and ω for angular speed; check the quantity, not just the letter.

    Choose a belt for the load and environment

    Choose a belt for the load and environment

    Belts can span separated shafts, soften vibration and avoid oil at the transmission contact. Flat and V-belts suit jobs where a small speed variation is acceptable. Choose a timing belt when the shafts must stay synchronized. Compare the alternatives in Belt, Chain and Gear Drives.

    Check belt section or tooth profile, width, minimum pulley size, available length, wrap, power rating, temperature and chemical compatibility. There is no single maximum speed or temperature range for every belt. Reinforcement cords limit stretch, but the belt still needs correct alignment and installation tension.

    Some specially designed flat-belt layouts connect nonparallel shafts. That does not make misalignment acceptable in an ordinary V-belt or timing-belt installation. Frictional slip may soften an overload, but it can also generate heat and destroy the belt; it is not a guaranteed overload-protection device.

    Use the wear pattern to find the cause; Practice

    Use the wear pattern to find the cause

    Fault clues to investigate with the drive safely isolated.
    SymptomPossible cause to check
    Squeal, glazing or excess heat on a friction beltLow tension, overload, contamination or worn pulley grooves can reduce grip.
    Frayed edges or the belt tracking to one sidePulley alignment, damaged flanges and shaft movement.
    Cracks or hardeningAge, heat, chemical attack or repeated bending around an unsuitable pulley.
    Missing timing-belt teeth or lost timingOverload, inadequate tension, poor engagement, debris or worn pulleys.

    Inspect the pulleys as well as the belt. Replacing the worn part without fixing its cause often repeats the failure. Follow the product's tension and inspection instructions; use Equipment Operating Procedure before touching the drive.

    Practice a timing-pulley speed

    Supporting detail: Addendum 40 — Manufacturer references for belt geometry and faults.

    Explore how pulley size and spacing change belt length and wrap; Interactive; Practice

    Explore how pulley size and spacing change belt length and wrap

    Use pitch diameters D (large) and d (small), and center distance C in one length unit. For an open belt, the approximate pitch length is L ≈ 2C + π(D + d)/2 + (D − d)²/(4C). The last term is the correction for unequal pulleys. Increasing C increases length and brings small-pulley wrap closer to 180°; the no-slip speed ratio stays D/d.

    Real belts come in standard lengths from the manufacturer's catalog. Pick the nearest stock length in the correct length convention, then use “Enter L → find C” to estimate the required shaft spacing. These calculations do not set installation tension or replace the manufacturer's selection procedure.

    Open belt: D = 200, d = 100 mm; n_small = 1200 r/min
    Belt pitch length L (approx., mm)1277.49
    Center distance C (mm)400
    Speed ratio n_small / n_large2
    Large-pulley speed (r/min)600
    Belt speed (m/min)376.991
    Small-pulley wrap (degrees)165.638
    Unequal-pulley correction (mm)6.25

    Less wrap means less grip for a friction belt and fewer teeth engaged for a timing belt. This geometry model does not rate load capacity.

    Worked example: D = 200 mm, d = 100 mm, C = 400 mm and n_small = 1200 r/min. L ≈ 800 + 150π + 6.25 = 1277.49 mm. The inverse returns C ≈ 400 mm. Ratio = 2; n_large = 600 r/min; v = π × 100 × 1200 / 1000 ≈ 376.99 m/min; wrap ≈ 165.64°.

    Engineering Fundamentals/Power Transmission

    Chain Drives

    Recognize chain components, decode ANSI pitch numbers, and distinguish ISO chain series before choosing sprockets.

    Sprocket teeth engage a chain of moving joints

    Sprocket teeth engage a chain of moving joints

    A chain drive is a positive drive: sprocket teeth engage the chain instead of relying on frictional grip. It can bridge separated shafts and carry substantial load, but its joints and sprockets need attention.

    Pitch, p
    The center-to-center distance between adjacent chain pins. A chain's pitch must match its sprocket.
    Roller
    A sleeve that turns around a bush as it contacts a sprocket tooth. Some small chains are bush chains and have no separate roller.
    Link
    A connecting unit of the chain. Ordinary roller chain alternates inner links, carrying bushes and rollers, with outer links, carrying pins and side plates.
    Sprocket
    The toothed wheel that engages the chain. Tooth count sets the speed relationship; tooth shape and width must suit the chain series.
    Master / connecting link
    The link used to join the ends into a loop. Use the specified type and installation method; retention and strength depend on the product.
    Read #25, #35 and #40 as pitch codes

    Read #25, #35 and #40 as pitch codes

    For the common ANSI short-pitch chain numbers here, remove the final digit of the base number and divide the remaining number by 8 to get pitch in inches. Thus #40 uses 4/8 in, not 40/8 in. #100 uses 10/8 in.

    Common ANSI designation examples, checked against Tsubaki's chain guide and sprocket catalog.
    Base numberPitch calculationPitchConstruction clue
    #252/8 in0.250 in = 6.35 mmFinal 5: bush chain, no separate rollers
    #353/8 in0.375 in = 9.525 mmFinal 5: bush chain, no separate rollers
    #404/8 in0.500 in = 12.70 mmFinal 0: roller chain
    #414/8 in0.500 in = 12.70 mmNarrow variation; not identical to #40
    #10010/8 in1.250 in = 31.75 mmTwo digits remain before dividing by 8

    A suffix such as -1 or -2 counts parallel strands: simplex or duplex. #40-2 still has a 0.500 in pitch. Heavy-series suffixes and manufacturer prefixes carry other information; do not apply the pitch shortcut to every chain product code.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 42 — Checked public wording behind the ANSI numbers.

    “Metric chain” still needs a series and a pitch

    “Metric chain” still needs a series and a pitch

    ISO chain data are commonly tabulated in millimeters. That does not make every pitch a whole number of millimeters. ISO 606 covers both A-series chains derived from American practice and B-series chains derived from European practice.

    Selected B-series simplex chains from Renold's public tables.
    DesignationPitch
    05B-18.000 mm
    06B-19.525 mm
    08B-112.700 mm
    10B-115.875 mm

    The common 06B, 08B and 10B sizes correspond to 6/16, 8/16 and 10/16 in pitch. Use the table for the exact designation: small sizes such as 05B do not follow that shortcut. B identifies the series; -1 identifies one strand.

    Same pitch does not mean interchangeable. #40 and 08B both have 12.7 mm pitch, but roller diameter and inner width differ. Check series, pitch, width, roller diameter and strand count when matching a sprocket or replacement link.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 43 — ISO scope and the source of the millimeter dimensions.

    Positive engagement still permits wear and speed ripple; Practice

    Positive engagement still permits wear and speed ripple

    Chain is worth considering when separated shafts need a fixed average ratio and lubricant and noise are acceptable. Select it for the actual power, speed, starts, shock loads and environment. Tensile breaking strength is not an allowable continuous working load.

    One-stage reminder: nout = nin × Ndriver / Ndriven; reduction i = Ndriven / Ndriver, written i:1. N counts teeth and n is rotational speed. For the reasoning and further stages, use Gear Ratios.

    The chain wraps a sprocket as a series of straight links, forming a polygon rather than a perfectly smooth circle. This chordal action produces speed ripple, especially with small sprockets. Backlash and elastic stretch also limit precise positioning, even without ordinary slip.

    • Wear elongation: pin/bush wear increases joint clearance and measured chain length. The worn chain rides poorly on sprocket teeth and can jump. Take-up removes slack; it does not restore worn joints.
    • Stiff or seized joints: check lubrication reaching the joints, contamination and corrosion.
    • Fractured plates or pins: investigate fatigue, overload, misalignment and connecting-link installation.
    • Hooked or uneven sprocket teeth: inspect the chain and sprockets together and follow replacement limits for that drive.

    Use the specified lubricant, alignment and slack. A chain is not installed taut like a belt. Set inspection intervals and wear limits from the maker's guide; isolate the drive before measuring or servicing it. See Equipment Operating Procedure.

    Practice reading chain pitch

    Supporting detail: Addendum 44 — Chain selection and maintenance reference.

    Few sprocket teeth make the chain surge and bob; Interactive

    Few sprocket teeth make the chain surge and bob

    A chain can bend only at its pins, so it wraps a sprocket as a polygon with one side per tooth. Even at a perfectly steady sprocket speed, the chain leaving that polygon speeds up and slows down once per tooth, and the span rises and falls with it. Predict how much, then turn the sprocket and watch.

    Pitch radiusR = p / (2 sin(180°/N))
    Speed rangeωR cos(180°/N) ≤ v ≤ ωR
    Ripple(vmax − vmin) / vmax = 1 − cos(180°/N)
    Span riseR (1 − cos(180°/N))

    Worked example: #40 chain (p = 12.7 mm) on a 9-tooth sprocket at 120 r/min. R = 12.7 / (2 sin 20°) = 18.57 mm. ω = 120 × 2π / 60 = 12.57 rad/s, so vmax = ωR = 0.233 m/s and vmin = ωR cos 20° = 0.219 m/s. Ripple = 1 − cos 20° = 6.03 %; the span rises and falls 1.12 mm, once per tooth: 18 times a second. With 21 teeth the same chain and speed give 1.12 % and 0.476 mm.

    Chordal speed variation by tooth count. Rise is for p = 12.7 mm (#40); ripple percentages do not depend on pitch or speed.
    Teeth NR / pRipple (vmax − vmin) / vmaxSame spread ÷ average speedSpan rise (mm)
    6113.40 %14.03 %1.7
    81.3077.61 %7.81 %1.26
    91.4626.03 %6.15 %1.12
    101.6184.89 %4.98 %1.01

    Read the trace: the speed peaks each time a pin passes the top of the sprocket and dips at the hand-over between pins. Chain speed as a fraction of ωR and span height as a fraction of R follow the same curve, cos θ, where θ is the leaving pin's angle from the top. The ripple percentage depends only on the tooth count. Speed and pitch change the size of the numbers, not the percentage.

    Engineering Fundamentals/Power Transmission

    Gear Drives and Tooth Geometry

    Compare spur and helical gears, identify tooth dimensions, and match pitch and pressure angle before choosing a gear pair.

    Spur teeth engage straight across; helical teeth engage progressively

    Spur teeth engage straight across; helical teeth engage progressively

    Gears transmit rotation by direct tooth contact. They make a compact positive drive, but accurate mounting, tooth compatibility and lubrication matter. This page compares external spur and helical gears on parallel shafts.

    Spur gear
    Teeth run parallel to the shaft. It is comparatively simple to make and produces no axial thrust from the ideal tooth mesh. Engagement can be noisy at higher speed.
    Helical gear
    Teeth run at a helix angle around the gear. Contact enters progressively across the face and overlapping teeth share load. This generally gives smoother, quieter operation, with added manufacturing cost.

    The inclined helical tooth force also pushes along the shaft. That axial thrust needs a suitable bearing arrangement. A spur gear still loads its bearings radially; “no axial thrust” does not mean “no bearing force.”

    The driver supplies power. The pinion is the smaller gear in a pair; it can be the driver or the driven member. An idler passes motion between gears and still needs a shaft or other bearing support. Follow Gear Ratios for direction, tooth-count ratios and compound trains.

    Measure teeth from the pitch circle

    Measure teeth from the pitch circle

    Pitch diameter, d
    The diameter of the reference pitch circle. In a standard unshifted pair at its standard center distance, the pitch circles roll together without slipping.
    Module, m
    Metric tooth size: m = d/N, with d in millimeters and N teeth. Larger module means larger teeth.
    Diametral pitch, Pd
    Inch-based tooth size: Pd = N/d, with d in inches. More teeth per inch of pitch diameter means smaller teeth. Do not confuse it with circular pitch, the distance along the pitch circle between successive teeth.
    Pressure angle, α
    The angle between the line of action (the contact-force direction, neglecting friction) and the common tangent to the pitch circles at the pitch point. It describes tooth geometry, not the helix angle.
    Addendum / dedendum
    Radial tooth height from pitch circle to tip / radial depth from pitch circle to root. Neither is a diameter difference by itself.
    Backlash
    Clearance between mating tooth flanks. It allows clearance in the mesh but creates lost motion when the load reverses.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 46 — Check the size definitions with one gear.

    Matching pitch is necessary, but not sufficient

    Matching pitch is necessary, but not sufficient

    Ordinary spur gears intended to mesh must share module or diametral pitch and pressure angle. Matching outside diameter or tooth count does not establish compatibility. Check the tooth system, center distance, clearance and manufacturer's mating information too.

    For external helical gears on parallel shafts, match tooth size, pressure angle and helix angle. Use one right-hand and one left-hand gear (teeth slanting in opposite directions), and confirm the manufacturer's mating specification. Equal tooth counts are not required.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 47 — Normal and transverse measurements use different planes.

    A larger tooth size can support more load when other conditions are comparable, but pitch alone cannot determine capacity, backlash or achievable reduction. Material, face width, heat treatment, alignment and speed remain part of the design.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 48 — Primary references for the geometry and helical mesh.

    Gear damage tells you where the load went

    Gear damage tells you where the load went

    Choose gears for compact packaging, a positive ratio and a supported shaft arrangement. Choose helical teeth when smoothness and noise justify their cost and thrust bearings. Check tooth bending strength, surface durability, speed, lubricant, seals and bearing loads before approving a pair.

    Common gear faults and conditions to investigate.
    DamageWhat to check
    Scoring or scuffing: streaked, torn tooth surfacesLubricant supply and type, excess temperature, contamination and load.
    Broken tooth or root crackOverload, repeated bending fatigue, impact and material condition.
    Pitting / spalling: small pits or flakes leaving the surfaceRepeated contact stress, lubrication and local load concentration.
    Wear concentrated at one edgeShaft/bearing alignment, deflection and tooth contact pattern.

    A symptom is a clue, not a unique diagnosis. Correct the cause before replacing parts. Most loaded metal gear sets need a controlled lubricant supply; some specially selected materials can run dry. Follow the product data and Equipment Operating Procedure for access.

    Compare family trade-offs in Belt, Chain and Gear Drives, and follow Power and Efficiency for power losses. A positive drive is not automatically lossless.

    Engineering Fundamentals/Power Transmission

    Screw Threads

    Choose a thread form for the load, read an inch or metric callout, and identify which way a screw advances.

    A fastener holds parts together; a power screw moves a load

    A fastener holds parts together; a power screw moves a load

    A thread is a ridge wrapped around a cylinder. A matching internal thread in a nut follows that ridge. Relative rotation can produce straight-line travel along the screw's axis.

    A machine screw usually holds parts together. A lead screw uses the thread to position or drive a load: a slide, a vise jaw, or a linear actuator. Belts, chains and gears commonly transfer rotation between shafts; a lead screw converts rotation into linear motion. See Lead Screws for the calculations.

    Keep four descriptions separate: form is the thread's cross-sectional shape; series selects diameter and pitch combinations; hand determines direction; starts count the separate helices. A helix is the spiral path around the cylinder.

    Match the thread form to fastening, repeated travel, or one-way thrust

    Match the thread form to fastening, repeated travel, or one-way thrust

    Thread-form trade-offs for sliding screw-and-nut contact.
    Form and useWhat it offersWhat it costs
    Square: power screws and jacksHigh efficiency relative to angled flanks under otherwise comparable conditions.Difficult, expensive machining; wear adjustment is difficult.
    V / machine-screw thread: bolts and fastening screwsWidely available fasteners; mass production by rolling makes standard parts economical.Flank wedging increases friction, so it is a poor choice for efficient repeated power transmission.
    ACME / metric trapezoidal: vises, clamps and linear actuatorsEasier machining than square; a broader thread root provides a sturdier profile than a comparable square thread. Split-nut (an adjustable, divided nut) arrangements can take up clearance.Flank wedging increases friction relative to square. A precision drive screw can cost more than an ordinary stock fastener.
    Buttress: heavy axial thrust (push along the screw) predominantly in one axial direction, such as a screw pressA nearly perpendicular working flank limits wedging in the intended load direction; the sloping back supports the thread.Its strength and efficiency advantages are directional. A special asymmetric profile and matching nut affect manufacturing and cost.

    No thread form wins every comparison. Actual strength also depends on diameter, pitch, engaged length, material and the failure being checked. ACME is not automatically stronger than every V thread. Nor does its name guarantee a larger lead. ACME and metric trapezoidal are related forms, not interchangeable parts.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 49 — Why the efficiency and strength comparisons need conditions.

    No radial wedging (outward force on the nut) does not mean no wear

    No radial wedging (outward force on the nut) does not mean no wear

    In the ideal square-thread geometry, axial load does not create the outward wedging associated with angled flanks. That reduces a source of radial loading on the nut. The loaded surfaces still slide against each other. Friction, lubrication, materials, load and speed still affect wear.

    Wear can increase backlash: clearance that must be taken up after reversing direction before the load moves. An adjustable nut can reduce that clearance; adjustment does not restore lost material or guarantee longer life. Do not infer nut life from the thread profile alone.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 50 — Where wear and operating limits enter the selection.

    Inch callouts count threads; metric callouts state pitch; Practice

    Inch callouts count threads; metric callouts state pitch

    Pitch is the axial distance between adjacent thread crests. Inch fastener callouts commonly give threads per inch (TPI), so pitch = 1 / TPI in inches. Metric callouts give pitch directly in millimetres.

    Selected callouts transcribed from checked public standard sources; pitches in the last column are calculated.
    CalloutRead it asPitch
    1/4-20 UNCNominal diameter 1/4 in; 20 threads per inch; Unified coarse series1/20 = 0.050 in
    1/4-28 UNFNominal diameter 1/4 in; 28 threads per inch; Unified fine series1/28 ≈ 0.03571 in
    M6 × 1.0Metric thread; nominal diameter 6 mm; pitch 1.0 mm1.0 mm

    Fine means a smaller pitch at the same nominal diameter. It does not mean a better-quality thread. Metric threads also have coarse and fine pitch choices. The 6 in M6 is a diameter, not a pitch; the 20 in 1/4-20 is a count per inch, not a lead.

    These are basic size-and-pitch callouts, not complete manufacturing specifications. Fit and tolerance information may follow them. A fastener-series label does not tell you the efficiency of a lead screw; for a multiple-start drive, obtain both pitch and starts, or the lead directly.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 51 — The exact standard entries used here.

    Practice reading an inch callout

    Right-hand and left-hand threads advance in opposite directions

    Right-hand and left-hand threads advance in opposite directions

    Fix the nut and look along the screw from the end you turn. Clockwise turns a right-hand screw away from you into the nut. The same clockwise rotation moves a left-hand screw toward you. Reverse the rotation and the travel reverses.

    If the screw is held against axial motion and the nut travels instead, the nut moves opposite to the screw travel just described. Handedness changes the direction, not the magnitude of travel per revolution.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 52 — Direction reference.

    Next, distinguish pitch from lead in Lead Screws.

    Engineering Fundamentals/Power Transmission

    Lead Screws

    Pitch times starts gives lead. Use lead to convert rpm into travel speed and torque into force, with efficiency applied only to the force conversion.

    Pitch is thread spacing; lead is travel per revolution

    Pitch is thread spacing; lead is travel per revolution

    Lead = pitch × number of starts. This is the distinction to get right before calculating either speed or force.

    A start is one continuous helical ridge. A single-start screw has one ridge, so its lead equals its pitch. A triple-start screw has three interleaved ridges: follow one ridge through a full turn and it advances three pitch distances.

    At the same pitch, adding starts increases travel per turn. At the same torque it reduces theoretical force. The thread's cross-sectional form and its number of starts are separate choices; see Screw Threads.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 53 — Check the definition, not just the label on a catalog.

    Multiply rpm by lead to find linear speed

    Multiply rpm by lead to find linear speed

    For an engaged screw and nut, with the nut restrained from rotating, v = nL. Here n is screw speed in revolutions per minute and L is lead in distance per revolution. The result is distance per minute. Divide by 60 for distance per second.

    A triple-start screw with 1.5 mm pitch has L = 1.5 × 3 = 4.5 mm/rev. At 480 rpm, v = 480 × 4.5 = 2,160 mm/min = 36 mm/s.

    Do not multiply that speed by efficiency. The teaching rule is: “RPM → velocity is 100% efficient unless the screw is malfunctioning; all efficiency losses are found in the torque → force conversion.” This describes a positive-drive motion relationship, not 100% energy efficiency. It is the same tooth-count principle used in Gear Ratios.

    Use the actual screw rpm. If the motor slows under load, the lower rpm gives a lower travel speed. Backlash at reversal and elastic deflection can affect positioning without being an efficiency factor on speed. These calculations describe steady engaged travel, after clearance is taken up. See Rotation and Linear Speed for the general rotation-to-travel connection.

    Divide torque times 2π by lead, then apply efficiency

    Divide torque times 2π by lead, then apply efficiency

    For steady motion driving a resisting axial load, Ftheoretical = 2πT / L and Factual = η × Ftheoretical. Here T is input torque and η (eta) is efficiency written as a decimal: 40% is 0.40.

    Make the length in torque match the length in lead.
    TorqueLead for force calculationForce
    N·mmetres per revolution (mm ÷ 1,000)N
    lbf·in (often written lb-in)inches per revolutionlbf

    To find the torque required for a target actual force, rearrange: T = FL / (2πη). For the same load and lead, lower efficiency requires more torque. Keep the efficiency boundary consistent: a whole screw assembly efficiency includes losses in the bearings or collar (a supporting thrust-contact surface) as well as the threads.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 54 — Derive the 2π from equal power, or one revolution of work.

    Experiment: more starts change speed and force in opposite ways; Interactive

    Experiment: more starts change speed and force in opposite ways

    Predict first: keep pitch, rpm, torque and efficiency fixed, then change from one start to three. Lead and speed triple; theoretical force falls to one third. The same force ratio holds when efficiency is held fixed.

    Static comparison / print example: pitch 2 mm, 300 rpm, torque 1.2 N·m, given efficiency 40%.

    Same pitch and input, different starts.
    StartsLeadSpeedIdeal forceActual force
    12 mm/rev10 mm/s3,770 N1,508 N
    36 mm/rev30 mm/s1,257 N503 N

    Changing efficiency to 20% halves each actual force; both speeds stay the same. Real efficiency can change with lead, lubrication and load. Here it is an independent input so the two effects can be studied separately.

    Worked actuator: keep inch torque and inch lead together; Practice

    Worked actuator: keep inch torque and inch lead together

    A single-start ACME actuator has 0.20 in pitch, runs at 900 rpm and receives 12 lbf·in of torque. Its assembly efficiency is given as 60%. Find travel speed and useful axial force.

    1. L = 0.20 × 1 = 0.20 in/rev.
    2. v = 900 × 0.20 = 180 in/min = 3 in/s.
    3. Ftheoretical = 2π × 12 / 0.20 = 376.99 lbf.
    4. Factual = 376.99 × 0.60 ≈ 226 lbf.

    The 60% belongs in step 4, not step 2. It is an example input, not an efficiency assigned to every ACME screw.

    Practice actuator force

    Worked vise: turn hand force into torque before finding clamp force; Practice

    Worked vise: turn hand force into torque before finding clamp force

    For an illustrative square-thread vise, a 120 N hand force acts perpendicular to the handle at a radius of 0.18 m from the screw axis. Pitch is 4 mm with one start. Assume a given overall tightening efficiency of 30%; this is not a measured or universal vise efficiency.

    1. Use torque = radius × perpendicular force: T = 0.18 × 120 = 21.6 N·m. Radius is the distance from the axis to the hand, not necessarily the full handle length.
    2. L = 4 mm/rev = 0.004 m/rev.
    3. Factual = 0.30 × 2π × 21.6 / 0.004 ≈ 10,179 N = 10.18 kN.

    This is a tightening estimate using the supplied efficiency. It is not a vise rating or a prediction of residual force after the hand stops turning. A separate free-travel calculation at 24 rpm gives 24 × 4 / 60 = 1.6 mm/s; the jaws do not continue at that speed through a rigid clamped part.

    Practice handle torque and clamp force Practice a triple-start CNC screw

    Engineering Fundamentals/Power Transmission

    Backlash and Lost Motion

    After a feed screw reverses, the handwheel turns through the thread clearance before the carriage moves. Predict that dead band from clearance and lead, and finish every approach in one direction.

    The dial counts screw rotation; the indicator finds the carriage

    The dial counts screw rotation; the indicator finds the carriage

    A handwheel dial does not measure the carriage. It counts how far the screw has turned and multiplies by the lead. That is the carriage's travel only while the screw keeps pushing the nut in one direction.

    A screw and its nut need some clearance between their thread flanks (a flank is the sloping side of a thread). After the screw changes direction, it must turn through that clearance before its other flank meets the nut and the carriage moves again. That clearance is backlash, the same idea defined for threads in Screw Threads and for gear teeth in Gear Drives and Tooth Geometry. The turn spent crossing it is lost motion: input that produces no output.

    • Dial reading: travel predicted from screw rotation, turns × lead. See Lead Screws.
    • Carriage position: where the carriage really is, as an indicator touching it would show.
    • The difference is zero after a forward approach (the direction the dial was zeroed in) and one full clearance after a reverse approach.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 55 — Where the definition comes from.

    Experiment: reverse the handwheel and watch the carriage wait; Interactive

    Experiment: reverse the handwheel and watch the carriage wait

    What the lab does: a handwheel turns an axially fixed lead screw. The dial reports travel calculated from screw rotation; an indicator on the carriage reports where the carriage really is. With a total axial clearance B between screw and nut flanks, the two agree only while the screw keeps pushing in the direction the dial was set in.

    Dead band after a reversal = clearance ÷ lead, as a fraction of a turn:

    angle = 360° × B ÷ L   dial divisions = B ÷ (L ÷ 100) on a dial with 100 divisions per turn.

    Worked example: lead L = 5 mm/rev, so one division is 0.05 mm. Clearance B = 0.20 mm. Angle = 360° × 0.20 ÷ 5 = 14.4°; divisions = 0.20 ÷ 0.05 = 4. For four divisions after the reversal the dial changes and the carriage does not.

    Landing on 25.00 mm after overshooting to 25.60 mm (lead 5 mm, clearance 0.20 mm). The dial was zeroed after a forward approach, so it equals the carriage position only for forward approaches:

    Same dial number, two approaches.
    MethodDial movesDialCarriageError
    Reverse straight to the number25.60 → 25.00 mm25.00 mm25.20 mm+0.20 mm
    Back past it, approach forward again25.60 → 24.50 → 25.00 mm25.00 mm25.00 mm0.00 mm

    Reversing straight to the number stops the carriage one full clearance away from the dial reading, still on the overshoot side: the dial shows 25.00 mm while the carriage is at 25.20 mm. Backing past the target by more than the clearance and finishing in the original direction puts the screw back on the flank the dial was set against.

    Model limits: rigid parts and a kinematic dead band only. Friction is assumed to hold the carriage still inside the clearance, and nothing else pushes it along the axis; there is no force, stiffness, preload or stick-slip model. Lead, clearance and the 3D dimensions are illustrative and exaggerated, not a standard thread or a measured machine.

    Predict the dead band: clearance divided by lead, as a fraction of a turn

    Predict the dead band: clearance divided by lead, as a fraction of a turn

    Once the screw reverses, the carriage stays still until the screw's helix has moved one full clearance B. One turn moves the helix one lead L, so the dead band is B ÷ L of a turn.

    dead-band angle = 360° × B ÷ L

    dead-band divisions = B ÷ (value of one division); with 100 divisions per turn, one division is L ÷ 100.

    Same clearance, two leads (illustrative values, 100-division dial).
    Lead LOne divisionClearance BDead band
    5 mm/rev0.05 mm0.20 mm4 divisions = 14.4°
    2 mm/rev0.02 mm0.20 mm10 divisions = 36°

    The carriage error after a reverse approach is the same 0.20 mm in both rows. A finer lead only spreads that same clearance over more of the handwheel turn.

    Land on a dimension: finish every approach in the direction the dial was set

    Land on a dimension: finish every approach in the direction the dial was set

    If you overshoot a target, turning straight back to the number leaves the carriage one clearance away from it, because the screw is now pushing on the other flank. Instead:

    1. Back the handwheel past the target by more than the backlash.
    2. Turn in the original direction again and stop on the number.

    The same reasoning applies when setting a dial. MIT's 2.670 milling notes say to “be certain that the backlash in the mechanism driving the table is taken up prior to setting the dial indicator”. A dial set with the clearance taken up in one direction reads true for approaches in that direction. For edge finding, Mill Indicators and Part Zero repeats the touch from the same direction for the same reason.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 56 — A readout that measures the slide, and when the clearance still matters.

    What the lab model includes and leaves out

    What the lab model includes and leaves out

    • Included: a rigid screw that turns but never slides along its axis, a nut fixed to the carriage, and a total axial clearance B. The carriage position c stays within B/2 of the screw's helical phase s = −Lφ/360° (right-hand thread, φ the screw rotation); inside that band it does not move.
    • Assumed: friction holds the carriage still inside the clearance, and no outside force pushes it along the axis.
    • Left out: forces, friction values, stiffness and elastic wind-up, preload, stick-slip and wear. Drives designed to remove the clearance, such as preloaded ball nuts or adjustable split nuts, are beyond this model.
    • Illustrative: the leads, clearances and the 3D screw (5 mm lead, 1.0 mm clearance, 30° flanks) are chosen to be seen, not taken from a standard thread or a measured machine.

    For drive design in depth, Alexander Slocum's Precision Machine Design (1992) covers actuators and transmissions in Chapter 10, including section 10.8, Linear Power Transmission Elements.

    Engineering Fundamentals/Power Transmission

    Bearing Types and Loads

    Choose the motion to allow, identify the load, then compare plain and rolling-element bearings.

    A bearing allows useful motion and restrains unwanted motion

    A bearing allows useful motion and restrains unwanted motion

    A loose rigid part can move in six independent ways: translate along three axes and rotate about those three axes. These are its degrees of freedom. A bearing transfers load to a support while allowing the motion the machine needs, with low friction.

    For a rotating shaft, the goal is usually one remaining freedom: rotation about its own axis. Two spaced radial supports resist sideways movement and tilting; axial location stops the shaft walking lengthwise. A single short bearing does not automatically provide that whole constraint system.

    Bearings guide motion; motors and drives supply it. Belt, chain and gear drives load their supporting shafts. See Torque for turning effort and Shaft Support and Axial Adjustment for the complete support arrangement.

    Radial load crosses the shaft; thrust acts along it

    Radial load crosses the shaft; thrust acts along it

    Radial load acts perpendicular to the shaft axis. Axial load, or thrust, acts parallel to it. Combined load has both components. A bearing's orientation and internal geometry determine which it can carry.

    First selection filter, not a load rating. Check the exact catalog design.
    TypeRadial loadAxial loadCombined load
    Plain journal, without thrust facesYesNo intended capacityNeeds a thrust bearing
    Plain footstep or thrust collar faceNeeds a journal guideYes, against the loaded faceWith a radial guide
    Deep-groove ballYesBoth directions, within ratingYes, within rating
    Angular-contact ball or tapered roller, single rowYesPrimarily one directionYes; opposing bearing needed for reverse thrust
    Cylindrical roller, NU or N designYesNo intended locating dutyUse another bearing for thrust
    Pure thrust ball or cylindrical thrust rollerNoYes; direction depends on arrangementNo

    Do not turn “roller” into “radial only,” or “thrust” into a rule for every product bearing that name. Tapered rollers carry combined loads; some spherical roller thrust designs also accept radial load under specified conditions.

    Plain and rolling bearings trade friction, upkeep and cost

    Plain and rolling bearings trade friction, upkeep and cost

    A plain bearing supports sliding surfaces, often with a replaceable sleeve called a bushing. A rolling-element bearing places balls or rollers between rings. “Anti-friction” is a traditional name, not a promise of zero friction.

    Compare the operating conditions as well as the purchase price.
    QuestionPlain bearingRolling-element bearing
    Starting versus running resistance?Breakaway friction can exceed running friction. A hydrodynamic film is not fully established at rest.Often low starting resistance and a smaller start/run difference; seals, grease and preload still matter.
    Lubrication and maintenance?Dry grades may need no added lubricant; oil-fed designs require the specified supply and cleanliness.Usually grease or oil lubricated. A sealed, prelubricated bearing still has a finite service life.
    Speed?Dry bushings have material-specific speed and pressure limits. Fluid-film bearings can serve high-speed machinery.Many suit moderate to high speeds; type, size, lubrication and heat limit speed.
    Load and cost?Simple bushings often cost little initially. Capacity depends on size, material, speed and heat removal.Precision rings and elements add cost. Roller designs often carry more load than ball designs of similar overall size.

    Rolling contact generally reduces resistance compared with sliding contact. It does not guarantee higher efficiency than every fluid-film bearing, nor does a cheap bushing guarantee lower lifetime cost. Include lubrication equipment, replacement, downtime and power loss. Bearing losses contribute to Power and Efficiency and the stage efficiencies discussed in Gear Ratios.

    Plain bearings differ in both lubrication and load direction

    Plain bearings differ in both lubrication and load direction

    Dry or self-lubricating
    A suitable polymer, composite or lubricant-containing material supplies a low-friction sliding surface. Follow that material's instructions; adding grease is not automatically an improvement.
    Hydrodynamic
    Relative motion draws lubricant into a converging gap, forming a pressure-supported film. Starts and stops require attention because the running film depends on motion.
    Hydrostatic
    An external pressure supply supports the load on a fluid film, including at rest while the supply operates. The pump, flow control and loss-of-pressure behavior are part of the system.

    Those are lubrication descriptions. Shape answers a different question: a journal surrounds a shaft to carry radial load; a footstep supports axial load at a shaft end; a thrust collar presents an annular face to carry axial load. An assembly can combine a journal and a collar to handle both components.

    Rings carry the load; the cage spaces the rolling elements; Practice

    Rings carry the load; the cage spaces the rolling elements

    The inner ring fits around the shaft; the outer ring fits in the housing. The rolling elements transfer load between their raceways. The cage maintains spacing and guides the elements.

    In a common arrangement the inner ring turns with the shaft while the outer ring stays still. The balls spin about their own axes and orbit around the shaft. The rings do not have to rotate in opposite directions.

    Balls have idealized point contact; rollers have idealized line contact. Under load these become finite contact patches. The longer roller contact generally supports more load in a similar overall size. Contact angle, not just element shape, determines thrust capability. Thrust ball and roller bearings place their contact geometry to support axial force.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 57 — Manufacturer reading for bearing selection.

    Practice identifying the load

    Double a ball bearing's load and its basic rating life falls to one eighth; Interactive; Practice

    Double a ball bearing's load and its basic rating life falls to one eighth

    L10 is the life that 90% of a large group of identical bearings are expected to reach or exceed. It is neither a guaranteed life nor an average. Change one input below and watch the life curve.

    Example bearing: C = 14.0 kN, given for this exercise. A real bearing's C comes from its manufacturer's catalog; this example does not represent a catalog part.

    Basic rating life: L10 = (C/P)p in millions of revolutions, with p = 3 for balls and p = 10/3 for rollers. C is the basic dynamic load rating; P is the equivalent dynamic load, taken as given here (for pure radial loading in this exercise, P = Fr). Use the same force units for C and P.

    At constant speed n in r/min, L10h = L10 × 10⁶/(60 × n) hours. The years conversion assumes a duty schedule you can change; it does not predict calendar aging.

    Static worked example (also used for printing).

    Example ball bearing: C = 14 kN (given), P = 2 kN, n = 1500 r/min
    C/P7
    L10 (million revolutions)343
    L10h (hours)3811
    Years at assumed duty1.906

    Duty assumption: 8 h/day × 250 days/year. Years = hours ÷ annual operating hours.

    C/P = 14/2 = 7; L10 = 7³ = 343 million revolutions. L10h = 343 × 10⁶/(60 × 1500) = 3811 h, or 1.906 years at 2000 h/year. At P = 4 kN, L10 = 42.875 million revolutions and L10h = 476.4 h.

    Adjusted life factors (a1, aISO), contamination, lubrication and combined-load X/Y factors are beyond this page.
