    Engineering Fundamentals/Power Transmission

    Shaft Support and Axial Adjustment

    Locate one end, allow thermal movement at the other, and distinguish end play from preload.

    Locate the shaft at one end and allow growth at the other

    Locate the shaft at one end and allow growth at the other

    In a locating/non-locating arrangement, also called fixed/floating here, both supports carry radial load. The locating support also carries the applied axial load and establishes the shaft's axial position. The non-locating support allows axial movement as the shaft expands relative to the housing.

    Location needs a load path from shaft to bearing to housing: shoulders, suitable spacers, nuts, retaining rings or covers can retain the rings. Which end is fixed follows the required position of the driven parts; it is not automatically the left end or the motor end.

    The floating end can accommodate movement inside a suitable bearing, such as an NU cylindrical roller bearing, or by controlled sliding of a ring in its seat. Do not loosen an arbitrary fit: see Tolerances and Fits and the bearing maker's mounting guidance.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 58 — Why two locating supports can create unwanted load.

    Heat the shaft and compare free travel with restraint; Interactive

    Heat the shaft and compare free travel with restraint

    Static comparison: at half the heating range, the shaft wants half the model's maximum free growth. A floating support with sufficient travel accommodates all of it. Two locating supports prevent it. With travel limited to 40%, half-range heating leaves 10% of maximum growth unaccommodated.

    The drawing exaggerates growth. Heating level is a relative teaching scale, not a temperature or a material property. The left support and housing stay in place; only the shaft is heated. The dashed outline shows the length the shaft would reach if free. The solid outline shows the ideal constrained length. This model shows incompatible motion, not a binding force, stress or safe operating limit.

    End play is free movement; preload is an initial internal load

    End play is free movement; preload is an initial internal load

    End play is the axial free movement available before the bearing arrangement takes up its clearance. Preload is a deliberately applied internal load before the external working load arrives. Reducing end play to a specified value and applying preload are different adjustments.

    Do not tighten a bearing until it merely “feels solid.” Excess preload increases friction and temperature. Some arrangements require positive operating clearance; others use specified preload for stiffness or running accuracy. Temperature and fits change the operating condition.

    A shim is a thin, accurately sized spacer. Changing its thickness sets a position in a rigid stack. Whether adding a shim increases or decreases end play depends on where the shim sits and which faces it separates.

    Avoid burrs and rubbing contact that could release debris. Use the material and placement specified for the assembly.

    A spring maintains force over travel; a shim sets distance; Checklist; Practice

    A spring maintains force over travel; a shim sets distance

    A shim sets distance and a spring maintains force.

    A Belleville washer is a conical disc spring. A wave washer has an undulating shape that compresses axially. Both can apply preload when selected for the required force and working deflection.

    A spring can accommodate small dimensional changes while maintaining load. “Very light load” is not a universal specification. Use the bearing's required preload and the spring's load-deflection data; an ordinary lock washer is not a calibrated preload spring.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 59 — Position preload versus spring preload.

    • Identify which support locates the shaft and trace its axial load path.
    • Find where the other support permits thermal movement and check available travel.
    • Read the specified end play or preload and its measurement conditions.
    • Choose the prescribed shim or spring arrangement and verify the final measured setting.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 60 — Manufacturer reading and open material questions.

    Continue with Linear Bearing Guides or practice locating a shaft.

    Engineering Fundamentals/Power Transmission

    Linear Bearing Guides

    Use the same degrees-of-freedom model to compare round shafts, profile rails and V-wheel carriages.

    A linear guide leaves travel along one axis

    A linear guide leaves travel along one axis

    A linear bearing guides sliding motion just as a rotary bearing guides turning. Let x point along the travel. The guide supports transverse loads and, where its geometry allows, resists moments that would tilt or twist the carriage. A screw, belt or other actuator supplies travel force; the guide does not drive itself.

    In the ideal model, translation along x is free. The desired constraints depend on whether rotation about x is acceptable. Real guide selection also checks load, moment capacity, stiffness, clearance, lubrication and alignment.

    A round shaft does not provide an anti-rotation key

    A round shaft does not provide an anti-rotation key

    A plain round sleeve or linear ball bushing guides motion along a cylindrical shaft. In the ideal geometry it leaves two freedoms: Tx and Rx. The four other motions are restrained by the support's length or spaced bearings. A second parallel guide can stop the carriage rotating.

    Geometric freedom is not a rotary service rating. A recirculating ball bushing may resist or wear under rotation even though its round shaft provides no positive anti-rotation feature. Use a product explicitly rated for combined linear and rotary motion when both are required.

    LMU is a common catalog family label associated with round-shaft linear ball bushings. Treat it as a catalog name, not a universal standard or proof of rotary capability. Check the supplier's construction, dimensions and limits.

    A profile rail constrains twist as well as sideways motion

    A profile rail constrains twist as well as sideways motion

    A shaped rail and matching carriage have separated contact paths that resist twisting and tipping. Within their moment ratings, they leave one degree of freedom: Tx. Mounting surfaces must keep the rail aligned; adding constraints can also make an assembly sensitive to misalignment.

    MGN commonly identifies a miniature, narrow-block profile-guide family. For example, HIWIN uses MGN within its miniature MG series, with recirculating balls. The label does not make every supplier's product interchangeable, and does not describe every plain or roller guide.

    Opposed V-wheels guide a carriage; one wheel does not; Practice

    Opposed V-wheels guide a carriage; one wheel does not

    A V-groove wheel runs on a matching edge or rail. A stable carriage commonly uses three or more wheels with contacts opposed across the rail and spaced along it. A triangular three-wheel arrangement can use an adjustable wheel to take up clearance.

    The assembled carriage should leave only travel along the rail. Three wheels placed arbitrarily do not guarantee that result: orientation, spacing, contact retention and adjustment determine which loads and moments it can resist. A carriage that can lift away from its track has not constrained that motion.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 61 — Manufacturer reading and the rotary-motion qualification.

    Compare rotary support on Bearing Types and Loads. Practice counting freedoms

    Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Quantities

    Current, Voltage, and Resistance

    The three quantities every schematic and nameplate uses, the units they are measured in, and the two equations that connect them.

    Three quantities, three units

    Three quantities, three units

    Almost every electrical number you will read off a nameplate, a meter, or a schematic is one of three quantities. Each has a name, a quantity symbol used in formulas, and a unit symbol written after a value.

    Current, I
    The rate at which electric charge flows past a point. Its unit is the ampere, symbol A — one of the seven SI base units. One ampere is one coulomb of charge per second.
    Voltage, V
    Also called electric potential difference: the difference in electric potential between two points. Its unit is the volt, symbol V, defined as power per unit of current.
    Resistance, R
    How strongly something opposes the flow of current. Its unit is the ohm, symbol Ω, defined as voltage per unit of current.
    How each unit is built out of the others.
    QuantityUnitSymbolIn other units
    Electric currentampereASI base unit; 1 A = 1 C/s
    Electric chargecoulombCs·A
    Potential differencevoltVW/A, and so (N·m)/(A·s)
    ResistanceohmΩV/A, and so W/A2

    Say “amp” if you like; write A. The unit name is the ampere, and the symbol is a capital A because the unit is named after a person. So is the volt (V) and the watt (W). Lower case changes the meaning of a prefix, not just the look of it: mA is a milliampere and MA is a megaampere, a billion times larger. See Measurement Language.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 62 — Why voltage and resistance are called derived units.

    Two equations, and everything else follows

    Two equations, and everything else follows

    For an ohmic resistor (constant resistance under the stated conditions), the set is generated by Ohm’s law and the power relationship:

    V = IR  —  P = VI

    Rearranging and substituting gives three expressions for each of the four quantities. There is nothing to memorise beyond the two above; the table is a lookup, not a list of new facts.

    Resistive-load magnitudes: steady DC, or RMS voltage and current for AC.
    To findFrom V and I or RUsing powerUsing power
    Voltage, VV = IRV = P/IV = √(PR)
    Current, II = V/RI = P/VI = √(P/R)
    Resistance, RR = V/IR = V2/PR = P/I2
    Power, PP = VIP = I2RP = V2/R

    P = VI gives real power in watts on direct current or a purely resistive load. For single-phase AC, RMS volts times RMS amps is apparent power in volt-amperes, and the real power is that multiplied by the power factor — see Power and Efficiency.

    Worked example: what a lamp draws

    Worked example: what a lamp draws

    How much current does a 100 W resistive lamp draw on a 120 V supply (RMS for AC)?

    1. Pick the form with the two quantities you have: I = P/V.
    2. I = 100 W ÷ 120 V = 0.833 A.

    Check the units rather than trusting the arithmetic. A volt is a watt per ampere, so watts divided by volts leaves amperes — which is what was asked for.

    Worked example: voltage drop along a cord

    Worked example: voltage drop along a cord

    A 100 ft extension cord has a total out-and-back conductor resistance of 0.1588 Ω. What is the resistive voltage drop across that path when 10 A flows through it?

    1. V = IR = 10 A × 0.1588 Ω = 1.588 V.

    About 1.6 V. That is 1.6 V that never reaches the tool: for DC or an AC resistive load, the supply voltage equals the cord drop plus the load voltage.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 63 — The dropped voltage does not disappear.

    The same method keeps working

    The same method keeps working

    These are not the last units you will meet. Each new quantity arrives the same way: it is defined as a combination of quantities you already have, and its unit is that same combination.

    A few more, and where each one comes from.
    QuantityDefined asSI unit
    Pressure or stressForce per unit areapascal, Pa = N/m2
    Volumetric flow rateVolume per unit timem3/s
    Specific weightWeight per unit volumeN/m3
    CapacitanceCharge per unit voltagefarad, F = C/V

    Read the middle column and the right-hand column together and the pattern is the whole point: the unit is the definition, written in symbols. Once that clicks, a unit you have never seen tells you what the quantity is.

    Sources

    Sources

    Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems

    AC and DC

    Current direction, sine-wave voltage, transmission losses, and conversion between AC and DC.

    DC flows one way; AC reverses direction

    DC flows one way; AC reverses direction

    Direct current (DC) flows in one direction. Its magnitude can change without making it AC. Alternating current (AC) reverses direction repeatedly. A battery supplies DC; a wall receptacle supplies AC.

    Electronics generally run from a DC supply. That does not mean a transistor cannot handle an AC signal: transistors can amplify changing signals and act as switches. The supply and the signal are different parts of the story.

    Start with Current, Voltage, and Resistance for the quantities and equations used here. For measurement, see Measuring Electric Circuits.

    A 120 V sine wave peaks near positive and negative 170 V

    A 120 V sine wave peaks near positive and negative 170 V

    The nominal 120 V of a US receptacle is an RMS value: root mean square. For a sine wave, Vpeak = VRMS × √2, and VRMS = Vpeak / √2. Thus 120 × √2 = 169.7 V. The instantaneous voltage swings between about +170 V and −170 V, or about 340 V peak to peak.

    Frequency counts complete cycles per second, in hertz (Hz). A 60 Hz waveform completes 60 whole cycles per second; a 50 Hz waveform completes 50. A cycle returns to the same phase, rather than ending at the opposite peak. US household mains is 60 Hz; many other countries use 50 Hz (DOE, Electricity 101).

    Supporting detail: Addendum 65 — Why use RMS instead of the average voltage?.

    Compare signed mean, RMS, and ideal-resistor heating; Interactive; Practice

    Compare signed mean, RMS, and ideal-resistor heating

    A sine can have a signed average of zero over one cycle and still produce heating. Add a DC offset and the signed mean moves with the waveform, while total RMS combines the offset and the changing component. Predict first, then compare the same sine centered on zero, shifted by an offset, kept above zero, or reduced to pure DC.

    Print / static comparison: use the analytic waveform v(t) = offset + amplitude × sin(2πft) over one complete cycle. The resistor is ideal and fixed at 100 Ω. These are low illustrative voltages, not mains or wiring examples.

    The same 2 V sine amplitude with different DC offsets
    WaveformSigned meanAC-component RMSTotal RMSMinimum / maximumAverage resistor power
    0 V offset0 V1.414 V1.414 V−2 / +2 V20 mW
    +1 V offset+1 V1.414 V1.732 V−1 / +3 V30 mW
    +3 V offset+3 V1.414 V3.317 V+1 / +5 V110 mW

    The centered sine has zero signed mean but nonzero RMS and average power. The +3 V offset keeps the total waveform positive even though it still contains a sine component. A constant pure-DC value has RMS equal to its magnitude and has no unique oscillation period.

    The live explorer evaluates one complete ideal sine cycle analytically; the drawn points only illustrate the equation. For v(t) = VDC + A sin(2πft), the signed mean is VDC, the sine component has RMS A/√2, and total RMS is √(VDC² + A²/2). In one ideal resistor, average power is VRMS²/R; “RMS power” is not the quantity being calculated.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 66 — Why RMS answers the heating question.

    Practice zero-mean RMS Practice RMS with offset Practice average resistor power

    Higher transmission voltage reduces current and line loss

    Higher transmission voltage reduces current and line loss

    For the same transmitted power, a higher voltage allows a lower current. The line's resistive heating is Ploss = I2Rline. Halve the current and the loss becomes one quarter, if line resistance stays the same. Here Rline includes the complete current path.

    Transformers made it practical to step AC voltage up for transmission and down for use. That advantage helped the AC systems associated with Westinghouse and Tesla prevail over Edison's early DC distribution system in the “war of the currents.” It was not one inventor winning every part of electrical engineering.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 67 — A comparison with the same power and the same line.

    A rectifier is one stage of an AC-to-DC power supply

    A rectifier is one stage of an AC-to-DC power supply

    A rectifier makes current flow in one direction from an AC input. Its output can still pulsate. Filtering smooths the output, and regulation controls the output voltage. A complete power supply may include all these functions as well as isolation.

    • Linear supply: commonly uses a line-frequency transformer, rectifier, filter, and linear regulator. The regulator dissipates excess voltage as heat.
    • Switch-mode supply: switches current rapidly and uses energy-storage components to convert voltage efficiently. An AC-input version also rectifies its input. Not every switch-mode converter provides isolation.

    Power-supply manufacturer ARCH gives illustrative typical efficiency categories: linear supplies about 50–60%, conventional switching supplies 75–85%, and modern high-efficiency designs 90–95%.

    Both lose some input energy as heat. Efficiency depends on the design, input voltage and load; compare published efficiency curves at the intended operating point rather than assuming one percentage for a whole category. See Power and Efficiency for the input/output calculation.

    An inverter makes AC from DC; the waveform matters

    An inverter makes AC from DC; the waveform matters

    A pure-sine inverter produces an output close to a sine wave. A modified-sine inverter produces a stepped approximation. Equipment may run differently, make more noise or heat, or fail to operate on a stepped waveform. Check the equipment manufacturer's compatibility guidance; equal RMS voltages do not make the waveforms interchangeable.

    For grid-tied PV inverters, efficiency is typically above 95% under most operating conditions, according to Sandia PVPMC’s CEC Inverter Test Protocol. Efficiency depends on AC output power, DC voltage and sometimes temperature.

    Every real conversion loses some energy. Several conversions in a row multiply their efficiencies rather than adding them. Much of what we use today runs on DC internally, even when it plugs into AC. Phones, computers, and microcontroller electronics bring the instructor's closing question into focus: who gets the last laugh?

    Motors, generation, and energy storage make use of both forms of electrical power.

    Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems

    Wire and Wire Gauge

    Separate the conductor from its insulation, and understand what a wire gauge does and does not tell you.

    The conductor carries current; insulation separates conductors

    The conductor carries current; insulation separates conductors

    The metal inside a wire is the conductor. Its resistance depends on material, length, cross-sectional area and temperature. The covering is insulation: it keeps the conductor from contacting other conductors or surrounding objects. The outside diameter includes that covering and does not by itself tell you how much metal is inside.

    Solid wire has one solid conductor; stranded wire has several smaller strands forming a conductor. Insulation type and condition matter separately from the metal size. See Electrical Safety for use and inspection guidance.

    A smaller AWG number means a thicker conductor

    A smaller AWG number means a thicker conductor

    American Wire Gauge (AWG) uses smaller numbers for larger conductor cross sections. For the same material, length and temperature, a thicker conductor has less resistance. See Adafruit’s wire-gauge explanation. Under comparable installation and temperature conditions, it can carry more current without exceeding its temperature limit.

    Ampacity means the allowable current under specified conditions. Gauge alone is not an ampacity rating: material, insulation temperature rating, ambient temperature, bundling and installation all matter. Use the applicable manufacturer data and installation requirements for a real selection; this page is not a wire-sizing table. IEWC explains these ampacity factors. Choosing a wire involves voltage drop as well as allowable current.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 68 — Why a long wire can matter even below its current limit.

    Count the return wire: explore voltage drop and heating; Interactive; Practice

    Count the return wire: explore voltage drop and heating

    A two-conductor circuit carries current out and back. Use twice the one-way run for its wire resistance. At the same current, longer or thinner wire drops more voltage and wastes more power as heat. Voltage drop is a separate check from ampacity: get the current rating from the applicable code table or manufacturer for the insulation and installation.

    AWG 18, 50 ft one way, 5 A, 24 V source
    Single wire: Ω / 1000 ft6.385
    Single wire: Ω / km20.95
    Loop resistance (Ω)0.6385
    Voltage drop (V)3.192
    Source voltage lost (%)13.3
    Load voltage (V)20.81
    Wire heating loss (W)15.96

    Worked example: 50 ft out + 50 ft back = 30.48 m of copper. R = ρL/A = 0.6385 Ω. At 5 A, IR = 3.192 V and I²R = 15.96 W.

    Outline = baseline; filled = now. Each pair shares its own scale; compare within a pair. Loss is heating power, not wire temperature.

    Doubling only current doubles the drop and quadruples heating loss. Doubling only length doubles both; a smaller AWG number lowers both at the same current.

    This model assumes solid copper at 20 °C, equal outgoing and return wires, and DC/resistive behavior. Current is an input, not a prediction of how a particular load responds. Heating loss is not a temperature prediction; copper resistance rises with temperature (approx. 0.393%/°C near 20 °C). Connections and AC reactance are omitted.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 69 — Definitions used to calculate every result.

    Practice: Loop resistance · Voltage drop · Percent drop · Load voltage · Choose a gauge.

    Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems

    Series and Parallel Circuits

    Trace current paths, combine resistances, and explore how opening a switch changes voltage, current and power.

    Series has one path; parallel has separate branches

    Series has one path; parallel has separate branches

    In a series circuit, the same current passes through every element. The voltage drops around the loop add up to the source voltage. One break stops current everywhere in that loop.

    In a parallel circuit, each branch connects to the same two supply nodes (a node is an electrically connected junction), so each complete branch has the same voltage. The branch currents add up to the supply current. A break in one branch leaves the other branches working, provided the source and shared wiring remain intact.

    Equal resistance gives equal drops in series and equal currents in parallel. Different resistances make the drops or currents different. The formulas for each individual resistor are on Current, Voltage, and Resistance.

    Add resistances in series; add their reciprocals in parallel

    Add resistances in series; add their reciprocals in parallel

    Equivalent resistance is the single resistance that would draw the same total current at the supply terminals.

    • Series: Req = R1 + R2 + R3.
    • Parallel: 1/Req = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3. A reciprocal is 1 ÷ R: one divided by the resistance. Include only connected branches.
    • Two parallel resistors: Req = R1R2 / (R1 + R2).

    Check the result: series resistance is greater than any one positive resistor; parallel resistance is smaller than the smallest connected resistor when two or more branches are connected. An open circuit has no conducting path and is represented by infinite equivalent resistance.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 70 — Why the parallel formula uses reciprocals.

    Change a resistor or open a switch and predict what changes; Interactive

    Change a resistor or open a switch and predict what changes

    Use this ideal DC model to compare two or three fixed resistors. Before moving a control, predict which current, voltage and power will change. Switches are ideal, wires have zero resistance and the source holds its set voltage.

    Static example: a 15 V source and 30 Ω and 60 Ω resistors, with both switches closed.

    The same resistors in two connections
    ConnectionEquivalent resistanceTotal currentR1: current / voltage / powerR2: current / voltage / power
    Series90 Ω0.1667 A0.1667 A / 5 V / 0.8333 W0.1667 A / 10 V / 1.667 W
    Parallel20 Ω0.75 A0.5 A / 15 V / 7.5 W0.25 A / 15 V / 3.75 W

    Opening either series switch makes both resistor currents and both resistor voltage drops zero. Opening the R1 parallel switch makes R1 current and power zero while R2 still draws 0.25 A. The voltage across the whole open branch remains 15 V; it falls across the open switch, not the resistor.

    The live table reports voltage across each resistor, excluding its switch. In an open series loop the source voltage is across the break or breaks. With several open switches, this ideal model does not determine how that voltage divides between the breaks.

    Power explains the bulb comparison, within the model; Practice

    Power explains the bulb comparison, within the model

    For fixed resistors in series, the larger resistance dissipates more power because both carry the same current. In parallel, the smaller resistance dissipates more power because both have the same voltage. Check the power column rather than assuming the same bulb wins in both arrangements.

    Greater electrical power is a useful brightness comparison for otherwise comparable incandescent bulbs. Real filaments change resistance as they heat, and LED lamps contain additional circuitry. The fixed-resistor model is not a universal lamp-brightness predictor.

    Build another circuit in PhET's Circuit Construction Kit: DC – Virtual Lab. Try an unequal pair of resistors, predict the effect of a break, and then test your prediction.

    Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems

    Measuring Electric Circuits

    Connect voltage, current, resistance and continuity measurements to the part of the circuit they describe.

    Voltage is measured across; current is measured through

    Voltage is measured across; current is measured through

    A voltmeter measures the potential difference between two points. Connect it across the component, in parallel. A series ammeter becomes part of the current path: open the path and insert it in series with the element whose current you want.

    A meter set for current has a low-resistance input; connecting that input across a source makes a short circuit. Read Electrical Safety before making physical measurements. The diagrams here explain connections, not a procedure for working on mains wiring.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 71 — Real meters change the circuit a little.

    Place both voltage probes, predict the sign, then reveal; Interactive; Practice

    Place both voltage probes, predict the sign, then reveal

    A DC voltmeter reports an ordered difference: V(red) − V(black). The two probes must touch the two named points you want to compare. Reversing them reverses the sign; putting both on the same conductor gives zero.

    Static example: an ideal 12 V source supplies 30 Ω and 60 Ω resistors in series. Each resistor has an ideal switch immediately before it.

    Signed readings from the same ideal circuit
    Circuit stateRed pointBlack pointReadingWhy
    S1 openSupply +After S1+12 VThe single open switch takes the source voltage; no current flows.
    Both closedAfter S1After R1+4 VCurrent is 12/(30+60) = 0.1333 A; R1 drops 4 V.
    Both closed, probes reversedAfter R1After S1−4 VThe two point potentials are unchanged; only the ordered subtraction reverses.
    S2 openAfter R1After S2+12 VThe upstream side stays at +12 V and the downstream side returns to 0 V.
    Any supported stateOne named pointThe same point0 VA point cannot have a potential difference from itself.

    With two open switches, the conductor between them floats in this ideal model. Its voltage is not assigned. The interactive intentionally offers no two-open state.

    This is a low-voltage ideal-circuit model with an infinite-impedance voltmeter. It does not authorize live work, mains measurements, or current-mode probing. Fluke's DC-voltage guide explains the V and COM inputs and the negative sign from reversed DC probes; its 381 meter manual shows that voltage probes touch the two desired test points.

    Practice choosing probe points Practice open-switch readings

    A shunt or clamp lets you measure current indirectly

    A shunt or clamp lets you measure current indirectly

    A shunt is a known small resistance in the current path. Measure the voltage across it and use the relationship in Current, Voltage, and Resistance to find current. The shunt is in series; the voltage measurement across it is in parallel. Many ammeters contain a shunt internally. An installed shunt avoids opening the circuit each time you read it; adding one still requires changing the path.

    A clamp meter senses the magnetic field around a conductor without breaking the circuit. Clamp around one conductor, not the outgoing and returning conductors together: their fields can cancel. The instrument must support the type of current being measured; an AC-only clamp does not measure steady DC.

    Resistance and continuity are measured with the circuit unpowered

    Resistance and continuity are measured with the circuit unpowered

    An ohmmeter applies its own small test signal. Use it on an unpowered circuit, with stored energy discharged as described in Electrical Safety. Other connected paths can change the result; isolating the component lets you measure its resistance instead of the whole network.

    Continuity is a resistance-threshold test. The beep means the measured resistance is below that meter's threshold. It does not prove exactly zero resistance, identify the intended path, or establish that a connection can carry its working current. The threshold comes from the meter's manual.

    A multimeter combines voltage, current and resistance functions, often with continuity too. Select the function, AC or DC mode, range and lead sockets for the measurement. In a schematic, follow the actual connection points rather than the physical positions of the symbols.

    Choose a drawing by the question it answers: appearance, connections, function, control logic, or physical location.

    Choose the drawing for the job

    Choose the drawing for the job

    One electrical system can need several drawings. Start with the question: What does the part look like? Where does this wire go? How does the circuit work? Where does the equipment fit?

    Choose the drawing for the question you need to answer.
    TypeShowsUsually leaves outWho uses it, and when

    BlockFunctions and the direction of signal or power flow.Individual terminals, component values, and return wires.A designer explaining a system before working out its circuits.
    WiringConnections between terminals; wire identifiers and routing where specified.The reason the circuit behaves as it does; scale may be omitted.An assembler or service technician connecting or tracing wires.
    SchematicElectrical function and connections using component symbols.Actual component positions, wire lengths, and enclosure geometry.A circuit designer or technician analyzing how a circuit works.
    IC / PCB layoutPhysical geometry: a PCB has footprints, pads and copper traces; an IC layout describes structures and interconnect on a chip.A convenient explanation of circuit operation.A board or chip designer checking placement and routing before manufacture.
    LadderRelay or PLC control logic arranged in rungs between rails.Exact equipment placement and wire routing.A controls technician tracing the conditions for an output.
    LogicGates and the relationships between logical inputs and outputs.Power wiring, package pin locations, and physical placement unless added.A digital designer following Boolean decisions through a circuit.
    Electrical floor planLocations of outlets, switches and fixtures on a building plan, interpreted with its legend.Internal circuit operation; complete routing may be on other drawings.An installer or building designer locating devices within rooms.
    RiserDistribution between building levels and the equipment serving them.Detailed room layouts and exact conduit paths unless specified.A building electrical designer or installer coordinating distribution across floors.

    Read the drawing title, legend, revision, and notes before treating a line or mark as an instruction. The same habit applies to mechanical drawings; see Choosing Drawing Views and The Alphabet of Lines.

    Compare one circuit in pictorial, wiring, and schematic views; Interactive

    Compare one circuit in pictorial, wiring, and schematic views

    This teaching example connects a battery, switch, resistor, and LED in one loop. The resistor is in series with the LED. The drawings explain identity and connections; they do not specify a buildable parts list, resistor value, battery rating, or package pinout.

    Choose a view. Choose a component to keep it marked when you change views.

    The wiring view retains every terminal connection. The block view deliberately removes that detail to explain each part's job. The schematic retains those connections while replacing part pictures with common symbols. Compare the three drawings together, or select one view to trace a part. On narrow screens the comparison stacks vertically.

    For the electrical quantities and circuit behavior, continue to Current, Voltage, and Resistance, Series and Parallel Circuits, and AC and DC. For programmable control, see Microcontroller Basics. For work on real equipment, use Electrical Safety.

    A layout, floor plan, and riser answer different location questions

    A layout, floor plan, and riser answer different location questions

    A PCB footprint is the land pattern where a component attaches to a board. Traces are the board's conductive paths. An IC is a chip; its internal layout is not the same drawing as the board that holds it.

    A floor plan places devices in rooms. Its legend tells you what each mark means. A riser makes the relationship between building levels easier to follow. Neither should be treated as a complete installation instruction by itself.

    Read control logic without assuming physical placement

    Read control logic without assuming physical placement

    A ladder diagram arranges control conditions and outputs in horizontal rungs between two vertical rails. A relay drawing and a PLC program may use a similar ladder shape, but a PLC instruction tests a stored state; it is not a picture of a physical contact.

    A logic diagram emphasizes operations such as AND, OR, and NOT. It helps answer which combinations of inputs produce an output. The diagram may omit supply connections and package pin numbers, so it does not replace a wiring drawing.

    Practice selecting a useful drawing

    Practice diagram selection

    Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems

    Reading Electrical Connections

    Follow conductors and node labels instead of judging connections by where components sit on the page.

    Read the connection convention before tracing a wire

    Read the connection convention before tracing a wire

    A schematic organizes electrical relationships, not the positions of parts on a bench. Stretching or bending a drawn wire does not change its connections. Moving a line onto a different terminal does.

    For the examples on this page, a filled dot at a crossing means the wires join. A crossing with no dot means they do not join. Other drawings may use a bridge or different conventions. Check the legend; an unclear or damaged junction mark is a reason to consult the drawing source.

    Count connected conductors, not corners or dots

    Count connected conductors, not corners or dots

    A node is a set of points joined by ideal conductors. Every point along an uninterrupted wire belongs to the same node, including its bends and branches. A dot marks a connection; it is not a separate component or an extra node.

    In the figure, the dotted cross is one node. The undotted cross is two nodes: the horizontal conductor and the vertical conductor. This count concerns the wires drawn in the figure; no connection elsewhere is implied.

    Do not trace through a resistor, diode, or open switch as if it were wire. If an ideal switch closes, its two sides become connected; state the switch position before counting nodes. Matching net labels can also indicate a connection without a continuous line across the page. Check the label scope and drawing notes before joining similarly named nets.

    Read component identity separately from its value

    Read component identity separately from its value

    A reference such as R1 identifies a particular part; a value such as 1 kΩ describes its resistance. D1 can identify a diode or LED, so its symbol and parts information still matter. A ground label identifies a reference or connection according to the drawing; it does not by itself establish a connection to protective earth.

    US practice (IEEE 315 / ANSI Y32.2) and international practice (IEC 60617) draw some symbols differently. Use the drawing legend; the forms below are teaching examples, not a claim of compliance with a standard.

    Trace a connection one terminal at a time; Checklist; Practice

    Trace a connection one terminal at a time

    • Read the legend, notes, revision, and stated switch positions.
    • Find the source and the named return or reference node.
    • Follow each conductor to a component terminal, junction, or net label.
    • Mark each uninterrupted group of conductors as one node.
    • Check crossings and similarly named labels before assuming they join.
    • Use the wiring drawing and parts documentation when physical terminal locations matter.

    Practice crossing wires

    Recognize common symbols before tracing their connections

    Use the symbol to identify the kind of component, then read its reference and value. The sheet includes both resistor forms and an unpolarized capacitor. A battery is one kind of DC source; other DC supplies may use a circle marked with polarity.

    Electric Motor Principles

    Find the stator and rotor, then follow the changing magnetic field that keeps a motor turning.

    The stator stays still; the rotor turns

    The stator stays still; the rotor turns

    An electric motor turns electrical input into mechanical motion. In a rotary motor, the stator is the stationary part and the rotor is the rotating part. An air gap separates them. Bearings support the rotating assembly; the shaft carries motion to the load.

    The stator is often outside the rotor, but it does not have to be. The names describe motion, not inside versus outside. See Electric Motor Types for both arrangements.

    Keep the magnetic target moving: carrot on a stick

    Keep the magnetic target moving: carrot on a stick

    Picture the rotor turning to align its magnetic field with the stator's field. If the fields simply settled into alignment, that turning effect would disappear. To keep turning, the motor switches a field or keeps the stator field rotating. Think carrot on a stick: keep moving the target ahead.

    Commutation means switching current between windings at the right time. Brushes and a commutator can do it mechanically, or a drive can do it electronically. A winding is a coil of wire that creates a magnetic field when current flows through it.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 73 — Where the alignment picture needs care.

    Why a DC motor keeps turning: coil, field and commutator; Interactive

    Why a DC motor keeps turning: coil, field and commutator

    The simplest brushed DC motor is one rectangular coil on a shaft between two magnet poles. Turn the coil, find where the field stops pushing it, and see how a split-ring commutator keeps the push going one way.

    Predict first: a coil carrying current sits between a north and a south pole. At which angles does the field give it no turning push at all, and where is the push largest?

    Torque on the coil. For an ideal rectangular coil in a uniform field, the torque about the shaft is τ = N·B·I·A·sin θ. N is the number of turns, B the field (T), I the current (A) and A the coil's area (m²), so τ is in N·m. θ is the angle from the field B to the coil's normal n, the line perpendicular to the coil's face. The coil's magnetic moment lies along n or against it, depending on which way the current circulates. That sets the direction of the torque, not its size.

    Why the angle matters. Whenever current flows, each long side of the coil feels a force F = BIL, the same size at every angle. What changes is its lever arm about the shaft, r·sin θ, where r is half the coil's width. As the coil approaches θ = 0° or 180°, with its face across the field in the neutral plane, the forces point almost straight through the shaft. The lever arm shrinks to zero, and so does the torque. With slip rings the current still flows at those angles and the forces point straight through the shaft. With an ideal split ring the brushes sit on the gaps at that instant, so there is momentarily no current and no force at all. Either way the torque there is zero. At θ = 90° and 270° the lever arm, and the torque, are largest.

    Why a commutator. If the coil were fed through slip rings, its current would never reverse. With the polarity drawn here, past 180° the torque would reverse too, pushing the coil back toward that neutral-plane position, and over a whole turn it would average zero. Reverse the supply or the magnets and the coil's resting position moves half a turn. A split-ring commutator turns with the coil. Its brushes change segments exactly as the coil crosses the neutral plane, which reverses the coil current. The torque becomes N·B·I·A·|sin θ|: it never points backward, but it still falls to zero twice a turn.

    Two coils. Add a second coil 90° ahead of the first, each with its own split ring. When one coil is in the neutral plane, the other is at its peak. The total, |sin θ| + |cos θ| in units of one coil's peak, runs from 1 to √2. Its smallest value is 1/√2 ≈ 0.71 of its largest, so the ripple shrinks and the zero-torque dead spot disappears.

    Worked example, with illustrative numbers rather than a real motor rating: N = 50 turns, B = 0.20 T, I = 2.0 A, and a coil 40 mm × 30 mm, so A = 1.2 × 10⁻³ m². The peak torque is N·B·I·A = 50 × 0.20 × 2.0 × 0.0012 = 0.024 N·m. At θ = 30°, τ = 0.024 × sin 30° = 0.012 N·m.

    Direction. Reversing the current reverses every force (F = I L × B), so the motor turns the other way. Swapping the magnets reverses B and does the same. Reversing both restores the original direction.

    Model limits. This is an ideal teaching model: one or two rectangular coils, a uniform field, and current switched exactly at the neutral plane. Torque is shown as a fraction of one coil's peak, N·B·I·A. It does not model back EMF, speed, magnetic saturation or brush sparking.

    For how a DC motor's speed falls as its load torque rises, see DC Motor Torque, Speed, and Power.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 74 — Sources for the torque formula and the commutator.

    Separate turning effort, speed, and power

    Separate turning effort, speed, and power

    Torque is turning effort. Angular speed tells how fast the shaft turns. Mechanical power combines the two. A stopped shaft can have torque and still deliver zero mechanical power.

    Start with Current, Voltage, and Resistance for the electrical quantities, then use DC Motor Torque, Speed, and Power to see what happens when a load asks a motor for more torque.

    Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems

    Electric Motor Types

    Compare how motors switch their fields, what wears, and how they control motion.

    Brushed DC: simple supply, wearing contacts

    Brushed DC: simple supply, wearing contacts

    A small permanent-magnet brushed DC motor has stationary magnets and rotating electromagnets. Carbon brushes press against a segmented copper commutator. As the segments rotate past the brushes, the connections change and reverse current in rotor windings. The torque keeps acting in the intended direction.

    Strength: inexpensive and simple to run from DC, useful in small toys, pumps, and actuators. Weak points: brushes wear through contact and electrical arcing; the commutator and spring contact system can also deteriorate. Switching current at the contacts can cause sparks and electrical noise. Permanent-magnet construction is common in small motors; some brushed motors use field windings instead.

    A microcontroller can command a power driver with pulse-width modulation (PWM), switching the supply on and off rapidly to control the motor. The driver handles motor current; a logic output is not a motor power supply.

    AC induction: the rotor follows a rotating field with slip

    AC induction: the rotor follows a rotating field with slip

    Stator windings arranged around the motor produce a rotating magnetic field. In a three-phase motor, the currents reach their peaks at different times, moving the combined field around the stator. That moving field induces current in conducting rotor bars. The rotor current and stator field interact to produce torque.

    The rotor runs slightly slower than the field during normal motoring. The difference is called slip. If the rotor caught the field exactly, there would be no relative motion to induce the rotor current needed for torque. For example, a field at 1,800 rpm and a rotor at 1,740 rpm differ by 60 rpm, or 3.33% of field speed.

    Strength: a squirrel-cage induction rotor needs neither brushes nor permanent magnets, making it useful for pumps, fans, and conveyors. Weak points: speed changes with load and slip; a variable-frequency drive is normally used when adjustable speed is needed.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 75 — Why alternating current alone is not the full explanation.

    Brushless permanent-magnet motors: switch the stator current

    Brushless permanent-magnet motors: switch the stator current

    Here the rotor carries permanent magnets and the stator carries windings. A drive switches the stator currents in sequence so the magnetic field turns. There are no commutator brushes to wear.

    BLDC means brushless DC; PMSM means permanent-magnet synchronous motor. A DC supply can feed an inverter, an electronic circuit that creates changing phase currents. Most BLDC/PMSM drive systems use this electronic switching. The labels often distinguish waveform and control choices; they do not mean one rotor needs AC magnets and the other needs DC magnets.

    A suitably designed line-fed synchronous motor instead follows a rotating field set by the AC supply frequency and pole count. It needs an appropriate starting arrangement. Do not assume an arbitrary BLDC motor can connect directly to an AC line.

    Strengths: no brush contact wear and controllable speed; common uses include cooling fans, drones, and controlled machine drives. Weak points: drive electronics and correctly timed switching are needed; bearings still wear and winding temperature still limits output.

    Inner-rotor and outer-rotor describe what rotates

    Inner-rotor and outer-rotor describe what rotates

    An inner-rotor motor, also called an inrunner, rotates inside the stator. An outer-rotor motor, or outrunner, rotates around the stator. These are the arrangements sometimes called “inboard” and “outboard.” Use inner-/outer-rotor when describing the construction.

    An inner rotor can have low rotational inertia, useful for rapid speed changes. An outer rotor puts magnetic force at a larger radius, useful for producing torque in fan and propeller drives, but its rotating shell contributes inertia. Dimensions and design still decide the actual performance.

    Stepper: count commanded steps, but allow for missed motion; Practice

    Stepper: count commanded steps, but allow for missed motion

    A stepper drive energizes stator phases in a sequence of magnetic positions. As a first approximation, picture an inner-rotor brushless motor with many magnetic poles or teeth. That helps explain the small steps; it is a simplification, since stepper constructions differ.

    Open loop means the controller sends a move without measuring whether it happened. A stepper can position and hold without feedback while energized and within its torque capability. It is useful for printer axes and small indexing mechanisms. Holding position still uses current and produces heat.

    The weak point is missed steps. Excessive load or acceleration can prevent commanded motion. Without feedback, the controller keeps counting commands and does not know the shaft fell behind. Step count is not a guarantee of exact position, and holding torque is not a guarantee against any load.

    Practice motor selection

    Servo: measure motion and correct the error

    Servo: measure motion and correct the error

    A servo is a motor used with feedback and closed-loop control, not one particular magnetic construction. A sensor such as an encoder measures motion. The controller compares measured position or speed with the command and adjusts the drive to reduce the error.

    Strength: responds to a load disturbance and detects position error, useful for robot joints and machine axes. Weak points: adds sensor, controller, tuning, and cost. Feedback does not create extra torque; a servo can still reach its limits. A brushed, brushless, or other suitable motor can be part of a servo system.

    Linear motors move directly along a track

    Linear motors move directly along a track

    Think of the magnetic layout of a rotary motor opened out into a straight line. A traveling field pushes or pulls a moving member along a track, producing linear force instead of shaft torque. One permanent-magnet arrangement uses a magnet track and a moving coil assembly. Linear induction designs also exist; a magnetized rail is not universal.

    Strength: direct linear motion without a rotary-to-linear screw or belt, useful for positioning stages and transport systems. Weak points: the magnetic track, drive, cooling, and position measurement can add cost. Separate guides support and constrain the moving assembly; a motor does not replace the guide system.

    Compare the basic field picture in Electric Motor Principles and the load calculation in DC Motor Torque, Speed, and Power.

    Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems

    DC Motor Torque, Speed, and Power

    Use an ideal linear torque-speed curve to find a load point and see why peak output power occurs halfway to no-load speed.

    More load torque means less speed on this curve

    More load torque means less speed on this curve

    This model approximates a permanent-magnet DC motor at a fixed supply voltage with a straight line between two endpoints. Stall torque is the torque at zero speed. No-load speed is the speed at zero external shaft load. It is not a universal curve for induction motors, steppers, or regulated drives.

    Let Ts be stall torque, n0 no-load speed, and T the constant resisting load torque. The steady operating point is where motor torque equals load torque:

    n = n0(1 − T/Ts).

    This is an assumed linear approximation, not a measured motor rating. It omits acceleration, current limiting, temperature changes, and supply voltage drop. At stall it predicts zero shaft power, not zero electrical input. A stall rating is not a continuous operating rating.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 76 — Manufacturer basis for the straight line.

    Explore the load point and the peak-power point; Interactive

    Explore the load point and the peak-power point

    Predict first: a model motor has 0.8 N·m stall torque and 3,000 rpm no-load speed. A constant load asks for 0.2 N·m. Does the motor run above or below half speed?

    Static example: n = 3,000(1 − 0.2/0.8) = 2,250 rpm. Angular speed is 2,250 × 2π/60 = 235.6 rad/s, so output power is 47.12 W. Peak power is 62.83 W at 1,500 rpm and 0.4 N·m.

    Ideal motor and constant load

    The solid line is torque / stall torque; the dashed curve is power / peak power. The circle marks load torque; the diamond marks output power. The square marks peak power.

    Peak power is halfway, not at either endpoint; Practice

    Peak power is halfway, not at either endpoint

    Use P = Tω, with torque in N·m and angular speed in rad/s. Convert rpm using ω = 2πn/60. The definitions and units are on Power and Efficiency and Angular Motion.

    At stall there is torque but no speed. At no load there is speed but no external load torque. Both endpoints therefore have zero shaft output power. Between them, torque times speed reaches a maximum.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 77 — Derive the halfway result from the straight line.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 78 — Manufacturer check on peak power.

    Practice operating speed Practice output power

    Peak efficiency needs electrical input as well as shaft output

    Peak efficiency needs electrical input as well as shaft output

    Efficiency is output power divided by input power. Peak output power and peak efficiency answer different questions. The torque-speed line alone does not give electrical input or losses, so this explorer deliberately does not calculate efficiency.

    For the brushed coreless DC motors described by Portescap, peak efficiency occurs at a lighter load and higher speed than peak output power. Its exact position needs loss or current data. No external load means no useful shaft output, even though a real motor draws current to overcome its internal losses. Consult the actual motor's efficiency and continuous-operation data before selecting a load point.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 79 — Manufacturer basis for the efficiency comparison.

    Match the motor, reduction, and the same output load; Interactive; Practice

    Match the motor, reduction, and the same output load

    A gearbox changes the torque demanded at the motor shaft for the same output load. That can move the motor to a different point on its torque–speed curve. Predict both operating points before revealing them.

    Static example: a motor has 0.8 N·m stall torque and 120 rpm no-load speed. The output load resists with 0.6 N·m. Compare direct drive with a 20-tooth driver, 40-tooth driven gear, and a stated 90% running mesh efficiency.

    The same motor and output load, two connections
    ConnectionTorque required at motorMotor speedOutput speedMotor shaft powerModeled output power
    Direct0.600 N·m30.0 rpm30.0 rpm1.885 W1.885 W
    2:1 reduction, 90%0.3333 N·m70.0 rpm35.0 rpm2.443 W2.199 W

    Result: the reduction runs the output faster under this load, even though it divides motor speed. It reflects less load torque to the motor, so the motor reaches a higher speed. The gearbox did not create power: motor shaft power changed before the 10% modeled mesh loss.

    This is a fixed-voltage steady-running comparison with a constant resisting torque. It does not establish starting ability, acceleration, thermal or continuous rating, back-driving, electrical input, or gear strength. At stall, speed and shaft output power are zero; if required motor torque exceeds stall torque, the model reports no forward steady operating point instead of assigning a fictitious speed.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 80 — Source and the standstill boundary.

    Real loads may demand different torque at different speeds. Their operating point is an intersection of a load curve and a motor curve. Practice reflected load Practice output power

    Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems

    Microcontroller Basics

    Read inputs, make decisions in a program, and control outputs using a classic Arduino Uno R3.

    A microcontroller reads inputs and controls outputs

    A microcontroller reads inputs and controls outputs

    A microcontroller is a small computer on a chip, with a processor, memory and connections to the outside world. Its program can read a switch, decide what that input means, and turn an output on or off. The Arduino Uno is a board that supplies the chip with power connections, a USB interface and accessible pins.

    This topic uses the classic Uno R3 with an ATmega328P, operating with 5 V logic. Other Arduino boards, including newer Uno models, can have different converters and electrical limits.

    The drawing groups functions; it is not a wiring pinout. Check the labels on the actual board. Start with Digital and Analog Signals, then Analog-to-Digital Conversion and Pulse-Width Modulation.

    A sketch runs setup once, then repeats loop

    A sketch runs setup once, then repeats loop

    An Arduino program is called a sketch. It uses C/C++ syntax: rules for names, parentheses, braces and statements. It is a programming language, not ordinary English. Capitalization matters: digitalRead and digitalread are different names.

    setup() runs once after startup or reset. loop() repeats while the program runs. This original example turns the built-in LED on for half a second and off for half a second.

    void setup() {
  pinMode(LED_BUILTIN, OUTPUT);
}
void loop() {
  digitalWrite(LED_BUILTIN, HIGH);
  delay(500);
  digitalWrite(LED_BUILTIN, LOW);
  delay(500);
}

    delay uses milliseconds and pauses normal progress through the sketch. The braces group the statements belonging to each function.

    Choose the pin mode before using the pin

    Choose the pin mode before using the pin

    Three pin modes
    ModeWhat it doesTypical use
    INPUTReads a voltage level without enabling the internal pull-up.A sensor that actively drives a compatible signal; do not leave the input floating.
    OUTPUTDrives the pin HIGH or LOW.An LED through a current-limiting resistor, or a control signal to a driver.
    INPUT_PULLUPReads an input with an internal resistor pulling it toward the logic supply.A button connecting the input to ground.

    pinMode(pin, mode) configures the pin. digitalRead(pin) returns HIGH or LOW. On an OUTPUT pin, digitalWrite(pin, HIGH) drives it toward the logic supply; LOW drives it toward ground. These are limited-current signals, not ideal power supplies. On an INPUT pin, digitalWrite instead controls the pull-up.

    A button to ground reads LOW when pressed

    A button to ground reads LOW when pressed

    With INPUT_PULLUP, an open switch reads HIGH. Closing the switch to ground reads LOW. This is called active-low: the action happens when the signal is low.

    void setup() {
  pinMode(2, INPUT_PULLUP);
  pinMode(LED_BUILTIN, OUTPUT);
}
void loop() {
  bool pressed = (digitalRead(2) == LOW);
  digitalWrite(LED_BUILTIN, pressed ? HIGH : LOW);
}

    The pull-up supplies a small current through the closed switch to ground. The switch sinks that current. A physical switch can bounce between states briefly; counting presses reliably needs debouncing beyond this simple state display.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 81 — Pull-up resistance and current.

    Use the official IDE and function reference; Checklist; Practice

    Use the official IDE and function reference

    Get the IDE from Arduino Software. Use the Arduino language reference to check spelling, arguments and return values. The Arduino getting-started guide introduces the programming environment.

    • Confirm the board model and choose its matching board entry in the IDE.
    • Select the port belonging to the connected board.
    • Verify the sketch to catch syntax errors, then upload it.
    • Check that the observed input and output match the program.

    Disconnect power before changing wiring. Keep signals within the board's ratings and use a suitable driver for a motor. See Electrical Safety for electrical precautions.

    Practice choosing a pin mode

    Digital and Analog Signals

    Decide whether a sensor communicates with two logic states, a changing voltage, or the timing of pulses.

    Digital uses two states; analog uses a range

    Digital uses two states; analog uses a range

    A digital input interprets two states: LOW/HIGH, or 0/1. The wire still carries a physical voltage; the receiving circuit decides which logic state it represents. A voltage in the undefined region between valid LOW and HIGH levels is not a useful third state.

    An analog signal represents a quantity by a continuous range of values. A potentiometer wired between ground and 5 V can provide a changing voltage at its middle terminal. On a classic Uno R3, the usual analog measurement range is nominally 0–5 V with the default reference. That is not a universal sensor range.

    Classify the sensor's output circuit, not just its name

    Classify the sensor's output circuit, not just its name

    Common examples
    Device and connectionSignal at the input
    Button or switch with a pull-upDigital open/closed state.
    Quadrature encoder with compatible logic outputsTwo digital pulse trains; their order gives direction.
    HC-SR04 ultrasonic module, Echo pinA timed digital pulse. Its duration represents distance; its voltage height does not.
    Potentiometer connected as a voltage dividerAnalog voltage from its wiper (middle terminal).
    Photoresistor in a voltage dividerAnalog voltage as resistance changes with light.
    Phototransistor with a load resistorAnalog response to light unless a threshold circuit converts it to digital.
    Pressure or proximity sensorDepends on the model: analog voltage, switching output, or digital data. Read its documentation.

    A bare resistive sensor does not generate a usable voltage by itself: its surrounding circuit matters. A module may offer both analog and thresholded digital outputs.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 82 — Phototransistor circuits can measure light or switch at a threshold.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 83 — Why an ultrasonic measurement can be digital.

    The ADC reads voltage; PWM controls time; Practice

    The ADC reads voltage; PWM controls time

    Analog-to-Digital Conversion turns an analog input into a number the program can use. Pulse-Width Modulation switches a digital output on and off for a controlled fraction of each cycle. Neither operation changes the fact that the processor stores and works with digital data.

    Practice identifying sensor signals

    Analog-to-Digital Conversion

    Relate an Uno R3's 10-bit ADC reading to its reference voltage, step size and approximate sampling time.

    Ten bits give 1024 codes, numbered 0 through 1023

    Ten bits give 1024 codes, numbered 0 through 1023

    An analog-to-digital converter (ADC) samples a voltage and reports a number. The classic Uno R3 has a 10-bit ADC: 210 = 1024 possible codes. analogRead(A0) reads analog input A0 and returns an integer from 0 to 1023.

    The reference voltage sets the scale. With an assumed exact 5.000 V reference, one nominal step is 5/1024 = 0.0048828125 V = 4.883 mV, or about 4.9 mV. Resolution describes the step size; it does not guarantee that a real voltage measurement is accurate to that amount.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 84 — Arduino's resolution and timing figures.

    Use 1024 for the nominal voltage step

    Use 1024 for the nominal voltage step

    For these exercises, use a clearly defined ideal bin model: divide the 0–5 V span into 1024 equal bins, round down to the bin number, and limit the top code to 1023.

    code = min(1023, floor(Vin × 1024 / Vref)). Here floor means round down. At 3.000 V with a 5.000 V reference: floor(614.4) = 614.

    To report the nominal voltage represented by a code, use its lower bin edge: V = code × Vref/1024. Code 800 represents 800 × 5/1024 = 3.90625 V. In this model its bin extends up to, but not including, 3.9111328125 V.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 85 — Why dividing by 1023 answers a different question.

    Explore the steps and check the units; Practice

    Explore the steps and check the units

    The two-way ADC controls in the PWM and ADC explorer let you enter a voltage or a code. Try nearby voltages within one bin, then cross its boundary. In reverse, code 1023 gives 4.9951171875 V as its lower edge, not proof that the input equals that value.

    The same explorer also separates when a voltage is sampled from how its code is calculated. It shows instantaneous raw PWM or settled RC values, the finite mean of the selected point samples, and the mean of their reconstructed lower-edge voltages. Those are different from the waveform's complete-cycle time mean. A held code is the latest point result, not a window average.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 86 — Quantize first or average first?.
