    Pulse-Width Modulation

    Explore duty cycle, frequency, average voltage and RC smoothing, then compare PWM output with ADC input.

    Duty cycle is the fraction of each cycle spent HIGH

    Duty cycle is the fraction of each cycle spent HIGH

    Pulse-width modulation (PWM) repeats a rectangular waveform. The period T is the time for one cycle; frequency f is cycles per second. Duty cycle D is the fraction of the period spent HIGH.

    T = 1/f, ton = D × T, and for ideal switching between 0 V and a supply Vs, Vaverage = D × Vs. Convert a percentage to a fraction: 25% means D = 0.25.

    At 500 Hz, T = 0.002 s = 2 ms = 2000 µs. At 25% duty, the on-time is 500 µs and the average of a 0–5 V output is 1.25 V. The pin itself still switches between 0 and 5 V.

    The stock Uno R3 uses six PWM pins

    The stock Uno R3 uses six PWM pins

    Use digital pins 3, 5, 6, 9, 10 and 11. Default PWM is approximately 490 Hz on 3, 9, 10 and 11, and 980 Hz on 5 and 6. These correspond to periods of about 2.04 ms and 1.02 ms.

    analogWrite(pin, value) requests duty using values from 0 (always off) to 255 (always on). A useful nominal mapping is value = round(255 × D): 25% gives 64. Hardware timer modes introduce small differences in the exact duty, particularly near the ends of the range.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 87 — Official frequency table and timer limitations.

    Change duty and frequency, then compare an ADC reading; Interactive

    Change duty and frequency, then compare an ADC reading

    Print / static comparison: 25% duty at 500 Hz gives a 2 ms period, 0.5 ms HIGH time and a 1.25 V complete-cycle time mean for an ideal 0–5 V waveform. A point sample is one instant, not that average.

    The same PWM waveform sampled at different phases
    Finite sample setEach raw sampleSelected-sample meanADC code / lower edge
    500 samples/s, phase 10%5 V5 V1023 / 4.995117 V
    500 samples/s, phase 60%0 V0 V0 / 0 V
    2000 samples/s, phases 1%, 26%, 51%, 76%5, 0, 0, 0 V1.25 VMean lower edge 1.248779 V

    An unloaded 10 kΩ / 1 µF RC filter has a 10 ms time constant. In the settled repeating response its 25%, 500 Hz ripple runs from about 1.1579 V to 1.3453 V while its cycle mean remains 1.25 V. Changing a control recomputes that settled response; this model does not show startup.

    With a separate 5.000 V ADC input, 3.000 V gives code 614; code 800 has lower edge 3.90625 V.

    The explorer is a model, not a board connection. Its frequency and sampling controls do not configure an Uno or claim a board throughput. A raw sample uses normalized phase with HIGH on [0, D) and LOW on [D, 1); the stated finite sample count defines the reported sample mean. ADC controls use the ideal bin convention on Analog-to-Digital Conversion; 5.000 V is assumed exact.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 88 — Why more samples can still give the wrong mean.

    An RC filter smooths PWM but leaves ripple

    An RC filter smooths PWM but leaves ripple

    Put a resistor in series with the PWM signal and a capacitor from the output node to ground; measure the voltage across the capacitor. This RC low-pass filter slows voltage changes. The capacitor charges while PWM is HIGH and discharges while it is LOW.

    The time constant is τ = R × C. A longer time constant relative to the PWM period reduces ripple but makes the output respond more slowly when duty changes. The explorer shows the settled waveform with τ = 10 ms, assuming an ideal source and no load. A load changes the result; the filter is not a motor power supply.

    Microchip's AVR131 PWM filtering note explains the tradeoff: the low-pass filter must reject PWM base-frequency ripple without removing the slower signal of interest, and a low-impedance load can discharge the capacitor unless buffered. This explorer deliberately assumes no load.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 89 — What the smoothed trace calculates.

    PWM changes LED brightness and motor drive; Practice

    PWM changes LED brightness and motor drive

    Rapid switching changes an LED's average light output while a resistor or driver limits its on-state current. Perceived brightness is not perfectly proportional to duty. For a DC motor, PWM commands a suitable power driver; the board pin does not supply the motor current. The driver must handle the motor and its inductive current.

    Increasing duty usually increases the available drive, but motor speed also depends on load. Use DC Motor Torque, Speed, and Power to connect speed, torque and current. See Electrical Safety before wiring.

    Practice PWM calculations

    Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems

    Electrical Generation

    How turbines and generators turn other forms of energy into electricity, how photovoltaics differ, and how to compare a generation mix.

    A generator converts motion into electrical energy

    A generator converts motion into electrical energy

    A generator does not create energy. It takes mechanical work at a shaft and delivers electrical energy to a circuit, with some energy becoming heat along the way.

    A turbine is a rotating machine driven by a moving fluid. Steam, flowing water, wind, or hot combustion gases can turn its blades. The turbine turns the generator; the generator supplies electricity. An engine can also drive a generator without a turbine.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 90 — How rotation produces electricity.

    See Power and Efficiency for losses and AC and DC for the electrical output forms.

    Different heat sources can feed the same steam cycle

    Different heat sources can feed the same steam cycle

    Burning fossil fuels or biomass can heat water to make steam. Nuclear fission supplies heat without combustion. Geothermal systems use heat from the Earth, and concentrated solar systems use mirrors to collect sunlight as heat. The equipment differs, but a steam-based plant follows the same basic chain: heat, moving steam, shaft rotation, electricity.

    Not every turbine uses steam. A hydroelectric turbine takes energy from water flowing downhill. A wind turbine takes energy from moving air. A combustion turbine uses hot gases directly; a combined-cycle plant also recovers exhaust heat for a steam cycle.

    Photovoltaic cells skip the turbine

    Photovoltaic cells skip the turbine

    A photovoltaic (PV) cell converts light directly into electrical energy through the photovoltaic effect in a semiconductor. A connected load receives DC electricity. An inverter can convert that DC to AC.

    Solar PV and concentrated solar thermal are different routes. PV produces electricity in the cell; solar thermal first collects heat. That distinction matters when considering thermal storage.

    A generation mix is more than a list of percentages

    A generation mix is more than a list of percentages

    A generation mix describes how much electricity comes from each source over a stated place and time. Installed capacity describes how much power equipment is rated to supply. Those are different measures: a large rated capacity does not mean a source supplied the same share of annual energy.

    Predict: which generator produces more energy?

    Compare two hypothetical generators over the same 365-day, 8760-hour period. Generator A is rated at 1 MW with a given 25% capacity factor. Generator B is rated at 0.5 MW with a given 60% capacity factor. Which produces more energy over the year? Decide before opening the check.

    Check the rated-power and period-energy comparison

    Period energy = rated power × period hours × capacity factor
    Capacity factor = period energy ÷ (rated power × period hours)

    Fixed stated ratings and given illustrative factors over 8760 hours
    GeneratorRated powerCapacity factorAverage powerPeriod energy
    A1 MW25% = 0.250.25 MW1 × 8760 × 0.25 = 2190 MWh
    B0.5 MW60% = 0.600.30 MW0.5 × 8760 × 0.60 = 2628 MWh

    Generator B has the smaller rating but produces more energy in this given example. MW measures power; MWh measures energy over time. Do not treat 1 MW as 1 MWh for the year, and write 25% as 0.25 in the multiplication, not 25.

    Capacity factor is not conversion efficiency, the percentage of hours switched on, dispatchability, reliability, or a source's share of an energy mix. Partial-load operation contributes too; the factor does not require a generator to alternate only between off and full power.

    These ratings and factors are fixed hypothetical inputs for the stated period, not real-plant data. EIA's published factors use time-adjusted capacity methods; this example does not reproduce that method. The EIA capacity and generation FAQ distinguishes rated power from energy produced over a period and defines the capacity-factor comparison.

    Compare cost, emissions, variability, and dispatchability — the ability to adjust output when requested. Wind and sunlight vary with weather and time. Fuelled generation and reservoir hydro can often be scheduled, but fuel, water, maintenance and operating limits still matter. Storage shifts energy in time; it is not an extra primary energy source.

    No current percentage mix is supplied here. For dated U.S. generation data, consult the U.S. EIA's Electricity explained: electricity in the United States, and record the reporting year and whether the figures describe generation or capacity.

    Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems

    Energy Storage Methods

    Pumped water, stored heat and rechargeable batteries hold energy for later use in different ways.

    Pumped hydro stores energy by lifting water

    Pumped hydro stores energy by lifting water

    Use electricity to pump water uphill, then let it flow downhill through a turbine and generator when electricity is needed. The stored energy is gravitational potential energy.

    The cycle returns less electrical energy than it consumed because pumping, flow and generation all have losses. It needs suitable elevations, reservoirs and water management; it cannot be placed wherever a battery can.

    For the energy and efficiency relationships, see Work and Energy and Power and Efficiency.

    Thermal storage saves heat for later

    Thermal storage saves heat for later

    Thermal storage holds energy in a hot material, such as a fluid or solid. A concentrated solar plant can collect heat while sunlight is available, store it, and later use it to produce steam and electricity. Stored heat can also serve heating loads directly.

    Insulation slows heat loss; it does not eliminate it. Returning heat to electricity adds conversion losses. Choose the storage route for the energy form the load needs.

    Rechargeable batteries store energy chemically

    Rechargeable batteries store energy chemically

    A battery supplies DC through electrochemical reactions. A primary battery is intended for a single discharge life and replacement. A secondary battery is designed to be recharged with a suitable charger, restoring chemical energy for another discharge.

    Primary cells are useful portable energy supplies, but they are not reusable storage for electricity from a generator. Do not try to recharge a primary cell. Rechargeable does not mean unlimited life: cycling and aging reduce usable capacity.

    See Battery Chemistries for the families and Battery Capacity and Packs for the arithmetic.

    Choose storage for the load and the site; Practice

    Choose storage for the load and the site

    A small portable instrument needs a compact energy supply, so a battery is a practical fit. A site with suitable upper and lower reservoirs can consider pumped hydro for large stationary storage. A solar thermal plant needing heat after sunset can store heat without first converting it to electricity.

    Compare the required power, the energy needed over time, the storage duration, available space and terrain, losses, and service life. These examples identify a good fit; they do not establish that one technology is always cheapest.

    Practise choosing storage
    Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems

    Battery Chemistries

    Compare primary alkaline, rechargeable nickel, lead-acid and lithium-ion batteries, and the short history behind them.

    Capacity, self-discharge and aging are different

    Capacity, self-discharge and aging are different

    A cell is one electrochemical unit. A battery may contain one cell or several. Its chemistry helps determine voltage, mass, charging needs and how well it holds charge.

    Self-discharge is loss of stored charge while no load is connected. Aging is loss of the ability to hold or deliver charge, even after recharging. Both depend on the cell design, temperature and storage conditions, so a chemistry name is not a shelf-life specification.

    A capacity rating also depends on discharge current, temperature and the voltage at which the test stops. Use the particular cell's data, not a single capacity assigned to every AA or D cell.

    Primary alkaline cells suit replaceable, modest loads

    Primary alkaline cells suit replaceable, modest loads

    Common primary alkaline cells serve devices such as clocks, remote controls and flashlights. They are widely available and retain charge relatively well in storage. Their useful capacity and terminal voltage fall more under heavy loads and cold conditions.

    They are not intended to be recharged. Leakage can damage equipment, especially when cells are exhausted or left in storage. Rechargeable-battery memory effect is not a useful concern for a primary cell.

    NiCd and NiMH are rechargeable nickel batteries

    NiCd and NiMH are rechargeable nickel batteries

    Nickel-cadmium (NiCd) and nickel-metal hydride (NiMH) use alkaline electrolytes, but they should not be confused with primary alkaline cells.

    Two rechargeable nickel families.
    FamilyUses and strengthsLimits
    NiCdLegacy cordless tools and industrial backup equipment; capable of substantial discharge currents in suitable designs.Cadmium is toxic and requires appropriate battery recycling. Repeated partial cycling can cause memory-related voltage depression. Self-discharge matters during storage.
    NiMHRechargeable consumer cells and hybrid-vehicle packs; generally more capacity than comparable NiCd cells and no cadmium.Conventional cells can self-discharge noticeably; low-self-discharge versions improve charge retention. Voltage depression can occur, but memory concerns are generally less pronounced than with NiCd.

    Use a charger designed for the chemistry and cell. Fast charging is appropriate only when the cell and charger support it. Do not deliberately drive a pack to zero volts to prevent memory effect: a weaker cell can be forced into reverse polarity by the others.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 91 — Why a remote-control recommendation needs more than a chemistry name.

    Lead-acid trades low mass efficiency for useful power and cost

    Lead-acid trades low mass efficiency for useful power and cost

    Lead-acid batteries appear in engine starting and stationary backup supplies. They can deliver high starting currents and are relatively inexpensive, but they are heavy for the energy stored.

    They self-discharge during storage. Prolonged storage while discharged promotes sulfation, which can reduce capacity; this is not the NiCd memory effect. Starting and deep-cycle designs serve different loads. Use the specified charging method: the electrolyte is acidic, lead is toxic, and charging can release gas. Flooded, absorbed-glass-mat and gel designs all exist; modern lead-acid does not always mean gel.

    Lithium-ion needs protection; LiPo is not automatically better

    Lithium-ion needs protection; LiPo is not automatically better

    Lithium-ion batteries power portable electronics, tools and electric vehicles. Their energy per unit mass is generally considerably higher than NiMH, with relatively slow self-discharge and no routine need for full discharge to prevent memory effect. They still lose capacity through calendar aging and cycling.

    Protection and charge control must keep voltage, current and temperature within the cell's limits. A bare cell may not contain its own protection circuit. The pack design must provide the required protection; a protection circuit is not a substitute for a compatible charger.

    Lithium-ion polymer, often called LiPo, commonly appears as a light pouch cell in portable devices and model aircraft. The packaging allows thin shapes; some designs support high discharge rates. It does not guarantee higher energy density, lower cost or better resistance to physical damage. Pouches need protection against puncture and crushing. Self-discharge and memory behaviour are broadly those of lithium-ion.

    Nominal voltage and charging limits depend on the particular chemistry and cell. Do not use a single voltage for every lithium-ion battery, and do not confuse rechargeable lithium-ion with primary lithium-metal cells.

    Battery history moves from a pile to portable rechargeable cells

    Battery history moves from a pile to portable rechargeable cells

    The important sequence is the change in what batteries made possible.

    • Volta, around 1800: the voltaic pile made a sustained electrochemical source practical to demonstrate.
    • Gaston Planté, 1850s: lead-acid introduced a rechargeable battery.
    • Carl Gassner, 1880s: dry-cell development made the electrolyte easier to contain for portable use. “Dry” means immobilized electrolyte, not absence of moisture.
    • Waldemar Jungner, 1890s: nickel-cadmium added another rechargeable chemistry.
    • Lewis Urry, 1950s: work on the modern alkaline cell improved portable primary batteries.
    • Lithium-ion, 1990s: commercialization enabled rechargeable products with high energy per unit mass, building on earlier work by several researchers.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 92 — Scope of this short chronology.

    Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems

    Battery Capacity and Packs

    Convert Ah to Wh, use C-rate and current to estimate performance, and predict the effect of series and parallel cells.

    Ampere-hours measure charge; watt-hours measure energy; Practice

    Ampere-hours measure charge; watt-hours measure energy

    A 2 Ah cell and a 2 Ah battery can store very different amounts of energy if their voltages differ. Ah tells you charge. To estimate energy, you also need voltage.

    Energy (Wh) ≈ capacity (Ah) × nominal voltage (V)
    Energy (J) = energy (Wh) × 3600

    For an ideal 2.4 Ah, 3.6 V cell: 2.4 × 3.6 = 8.64 Wh, or 8.64 × 3600 = 31,104 J. Convert mAh to Ah by dividing by 1000 before multiplying by voltage.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 93 — Why the battery estimate uses an approximate sign.

    See Work and Energy for energy units and Current, Voltage, and Resistance for voltage and charge.

    Practise battery energy
    C-rate sets a current scale; load current sets ideal runtime; Practice

    C-rate sets a current scale; load current sets ideal runtime

    A discharge rate of 1C means a current numerically equal to the capacity in Ah divided by one hour. The rate has units of h−1. Here C is a rate notation, not the coulomb symbol.

    Rated maximum current (A) ≈ maximum discharge C-rate (h⁻¹) × capacity (Ah)
    Ideal runtime (h) = capacity (Ah) ÷ load current (A)

    A 2.4 Ah cell rated for continuous 3C discharge has a rated current estimate of 3 × 2.4 = 7.2 A. At a constant 1.2 A load, ideal runtime is 2.4 ÷ 1.2 = 2 h. At 3C, the ideal duration is one-third of an hour, or 20 minutes.

    A C-rate may describe a test rate, a charge rate, a continuous limit or a short pulse limit. Only a specified maximum discharge rating belongs in the maximum-current equation. Actual pack limits may be lower because of wiring, temperature or protection hardware. A constant-power load also changes current as voltage changes.

    Practise ideal runtime
    Series adds voltage; parallel adds charge capacity

    Series adds voltage; parallel adds charge capacity

    For matched cells, connect cells in series to increase voltage. Put identical series strings in parallel to increase Ah at the same voltage. 3s2p means three cells per series string and two strings in parallel: six cells altogether.

    Pack V = series count × cell V
    Pack Ah = parallel count × cell Ah
    Pack Wh ≈ pack V × pack Ah

    With 3.6 V, 2.4 Ah cells, a 3s2p pack is 10.8 V, 4.8 Ah and 51.84 Wh. At 3C it has an ideal rated-current estimate of 14.4 A. A 1.2 A pack load gives 4 h ideal runtime.

    This is an electrical model, not a pack assembly procedure. It assumes matched cells, balanced series operation and equal current sharing between parallel strings. Real packs need appropriate cell matching, interconnections and protection. See Series and Parallel Circuits.

    Explore a pack by changing one input at a time; Interactive; Practice

    Explore a pack by changing one input at a time

    First double the series count: voltage and energy double, but Ah and runtime at the same pack current do not. Reset it, then double the parallel count: Ah, energy, rated current and ideal runtime double. The load current below is measured at the pack terminals.

    Predict first: same current or same ideal power?

    Before checking the results, predict whether ideal runtime will stay the same or double in each comparison, and explain what must happen to current. Start with 3.6 V, 2.4 Ah cells in a 3s2p pack at 1.2 A, then try two different meanings of “the same load”:

    1. Same pack current: change only the series count from 3 to 6 and leave the load-current input at 1.2 A.
    2. Same ideal nominal pack power: keep 6s2p, calculate I = P ÷ V = 12.96 W ÷ 21.6 V = 0.6 A, then enter 0.6 A in the existing load-current input.

    Paper example: 3.6 V, 2.4 Ah cells; 3s2p; continuous discharge rating 3C; load 1.2 A.

    V = 3 × 3.6 = 10.8 V; Ah = 2 × 2.4 = 4.8 Ah; Wh = 10.8 × 4.8 = 51.84 Wh; Imax = 3 × 4.8 = 14.4 A; t = 4.8 ÷ 1.2 = 4 h.

    With no JavaScript, use these equations to explore other packs. This example remains in the print view.

    Check the fixed-current and fixed-power comparison
    Same cells and parallel count, with two different load bases
    CaseNominal voltageCapacityNominal energyPack currentNominal load powerIdeal runtime
    3s2p starting case10.8 V4.8 Ah51.84 Wh1.2 A12.96 W4 h
    6s2p, same current21.6 V4.8 Ah103.68 Wh1.2 A25.92 W4 h
    6s2p, same ideal power21.6 V4.8 Ah103.68 Wh0.6 A12.96 W8 h

    Check: at the same current, both packs still have 4.8 Ah, so t = Ah ÷ I stays at 4 h while the 6s2p pack supplies twice the nominal power. At the same ideal power, twice the nominal voltage needs half the current, so the ideal runtime becomes 8 h.

    The 6s2p case uses twelve cells instead of six and stores twice the nominal energy. The longer fixed-power runtime is not a free benefit.

    This comparison assumes matched cells, constant nominal voltage, the stated Ah is available and the entered load is ideal. It does not predict changing discharge voltage, load or converter losses, reserve capacity, aging, cutoff or protection behavior. The model reports when the requested current exceeds the entered rating; a result below that rating is not a safety certification.

    Practise series and parallel packs
    Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems

    Soldering Equipment and Setup

    Choose solder, flux, and a tip that transfers heat, then prepare a stable bench and a tinned iron.

    Solder melts; the parts being joined do not

    Solder melts; the parts being joined do not

    Soldering joins metal parts with a filler metal that melts below the parts' melting temperatures. It is closer to brazing than welding: the base metals do not melt. Electrical soldering connects wires, printed circuit boards (PCBs), and electronic components.

    A good connection must be mechanically secure and conduct electricity. The molten solder must wet both surfaces: spread onto and bond with them, rather than sit on top as a ball. Clean surfaces, flux, and heat at both parts make that possible.

    Start here, then follow Making and Inspecting Solder Joints and Soldering Wire Splices and Through-Hole PCBs.

    Choose the tip for contact, not just access

    Choose the tip for contact, not just access

    A temperature-controlled station regulates the iron's tip temperature. A basic iron may have no temperature control; a cordless iron changes how it is powered, not how a joint is made. Check the tool's instructions and choose settings suitable for the solder and components.

    Tip shape and size matter. A fine point reaches small spaces, but a chisel's broad face often transfers heat more effectively. Use the largest tinned contact face that fits the joint without touching neighboring connections. Interchangeable tips let one iron handle different work; change them according to the tool's instructions.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 94 — What the iron's “sweet spot” means.

    Match the solder and flux to electrical work; Practice

    Match the solder and flux to electrical work

    • Leaded solder: common tin-lead alloys melt at lower temperatures than common tin-copper or tin-silver-copper lead-free alloys. Leaded solder is still sold, but lead is restricted in many products. Follow the specified alloy for the work.
    • Lead-free solder: common electrical alloys use tin with copper and/or silver. They may need a different heating process and can solidify with a duller finish. “Lead-free” does not mean “no fumes.”
    • Diameter: fine solder wire makes it easier to meter a small amount into a small joint. Thick solder feeds more metal for the same length; it is easy to overfill a small pad.
    • Flux: helps remove surface oxides during heating so solder can wet the metal. Rosin-core solder carries flux inside the wire; additional compatible electronics flux may help. Do not substitute plumbing acid flux.

    Read the alloy and flux label, including any residue-cleaning instructions. See Chemicals and Safety Data Sheets for handling information.

    Practice choosing solder

    Support the work and control the heat and fume

    Support the work and control the heat and fume

    Helping hands or a PCB vise hold the parts still while your hands hold the iron and solder. Keep a proper stand or cradle within reach. Use a damp soldering sponge or brass wool for tip cleaning, and have solder wick (copper braid) or a desoldering pump available for removing excess solder.

    It gets hot. Really hot. Park the iron in its stand, and allow the work to cool before touching it. Use ventilation or fume extraction that keeps the plume away from your face and other people; most visible fume comes from flux. Wash your hands after handling leaded solder, and do not eat or drink at the bench.

    SHOP RULE: NEVER SOLDER BATTERIES.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 95 — Why the battery rule stays absolute.

    Work on disconnected circuits. Follow Electrical Safety and Personal Protective Equipment; flux and fume handling belongs with Chemicals and Safety Data Sheets.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 96 — Further reading on flux fume.

    Clean, tin, and keep the working face coated

    Clean, tin, and keep the working face coated

    With the iron at working temperature, briefly clean the tip on brass wool or a damp soldering sponge. Apply fresh solder to coat its working face, then remove the excess on the cleaner. Leave a thin coating; do not wipe it bare and let it sit hot. Re-tin as needed and before storage as directed by the tool manufacturer.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 97 — Why tinning helps heat transfer.

    Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems

    Making and Inspecting Solder Joints

    Heat both parts, feed solder into the joint, let it cool without movement, and inspect the bond rather than its shine alone.

    Heat both parts, then feed solder into the joint

    Heat both parts, then feed solder into the joint

    Prepare the iron and bench using Soldering Equipment and Setup. The iron heats the parts; the heated parts melt the solder. Touch the tinned working face to both wires, or to both the pad and the component lead. Feed solder into the joint, away from the iron's contact point when access allows.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 98 — A one-second count is a rhythm, not a temperature test.

    Work through the joint in this order; Checklist; Practice

    Work through the joint in this order

    • 1. Strip and clean. Expose only the conductor needed for the connection without nicking it. Clean the surfaces to be joined.
    • 2. Support the parts. Form the connection and secure it so it cannot move during soldering.
    • 3. Flux if needed. Use flux compatible with the solder and electrical work.
    • 4. Heat BOTH parts. Put the tinned working face of the iron against both parts at the joint.
    • 5. Feed solder into the heated joint. Let it wet both surfaces. Do not melt a blob on the iron and wipe it onto cold parts.
    • 6. Remove the solder, then the iron. Stop feeding once the connection has enough solder and both surfaces are wetted.
    • 7. Hold still while it cools. Let the solder solidify without moving the connection.
    • 8. Inspect. Check wetting, coverage, clearance from adjacent connections, and damage before powering the circuit.

    Practice the sequence

    Look for wetting and shape; shine alone is not a verdict; Practice

    Look for wetting and shape; shine alone is not a verdict

    A good joint flows onto both surfaces. On a typical through-hole pad, look for a smooth transition from pad to lead, often a concave fillet (an inward-curving slope). Tin-lead joints are often shiny. A sound lead-free joint may be dull; dullness alone does not diagnose a cold joint.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 99 — Why lead-free solder may look different.

    Cold or poorly wetted
    Solder balls up or fails to bond to one surface, often because the parts were not heated adequately. A rough or dull appearance can be a clue, but inspect the contact and shape too.
    Disturbed
    The connection moved while solidifying, leaving a cracked or disrupted joint. Secure it before reworking.
    Too much solder
    A large mound hides the connection and makes bridges easier to miss. Remove excess so the joint can be inspected.
    Too little solder
    The intended connection lacks coverage or a continuous bond. Reheat both surfaces and add only what is needed.
    Bridge
    Solder joins connections that should be electrically separate. Remove it before applying power.

    Practice joint inspection

    Correct the cause before reheating

    Correct the cause before reheating

    Keep the circuit disconnected. Secure loose parts, clean and re-tin the tip, and use compatible flux if needed. Reheat both surfaces to remake a poorly wetted or disturbed joint. Use wick or a pump to remove excess solder or a bridge; do not pry at a pad while the solder is solid.

    Repeated heating can damage components or lift copper pads from the board. If a joint still will not wet, let it cool and get help finding the cause. Inspect again after repair. A continuity check can help find an open connection or an unintended short, but it does not prove mechanical strength.

    See Soldering Wire Splices and Through-Hole PCBs for splice support and through-hole work.

    Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems

    Soldering Wire Splices and Through-Hole PCBs

    Form a supported wire splice, insulate it with heat-shrink, or heat a circuit-board pad and lead together for a through-hole connection.

    Make the splice mechanically sound before soldering; Practice

    Make the splice mechanically sound before soldering

    Solder should not be the only thing holding loose wires in position. Form a stable splice, support it during soldering, and provide strain relief so pulling or bending the cable does not load the soldered joint. Follow the wire and assembly requirements; these sketches show splice shapes, not a qualification standard.

    • Lay-over or lap: stripped ends overlap alongside one another. Support and strain relief are especially important because the overlap does not lock itself together.
    • Twist or pigtail: stripped ends twist together and leave the connection on the same side. Cover the joined end completely when insulating it.
    • Western Union: an inline connection with each free end wrapped around the opposite wire. It is a commonly used, strong splice when properly formed; it is not automatically the best choice for every wire or assembly.

    For conductor sizing, see Wire and Wire Gauge. Use the heating and inspection method on Making and Inspecting Solder Joints.

    Practice identifying splices

    Put heat-shrink on before closing the splice

    Put heat-shrink on before closing the splice

    Slide suitable heat-shrink tubing onto a wire before joining it, and keep it away from the soldering heat. After soldering, allow the joint to cool and inspect it. Move the tubing over all exposed conductor, overlapping intact insulation at both ends of an inline splice, then shrink it with the appropriate heat source according to its instructions.

    Choose tubing whose unshrunk size passes over the splice and whose recovered size fits the wire. Avoid sharp wire ends that could puncture it. Ordinary heat-shrink provides insulation; do not assume it makes a waterproof connection or replaces strain relief.

    Supporting detail: Addendum 100 — When pre-tinning helps.

    On a PCB, heat the copper pad and component lead together; Practice

    On a PCB, heat the copper pad and component lead together

    A pad is the exposed copper connection area on a printed circuit board. A component's lead is its metal leg. In through-hole assembly, the lead passes through a hole in the board. Insert the correct component in the correct orientation and support the board and component before heating.

    Place the tinned working face against both the pad and lead. Feed solder into the heated connection and let it flow onto both, then remove solder and iron in that order. Hold still while it cools. Inspect the joint and the gaps to neighboring pads.

    Where the component's assembly instructions call for trimming, cut the excess lead above the cooled joint without cutting into the solder fillet. Wear the required eye protection and control the clipped end so it does not fly away or remain on the board. Do not shorten connector pins that must still mate with another connector.

    Soldering header pins is one bridge to Microcontroller Basics. A stray bridge changes the intended circuit connections; review Series and Parallel Circuits when tracing those paths.

    Practice through-hole technique

    Supporting detail

    Addendum

    Additional evidence, standards context, and background referenced from the main text.

    1. Safety/Universal Rules/Electrical Safety

      Addendum 1. “It’s not the voltage that gets you, it’s the current”

      The saying is true. What usually gets taken from it — that the voltage does not matter — is not. Current is electricity actually moving through you, and it takes very little of it to do real harm. Volts sitting on a wire nobody is touching do nothing at all.

      Two things together decide how much current you get: how hard the electricity is being pushed, which is what voltage measures, and how hard your body holds it back, which is called resistance. Harder push, more current. More resistance, less.

      Your resistance is not a fixed number — wet skin holds current back far less than dry skin does, so the same push moves much more current through you. That half of it cannot be relied on, which is why the line is drawn on the half that can be: the push.

      Back to reference 1

    2. Safety/Universal Rules/Electrical Safety

      Addendum 2. The international standards are not one number

      On datasheets you will meet a different set of figures, and there the AC and DC limits are not the same:

      50 V AC / 120 V DC
      Extra-Low Voltage under IEC 61140 and IEC 60364-4-41 — 50 V AC rms, or 120 V ripple-free DC. “Ripple-free” is a real condition, not a figure of speech: past roughly 10 % rms ripple the supply is treated as AC and the lower number applies.
      30 V AC / 60 V DC
      Class ES1 in IEC 62368-1, the standard behind most benchtop and consumer equipment. ES1 is the class that needs no safeguard at all; ES2 runs up to 50 V AC / 120 V DC and requires one.

      Back to reference 2

    3. Safety/Universal Rules/Chemicals and Safety Data Sheets

      Addendum 3. All sixteen sections, and the four OSHA does not enforce

      This is OSHA's own list, from Appendix D to 29 CFR 1910.1200. The numbers and headings are fixed; a manufacturer cannot renumber them or reorder them.

      Section 1
      Identification — product identifier, recommended use and restrictions on use, who made it, emergency phone number.
      Section 2
      Hazard(s) identification — classification, signal word, hazard statement(s), symbol(s) and precautionary statement(s).
      Section 3
      Composition / information on ingredients — chemical name, CAS number, and for a mixture, the ingredients classified as health hazards and how much of each.
      Section 4
      First-aid measures — by route of exposure, plus the symptoms that matter and when to get medical attention.
      Section 5
      Fire-fighting measures — suitable and unsuitable extinguishing media, and what the chemical gives off when it burns.
      Section 6
      Accidental release measures — the spill response.
      Section 7
      Handling and storage — "conditions for safe storage, including any incompatibilities".
      Section 8
      Exposure controls / personal protection — the OSHA permissible exposure limit, the ACGIH threshold limit value, engineering controls, PPE.
      Section 9
      Physical and chemical properties — physical state, odor, flash point, auto-ignition temperature, density, pH and the rest.
      Section 10
      Stability and reactivity — reactivity, conditions to avoid, "incompatible materials", hazardous decomposition products.
      Section 11
      Toxicological information — the health effects and the data behind them, including any carcinogen listings.
      Section 12
      Ecological information
      Section 13
      Disposal considerations
      Section 14
      Transport information
      Section 15
      Regulatory information
      Section 16
      Other information — "the date of preparation of the SDS or the last change to it".

      Twelve through fifteen are the odd ones out. The headings have to be there: a note to the standard says an SDS "must also include the headings" for those four, "in order", to stay consistent with the international system the format comes from. What goes under them is a different question. Appendix D says "Sections 12-15 may be included in the SDS, but are not mandatory", and a second note to the same paragraph says "OSHA will not be enforcing information requirements in sections 12 through 15, as these areas are not under its jurisdiction."

      Those four cover the environment, waste, shipping and other agencies' regulations — EPA and DOT ground, not OSHA's. So Section 13 tells you what the manufacturer suggests doing with the leftovers. It does not tell you what happens to them here. Ask.

      Two more things about the shape of the document. The section order is fixed but the order within a section is not — preparers "are not required to present the information in any particular order within each section", so two sheets can look different inside the same numbered box. And a heading with nothing under it is not an oversight: where there is no relevant information, "the SDS shall clearly indicate that no applicable information is available." Read that as nobody has the data — not as nothing to worry about.

      Back to reference 3

    4. Safety/Universal Rules/Chemicals and Safety Data Sheets

      Addendum 4. Signal words, pictograms and H-numbers — how Section 2 is written

      There are exactly two signal words, and OSHA defines them in 1910.1200(c): a signal word indicates "the relative level of severity of hazard", and "'Danger' is used for the more severe hazards, while 'warning' is used for the less severe."

      Severity is relative to the same kind of hazard, and that is the part that catches people. Flammable liquids in OSHA's Appendix C are the clean example — all three categories carry the same Flame pictogram, and the signal word is the only thing separating them:

      Category 1
      Danger — "Extremely flammable liquid and vapor"
      Category 2
      Danger — "Highly flammable liquid and vapor"
      Category 3
      Warning — "Flammable liquid and vapor"

      So “warning” does not mean mild. A Category 3 flammable liquid still catches fire. The signal word ranks a hazard against others of its own kind; it is not a statement that the chemical is safe.

      The pictograms are a fixed set of eight — a black symbol in a red-bordered diamond standing on a point. OSHA names them: Flame, Flame Over Circle, Exclamation Mark, Exploding Bomb, Corrosion, Gas Cylinder, Health Hazard, and Skull and Crossbones.

      The H-numbers are an index, not the warning. Real sheets often print a code such as H225 beside a hazard statement. Those codes come from the international GHS scheme this format is built on, which treats them as reference labels rather than as a substitute for the statement itself. OSHA's Appendix C does not use them at all — it specifies the sentence. Read the sentence.

      Back to reference 4

    5. Safety/Universal Rules/Chemicals and Safety Data Sheets

      Addendum 5. Telling a current sheet from an old one

      Section 16 carries "the date of preparation of the SDS or the last change to it." That is the only date on the document, and it is how you tell a live sheet from one that has sat in a binder for a decade.

      Keeping it current is the manufacturer's job, not yours. Under 1910.1200(g)(5), when a manufacturer or importer "becomes newly aware of any significant information regarding the hazards of a chemical, or ways to protect against the hazards, this new information shall be added to the safety data sheet within three months."

      Back to reference 5

    6. Safety/Universal Rules/Chemicals and Safety Data Sheets

      Addendum 6. What makes a flammables cabinet “approved”, and how to spot one

      OSHA calls it a storage cabinet and defines it by a fire test rather than by how solid it looks. 29 CFR 1910.106(d)(3) requires cabinets to "limit the internal temperature to not more than 325 °F. when subjected to a 10-minute fire test", with all joints and seams staying tight and the door staying closed throughout.

      The same paragraph requires the marking, which is the fastest way to recognise one: "Cabinets shall be labeled in conspicuous lettering, 'Flammable - Keep Fire Away.'"

      Back to reference 6

    7. Safety/Universal Rules/Machine Hazards and Housekeeping

      Addendum 7. The word for this, and where it comes from

      “Nip point” is not shop slang. It is the term the machine-guarding standard uses. 29 CFR 1910.212(a)(1) requires guarding against “hazards such as those created by point of operation, ingoing nip points, rotating parts, flying chips and sparks.”

      OSHA’s Machine Guarding eTool puts it plainly: “In-running nip point hazards are caused by the rotating parts on machinery.” Its longer treatment, Concepts and Techniques of Machine Safeguarding (OSHA 3067), gives three kinds:

      • “Parts can rotate in opposite directions while their axes are parallel to each other. These parts may be in contact (producing a nip point) or in close proximity.” — meshing gears.
      • “Nip points are also created between rotating and tangentially moving parts. Some examples would be: the point of contact between a power transmission belt and its pulley, a chain and a sprocket, and a rack and pinion.”
      • “Nip points can occur between rotating and fixed parts which create a shearing, crushing, or abrading action.”

      So belts, chains, sprockets and gears are rotating hazards by name. What makes them dangerous is that they draw material in — not that two parts close on each other.

      OSHA is just as direct about the plain shaft: “Rotating motion can be dangerous; even smooth, slowly rotating shafts can grip hair and clothing, and through minor contact force the hand and arm into a dangerous position.”

      These parts are meant to be behind covers, and the standard is specific about it — 29 CFR 1910.219(f)(3): “All sprocket wheels and chains shall be enclosed unless they are more than seven (7) feet above the floor or platform.”

      Back to reference 7

    8. Safety/Universal Rules/Machine Hazards and Housekeeping

      Addendum 8. What the investigations actually describe

      Oregon’s state fatality-investigation program, summarizing the record for this class of machine: “The most common causes of death and injury from metal lathes include entanglement of clothing in moving parts, being hit by loose objects on the lathe (e.g., chuck keys, tools, metal shavings) and being struck by a part that has not been adequately secured.” (OR-FACE 2012-18-1, Experienced Journeyman Machinist Killed While Operating an Engine Lathe, 2014.)

      Four investigated deaths, all the same event — something attached to a person touched something turning, and the machine did the rest:

      • Smoothing a part while it turned. A 69-year-old machinist with over 30 years’ experience “reached over the work piece to smooth out a radiused transition with emery cloth and a file in hand” and “his loose clothing (left arm sleeve) became entangled around the rotating work piece”. A co-worker 30 feet away heard “a strange ‘winding-up’ sound”. Of that same part, the shop foreman had said that “the rough surface could grab clothing or gloves”. (OR-FACE 2012-18-1.)
      • Stock sticking out the back of the spindle. A 52-year-old machinist was set up on a 103-inch steel bar: “Due to the length of the material, 24 inches were sticking out the back of the lathe, unguarded, and held in place with a clamping device that rotates as the lathe rotates.” He reached across the running machine and “the sleeve of his shirt became entangled”. (Kentucky FACE 21KY002, 2021.)
      • A burr on the end of the bar. A lathe operator in his twenties had a 1 7/8-inch stub of 1-inch bar standing past the tailstock. “The right pocket of his shirt was caught by the rotating tailstock burr. His shirt wrapped around the stock and tightened at the decedent’s neck and chest.” The listed contributing factor is “walking to and/or reaching over unguarded rotating bar stock”. OSHA makes the same point in general: the danger “increases when projections such as set screws, bolts, nicks, abrasions, and projecting keys… are exposed on rotating parts.” (Michigan FACE 14MI034, 2014; OSHA Machine Guarding eTool.)
      • A drill press. “As Employee #1 reached into the unguarded point of operation, his shirt sleeve or gloves became entangled in the drill bit. Employee #1 was pulled toward the machine, entangling Employee #1’s long hair. The drill press continued to spin, completely pulling Employee #1 into the operating area.” She died of her injuries. The same report records that the spindle “had speeds that ranged from 45 to 1115 rotations per minute”. (OSHA accident 114097.015, 20 February 2019.)

      Why abrasive cloth keeps appearing. The UK Health and Safety Executive publishes a sheet on this one task: “Every year there are serious accidents involving the use of emery cloth on metalworking lathes. These accidents result in serious injuries such as broken bones, dislocations, lacerations, amputations and occasionally death.” The mechanism it names is the one above: “Accidents occur when hand-held emery cloth is entangled in the rotating parts of the machine or where the emery cloth is snagged on the rotating component dragging the operator into the danger zone.” Its own rules are that emery cloth “should NEVER be applied directly by hand on manual metalworking lathes”, and that gloves “increase the risk of entanglement and” are “never acceptable near rotating parts of machinery”. (HSE Engineering Information Sheet No 2, rev 1, 2015 — that is HSE’s guidance; ask what the procedure is in the shop you are standing in.)

      And the drill press is not the exception it looks like. OSHA’s own drill-press training script lists, among the ways accidents happen, “getting dangling jewelry, loose clothing, or hair caught in the drill chuck (rotational hazard)”, and states: “The primary hazards of drill presses are contact at the point of operation and rotational hazards. An operator can risk serious hand injury when working too close to the drilling area, wearing gloves, loose clothing, loose hair, or jewelry.”

      Back to reference 8

    9. Safety/Universal Rules/Machine Hazards and Housekeeping

      Addendum 9. Why belts and chains count as rotating, not pinching

      OSHA sorts machine hazards by the motion that causes them, and “pinch point” is the vocabulary it attaches to parts that travel, not to parts that turn. From Concepts and Techniques of Machine Safeguarding (OSHA 3067):

      • Reciprocating motion — “Reciprocating motions may be hazardous because, during the back-and-forth or up-and-down motion, a worker may be struck by or caught between a moving and a stationary part.”
      • Transverse motion, which means movement in a straight continuous line — “Transverse motion (movement in a straight, continuous line) creates a hazard because a worker may be struck or caught in a pinch or shear point by the moving part.”

      A belt on a pulley is a rotating hazard that draws material in; a table running up against a column is a moving hazard that closes on it. Both can take a hand, and the vocabulary is worth keeping straight because the two do not have the same tell. You avoid the first by giving it nothing to grip. You avoid the second by knowing where the gap is going.

      Back to reference 9

    10. Safety/Universal Rules/Machine Hazards and Housekeeping

      Addendum 10. Why the rule has no exceptions in it

      Guarding is not a local preference. 29 CFR 1910.212(a)(1) — quoted already in Rotating machinery above for its definition of a nip point — is a guarding requirement first: one or more methods of machine guarding shall be provided to protect the operator and other employees from hazards including those created by point of operation, ingoing nip points, rotating parts, flying chips and sparks.

      The reason a rule like this is written without exceptions is that the exceptions are exactly where people get hurt. A guard comes off for a legitimate setup, the setup takes longer than expected, somebody else walks up to a machine that looks normal and is not. The standard's own answer to “but this task genuinely needs the guard off” is not a more careful operator — it is Lockout/Tagout, the next card on this page, which is a procedure rather than a permission.

      Back to reference 10

    11. Safety/Universal Rules/Machine Hazards and Housekeeping

      Addendum 11. What the standard actually covers

      29 CFR 1910.147(a)(1)(i): “This standard covers the servicing and maintenance of machines and equipment in which the unexpected energization or start up of the machines or equipment, or release of stored energy could cause injury to employees.”

      Two things are worth reading twice. Unexpected is the whole point — the hazard is not that the machine runs, it is that it runs while someone has a hand inside it. And stored energy is named alongside energization, because a machine that has been switched off and unplugged can still contain everything it needs to move once.

      “Servicing and maintenance” is much broader than it sounds. The standard defines it as “constructing, installing, setting up, adjusting, inspecting, modifying, and maintaining and/or servicing machines or equipment”, and adds: “These activities include lubrication, cleaning or unjamming of machines or equipment and making adjustments or tool changes, where the employee may be exposed to the unexpected energization or startup of the equipment or release of hazardous energy.” Setting up, clearing a jam and changing a tool are all on that list.

      Stored energy gets its own requirement — 1910.147(d)(5)(i): “Following the application of lockout or tagout devices to energy isolating devices, all potentially hazardous stored or residual energy shall be relieved, disconnected, restrained, and otherwise rendered safe.” The lock comes first, and then the energy already in the machine is dealt with. Both, in that order.

      Back to reference 11

    12. Safety/Universal Rules/Machine Hazards and Housekeeping

      Addendum 12. Why the chuck key rule is worded as a grip and not as a reminder

      A key left in a chuck is launched the instant the machine starts. Written as “remember to remove the key” the rule depends on you remembering at the one moment you are busy with something else; written as the key never leaves your hand there is nothing to remember, because a key that is still in the chuck is still in your hand and you cannot start the machine.

      Do not let a spring be the thing that saves you. Some chuck keys are spring-loaded and eject themselves when you let go — ours are, on the lathe. Not all keys are, and our Jacobs chuck keys are not. So the habit has to be the same on every machine, or it is a habit that works until you walk up to a different chuck.

      A drill-press chuck key is lighter than a lathe chuck key and carries far less energy. It is still dangerous: it is in the list of things that become projectiles in Rotating machinery above, and “less mass” is not the same as “will not hurt you” when it leaves a spinning chuck at the distance you are standing.

      Back to reference 12

    13. Safety/Universal Rules/Fire Safety

      Addendum 13. Why dry sand is on the list, and why it is probably not on yours

      Sand does work. The Aluminum Association’s Guidelines for Handling Aluminum Fines (F-1) lists fine dry sand, “preferably finer than 20 mesh,” next to approved dry powders as effective for isolating an aluminum fines fire. It also says what has to be true first.

      • Dry. F-1 says dry sand. Damp sand is water, and water “will react with the aluminum fines to form flammable hydrogen gas.”
      • Already in the room. “A plentiful supply should be easily available in the operating area and stored in covered bins or drums.” Sand fetched after the fire starts is not that.
      • With the right tool waiting beside it. “Long handled shovels should be available at each bin or drum, and should be constructed of non-sparking metal.”
      • Laid, not thrown. The shovels “lay the sand or powder around the edge or perimeter of the fire.” You are walling it in. Anything thrown at the pile raises the dust cloud that is the actual explosion.
      • Decided before it started, by someone senior. “Qualified supervisory personnel should decide in advance whether it is better to attempt to fight the fire or to withdraw to a safe location and allow it to burn itself out.”

      Those are preconditions, not tips. If you cannot point at the covered sand bin and the non-sparking shovel beside it right now, you do not have this option — and the call to fight it was never yours to make on the spot. Alarm, evacuate, report.

      Back to reference 13

    14. Engineering Fundamentals/Units and Measurement/Measurement Language

      Addendum 14. Why technical writing cares about the space

      Leave a space between a numerical value and its unit symbol: 8 m, 15.0 kg, and 0.50 s. SI also uses a space before °C and %. Consistent notation is a low-cost way to keep a drawing, a spreadsheet, and a controller reading the same thing.

      Back to reference 14

    15. Engineering Fundamentals/Units and Measurement/Measurement Language

      Addendum 15. Sources and definitions

      The BIPM SI prefix table is the primary list used here, including the 2022 ronna, quetta, ronto, and quecto additions. The NIST SI Units reference explains SI base and derived units and their technical-writing role.

      Back to reference 15

    16. Engineering Fundamentals/Units and Measurement/Dimensional Analysis

      Addendum 16. Dimensional analysis is also a design check

      If a mass density is in kg/m3 and a CAD model volume is in m3, the cubic meters cancel and the result is kilograms. That is why CAD mass-property settings, material cards, and drawing units must be read together rather than as separate menus.

      Back to reference 16

    17. Engineering Fundamentals/Units and Measurement/Dimensional Analysis

      Addendum 17. Two more conversion cases from the unit

      Machine run time: an automated machine has operated for 15 years and 150 days. With the stated classroom assumption of 365 days per year, (15 × 365 + 150) d × (24 h / 1 d) = 135,000 h. Real maintenance records should use actual calendar dates and include leap days.

      Supply-chain fuel: a truck rated 15 mpg has 15 mi/U.S. gal × (1.609344 km / 1 mi) × (1 U.S. gal / 3.785411784 L) = 6.37716 km/L. A 150 km one-way route is a 300 km round trip, requiring 300 km / 6.37716 km/L = 47.0429 L, or 47.0 L, assuming the quoted fuel economy holds for the trip.

      Back to reference 17

    18. Engineering Fundamentals/Units and Measurement/Dimensional Analysis

      Addendum 18. Sources and exact factors

      The NIST SI Units reference documents SI base and derived units. The NIST conversion conventions define the inch as exactly 0.0254 m; this page derives square and cubic factors from that exact value. U.S. liquid gallon values are explicitly labeled whenever they are used.

      Back to reference 18

    19. Engineering Fundamentals/Motion and Rotation/Motion Quantities

      Addendum 19. The calculus idea, after the practical one

      Over a smaller and smaller time interval, average velocity approaches instantaneous velocity. In calculus notation, velocity is the derivative of position with respect to time: v = dx/dt. For this course, begin by naming the interval, position change, and direction correctly; the derivative notation is a compact extension of the same idea.

      Back to reference 19

    20. Engineering Fundamentals/Motion and Rotation/Motion Quantities

      Addendum 20. Source note

      The NIST SI Units reference lists velocity as a derived unit example. Direction is an added physical requirement: two motions may have the same speed but different velocities because their directions differ.

      Back to reference 20

    21. Engineering Fundamentals/Motion and Rotation/Acceleration and Squared Time

      Addendum 21. Source note

      NASA’s Newton’s second-law resource connects force, mass, and acceleration for grades 9–12. The calculation here uses the average velocity-change form first; a real machine profile may have changing instantaneous acceleration within the same interval.

      Back to reference 21

    22. Engineering Fundamentals/Force and Power/Geometry, Mass, and Force

      Addendum 22. Check the CAD assumptions before trusting mass properties

      Confirm the assigned material, density, document unit, bodies included, and whether the model represents solid material or an internal void. A precise calculation based on the wrong material card is still wrong.

      Back to reference 22

    23. Engineering Fundamentals/Force and Power/Geometry, Mass, and Force

      Addendum 23. Sources and engineering context

      NASA Glenn’s weight-and-mass explanation distinguishes F = ma from W = mg. The NIST SI Units reference lists kilograms as an SI base unit and newtons as a derived unit. Those conventions are used here with g0 = 9.80665 m/s2 for the standard-gravity examples.

      The density conversion is from NIST SP 811, Appendix B, which lists slug per cubic foot to kilogram per cubic meter as 5.153 788 E+02; 0.00194032 is its reciprocal.

      Back to reference 23

    24. Engineering Fundamentals/Motion and Rotation/Angular Motion

      Addendum 24. Why a radian is barely a unit at all

      A radian is an arc length divided by a radius — a length over a length. The two cancel, so NIST gives the base-unit expression for the radian as m/m and its value as simply 1: the radian and steradian are “special names for the number one that may be used to convey information about the quantity concerned.”

      That is not trivia. It is why a torque in N·m multiplied by an angle in rad comes out as energy in joules with no conversion factor anywhere, and why a formula that mixes rotation with straight-line motion works only when the angle is in radians. Degrees and revolutions are counts somebody picked; the radian is the ratio the geometry already contains.

      Back to reference 24

    25. Engineering Fundamentals/Motion and Rotation/Angular Motion

      Addendum 25. Where 0.1047198 comes from

      One revolution is 2π radians and one minute is 60 seconds, so one revolution per minute is 2π/60 = 0.104719755… radians per second. It is not a measured constant; it falls straight out of the two definitions. Turning it over gives 60/(2π) = 9.5492966… revolutions per minute in one radian per second.

      Back to reference 25

    26. Engineering Fundamentals/Motion and Rotation/Angular Motion

      Addendum 26. Where these values were checked

      NIST SP 811, Appendix B gives revolution per minute to radian per second as 1.047 198 E−01, revolution to radian as 6.283 185 E+00, and degree to radian as 1.745 329 E−02. The 9.549297 r/min in one rad/s is the reciprocal of the first of those.

      NIST SP 811, Chapter 4, Table 3, lists the radian with symbol rad, value 1, and base-unit expression m/m. The rule that every unit symbol takes a space except the degree, minute, and second of plane angle is NIST SP 811, section 7.2.

      Back to reference 26

    27. Engineering Fundamentals/Motion and Rotation/Rotation and Linear Speed

      Addendum 27. Why the radian is the only angle unit that works

      A radian is defined as arc length divided by radius. Multiply an angle in radians by a radius and you get the arc length back — which is exactly the distance the rim travelled. Do the same thing per second and you have the rim speed. Degrees and revolutions carry an extra arbitrary count inside them, so they need a conversion factor first. The radian does not, because it was built out of the same geometry the formula describes.

      Back to reference 27

    28. Engineering Fundamentals/Motion and Rotation/Rotation and Linear Speed

      Addendum 28. Where these values were checked

      Conversion factors from NIST SP 811, Appendix B: revolution per minute to radian per second 1.047 198 E−01, inch to meter 2.54 E−02 (exact), and mile per hour to meter per second 4.4704 E−01 (exact).

      The grinding-wheel requirement is quoted from 29 CFR 1910.215(d)(1): “The spindle speed of the machine shall be checked before mounting of the wheel to be certain that it does not exceed the maximum operating speed marked on the wheel.”

      Back to reference 28

    29. Engineering Fundamentals/Force and Power/Torque

      Addendum 29. Where these values were checked

      NIST SP 811, Appendix B lists pound-force foot (lbf·ft) to newton meter as 1.355 818 E+00, and separately lists foot pound-force (ft·lbf) to joule as the same 1.355 818 E+00 — the two entries that establish the word-order convention used above. The reciprocal, 0.7375621, gives newton metres to pound-force feet.

      That M is the prefix symbol for 106 and m the symbol for the metre is from the prefix and base-unit tables in NIST SP 811, Chapter 4.

      Back to reference 29

    30. Engineering Fundamentals/Motion and Rotation/Gear Ratios

      Addendum 30. Why tooth counts work, and what the dashed circles mean

      The gears here share one tooth size, called module, and a 20° pressure angle. Their pitch diameters are proportional to tooth count. The dashed pitch circles roll together at equal tangential speed, so nA × NA = −nB × NB when clockwise is positive on both shafts. Here n is signed rotational speed and N is tooth count.

      Tooth flanks are involute curves. Actual tooth surfaces can slide during contact even though the pitch circles roll. The drawing samples those curves, simplifies the tooth roots and adds a small visual clearance. It is a motion model, not a manufacturing drawing.

      Back to reference 30

    31. Engineering Fundamentals/Motion and Rotation/Gear Ratios

      Addendum 31. Primary references and model boundaries

      • KHK: Idler gear. The intermediate tooth count cancels from the overall speed ratio.
      • KHK: Calculation of Gear Dimensions, section 4.1 and Table 4.1. Standard spur-gear pitch, base, tip and root dimensions and center spacing.
      • MIT OpenCourseWare: Gear Trains. Gear bodies, shared shafts, and force and torque balance.

      The lab assumes rigid external spur gears, fixed shaft centers, matched tooth size and steady transmitted load. It starts lossless; its efficiency control applies the same specified loss to every actual mesh, including both meshes around an idler. Acceleration, elasticity, backlash dynamics, detailed friction, noise and tooth strength are omitted. Changing tooth counts moves the centers to maintain the correct mesh; it does not represent swapping a gear into a fixed gearbox housing.

      Back to reference 31

    32. Engineering Fundamentals/Motion and Rotation/Gear Ratios

      Addendum 32. Why adding losses is only an approximation

      For a 1000 W input and three 96% stages, the losses are 40 W, 38.4 W and 36.864 W. Each 4% applies to a smaller incoming power. Adding 4% + 4% + 4% incorrectly takes every loss from the original 1000 W.

      Back to reference 32

    33. Engineering Fundamentals/Motion and Rotation/Gear Ratios

      Addendum 33. Follow both stages of one loaded train

      A 24-tooth driver at 1440 rpm and 4 lbf·ft drives 48 teeth. That shaft also carries a 15-tooth driver for a 45-tooth output. Both stages are 96% efficient, with no other losses. After stage 1: 720 rpm and 4 × 2 × 0.96 = 7.68 lbf·ft. The shared shaft carries that same 720 rpm into stage 2. Final output: 1440/(2 × 3) = 240 rpm and 7.68 × 3 × 0.96 = 22.1184 lbf·ft, versus 24 lbf·ft ideally. Overall efficiency is 0.9216.

      Back to reference 33

    34. Engineering Fundamentals/Motion and Rotation/Gear Ratios

      Addendum 34. Worked design: a winch with a speed ceiling and torque floor

      A motor supplies 1680 rpm and 24 lbf·ft. The output must be at most 40 rpm and at least 950 lbf·ft. Available gears have 10–60 teeth, with unlimited copies; each reduction stage is at most 6:1 and 97% efficient. There are no idlers or other losses.

      1. Speed requires i ≥ 1680/40 = 42. Two stages give at most 6² = 36, so try three.
      2. Three stages give ηtotal = 0.97³ = 0.912673. Torque requires i ≥ 950/(24 × 0.912673) ≈ 43.3708. Torque controls.
      3. Choose 12 → 48, 15 → 45, and 16 → 60 teeth: i = 4 × 3 × 3.75 = 45. Every tooth count and stage ratio meets its limit.
      4. ωout = 1680/45 ≈ 37.33 rpm ≤ 40 rpm. τout = 24 × 45 × 0.912673 = 985.68684 lbf·ft ≥ 950 lbf·ft. Both pass. Three external meshes make the output opposite to the input.

      This is one feasible train, not a claim of an optimum or a complete winch specification. For load force at a drum, continue to Torque; for travel speed, use Rotation and Linear Speed.

      Back to reference 34

    35. Engineering Fundamentals/Force and Power/Work and Energy

      Addendum 35. Turning a torque into work, and where the radian goes

      A constant torque about a fixed axis that turns through an angle does work: W = τθ, with the angle in radians. Because the radian is a ratio of two lengths, NIST gives its base-unit expression as m/m and its value as 1. Nothing is added to the units, so:

      1 J = 1 N·m (torque) × 1 rad  ·  1 ft·lbf = 1 lbf·ft (torque) × 1 rad

      This is the practical payoff of the radian being dimensionless: a motor rated in N·m turning through an angle in rad gives you joules directly, with no factor to look up. Use degrees or revolutions instead and the relationship breaks, because both of those carry a chosen count inside them.

      Back to reference 35

    36. Engineering Fundamentals/Force and Power/Work and Energy

      Addendum 36. Where these values were checked

      All conversions from NIST SP 811, Appendix B: foot pound-force to joule 1.355 818 E+00; watt hour to joule 3.6 E+03 (exact); kilowatt hour to joule 3.6 E+06 (exact); British thermal unitIT to joule 1.055 056 E+03, with Btuth 1.054 350 E+03, Btu (mean) 1.055 87 E+03, Btu (39 °F) 1.059 67 E+03, Btu (59 °F) 1.054 80 E+03 and Btu (60 °F) 1.054 68 E+03 listed separately; calorieIT to joule 4.1868 E+00 (exact).

      The horsepower hour figure is derived rather than quoted: one horsepower is 7.456 999 E+02 watts in the same table, and an hour is 3,600 s, so 745.6999 W × 3,600 s = 2,684,520 J to six figures.

      NIST SP 811, Chapter 4, Table 3, gives the joule as J, expressed as N·m and in base units as m2·kg·s−2, and the radian as rad, value 1, base-unit expression m/m.

      Back to reference 36

    37. Engineering Fundamentals/Force and Power/Power and Efficiency

      Addendum 37. Where 63,025 comes from

      One horsepower is 550 ft·lbf/s, which is 550 × 12 = 6,600 lbf·in per second. One revolution per minute is 2π/60 rad/s. Putting a torque τ in lbf·in and a speed N in rpm into P = τω gives τN(2π/60) lbf·in per second, and dividing by 6,600 converts that to horsepower:

      hp = τN × (2π/60) ÷ 6,600 = τN ÷ (6,600 × 60 ÷ 2π) = τN ÷ 63,025

      Every constant in the shortcut is a unit conversion. Nothing about the physics is buried in it, which is why the same relationship in coherent SI units needs no constant at all.

      Back to reference 37

    38. Engineering Fundamentals/Force and Power/Power and Efficiency

      Addendum 38. Where these values were checked

      NIST SP 811, Appendix B lists horsepower (550 ft·lbf/s) to watt as 7.456 999 E+02 and horsepower (electric) to watt as 7.46 E+02 — two separately defined units, which is why 745.6999 and 746 both appear above. The 0.001341022 hp in one watt is the reciprocal of the first. Foot pound-force to joule is 1.355 818 E+00 in the same table.

      NIST SP 811, Chapter 4, Table 3, gives the watt as W, expressed as J/s and in base units as m2·kg·s−3.

      Power factor is defined by Fluke as “the ratio of working power, measured in kilowatts (kW), to apparent power, measured in kilovolt amperes (kVA).” The 63,025 constant is derived above from the horsepower definition and the rpm-to-rad/s conversion, not quoted.

      Back to reference 38

    39. Engineering Fundamentals/Power Transmission/Belt, Chain and Gear Drives

      Addendum 39. What the explorer assumes, and where to check a selection

      The explorer compares ordinary drives on parallel shafts. “Separated” means a belt or chain span is practical but a single compact gear pair cannot reach. Speed labels are relative to the chosen component's rating, with no universal rpm cutoff. It excludes load sizing, life prediction, efficiency percentages and automatic cost rankings. “Candidate” means worth sizing, not approved for use.

      Its rules synthesize Gates' belt maintenance manual, Renold's transmission-chain installation and maintenance guide, and KHK's helical gear selection notes. Each manufacturer requires details beyond the four classroom choices.

      Back to reference 39

    40. Engineering Fundamentals/Power Transmission/Belt Drives

      Addendum 40. Manufacturer references for belt geometry and faults

      Gates, Preventive Maintenance Manual, “Belt identification,” “Installation,” and “Belt drive problem diagnosis,” supplies the length/profile distinctions and troubleshooting checks. Gates' industrial synchronous-belt guide explains toothed engagement and dry belt contact. Use the exact belt's data for a real selection.

      Back to reference 40

    41. Engineering Fundamentals/Power Transmission/Belt Drives

      Addendum 41. Derive the inverse and check speed and wrap

      Multiply the length approximation by 4C: 4CL = 8C² + 2π(D + d)C + (D − d)². Set B = 4L − 2π(D + d), giving 8C² − BC + (D − d)² = 0. The quadratic formula gives C = [B + √(B² − 32(D − d)²)]/16. Use this larger root and require C > (D + d)/2 so the pitch circles are separated. An impossible length produces no valid layout.

      Assuming no slip, n_small / n_large = D/d and v = πd n_small. With d in mm, divide v by 1000 to get m/min; with d in inches, multiply by 0.0254. Speed n is in r/min; N remains the symbol for teeth.

      The tangent-span angle is α = asin((D − d)/(2C)); small-pulley wrap is θ = 180° − 2α, with α expressed in degrees. Less wrap means less grip. The drawing uses circular arcs and tangent spans; the length equation approximates that geometry. Its error grows as (D − d)/(2C) grows, so very unequal, closely spaced pulleys need a more exact calculation for final selection.

      Back to reference 41

    42. Engineering Fundamentals/Power Transmission/Chain Drives

      Addendum 42. Checked public wording behind the ANSI numbers

      Tsubaki, The Complete Guide to Chain, printed page 86, states: The numbers to the left of the right-hand digit refer to the chain pitch in eighths of an inch. It also identifies the final 5 as bush construction and #41 as the narrow #40 variation. Tsubaki's Sprocket Catalog, “How to Order”, lists the pitch sizes independently.

      The checked ASME public listing names B29.1 as Precision Power Transmission Roller Chains, Attachments, and Sprockets, edition 2011 (R2022). See ASME B29.1. The examples above come from public manufacturer tables, not an unread clause of the paid standard.

    43. Engineering Fundamentals/Power Transmission/Chain Drives

      Addendum 43. ISO scope and the source of the millimeter dimensions

      The ISO 606:2015 public abstract describes short-pitch precision roller and bush chains with associated sprockets. Its scope includes dimensional and strength characteristics; a chain number alone is not a load rating. The dimension examples are from Renold Roller Chain tables, “European (BS) Standard — Simplex.” Renold's Chain Standards guide explains series and strand suffixes.

      Back to reference 43

    44. Engineering Fundamentals/Power Transmission/Chain Drives

      Addendum 44. Chain selection and maintenance reference

      Renold's transmission-chain installation and maintenance guide covers installation, lubrication, wear measurement and sprocket condition. Compare other drive families in Belt, Chain and Gear Drives.

    45. Engineering Fundamentals/Power Transmission/Chain Drives

      Addendum 45. Where the formulas come from, and what this model leaves out

      Geometry. The pin centres sit on a circle of radius R = p / (2 sin(180°/N)). The leaving pin turns at ω, so its horizontal speed is ωR cos θ and its height above the sprocket centre is R cos θ. The pin hands over to the next one when θ reaches ±180°/N, so v runs from ωR cos(180°/N) to ωR. One pitch leaves per tooth, so the average chain speed is N·p·n. Shigley's text derives the same maximum and minimum exit speeds: Budynas and Nisbett, Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design, 8th ed., section 17-5, Eqs. 17-30 and 17-31.

      Two ways to state the same spread. Tsubaki's Complete Guide to Chain, section 2.2.1 (printed page 15), divides by the fastest speed: (Vmax − Vmin) / Vmax = 1 − cos (180°/N). Shigley's Eq. 17-31 divides the same spread by the average speed. For 9 teeth that gives 6.03 % and 6.15 %. The table shows both columns, and the prediction bands accept either.

      Design guidance. Shigley's text adds: For smooth operation at moderate and high speeds it is considered good practice to use a driving sprocket with at least 17 teeth. Follow the chain maker's selection procedure for a real drive.

      Left out on purpose. This model has one sprocket with rigid links, pins seated exactly on the pitch polygon, and a taut span kept level. In a real drive the span's far end rides on a second sprocket, so the span also tilts. Tsubaki notes that the centre distance relative to the chain pitch, plus manufacturing and alignment errors, changes how much chordal action you get. The model does not include chain stretch, joint clearance, wear, lubrication, vibration or resonance. The tooth form is drawn schematically, not to a standard tooth profile. Pitch follows the pin-to-pin definition in the first card; the governing standard for these chains is ASME B29.1, linked there.

      Back to reference 45

    46. Engineering Fundamentals/Power Transmission/Gear Drives and Tooth Geometry

      Addendum 46. Check the size definitions with one gear

      A spur gear with 30 teeth and 60 mm reference diameter has m = 60/30 = 2 mm. The diameter is 60/25.4 in, so its equivalent diametral pitch is 30/(60/25.4) = 12.7 teeth/in. In general, m = 25.4/Pd. Two gears can have different diameters and tooth counts while sharing the same tooth size.

      Back to reference 46

    47. Engineering Fundamentals/Power Transmission/Gear Drives and Tooth Geometry

      Addendum 47. Normal and transverse measurements use different planes

      The normal plane cuts across a tooth at right angles to its slant; the transverse plane cuts across the gear at right angles to its shaft. Module (tooth size) and pressure angle can be specified in either plane, so compare values measured in the same plane. For this helical pair, match normal module, normal pressure angle and helix-angle magnitude, with opposite helix hands.

      Back to reference 47

    48. Engineering Fundamentals/Power Transmission/Gear Drives and Tooth Geometry

      Addendum 48. Primary references for the geometry and helical mesh

      KHK, Calculation of Gear Dimensions, sections 4.1 and 4.3, distinguishes reference geometry, profile shifts, and normal/transverse helical dimensions. KHK, ABCs of Gearing, B, develops tooth terminology and spur/helical calculations. KHK's helical-gear catalog gives mating-series and bearing-thrust cautions. Use the mating table for the exact product.
