    49. Engineering Fundamentals/Power Transmission/Screw Threads

      Addendum 49. Why the efficiency and strength comparisons need conditions

      The IIT Kharagpur lesson Power Screw Drives and Their Efficiency (sections 6.1.1–6.1.2, hosted by IDC) explains square-thread machining cost, trapezoidal sturdiness, and added friction from inclined flanks. Its force model supports a conditional comparison: hold lead angle, contact friction and other losses comparable. It does not establish a universal ranking against V-thread fasteners.

      Pratt & Whitney's ACME explanation describes the manufacturing and split-nut advantages. IIT Kharagpur's thread manufacturing lesson explains fastener rolling and other production routes. For thread cutting on a machine tool, see Lathe Operations.

      The buttress working flank makes efficient thrust transmission possible in its intended direction; that is a geometry-based explanation, not a promise of the same measured efficiency as square. Reverse travel is possible, but heavy loading on the opposite flank does not retain the same advantages. Compare actual screw-and-nut ratings, not shape alone.

      Back to reference 49

    50. Engineering Fundamentals/Power Transmission/Screw Threads

      Addendum 50. Where wear and operating limits enter the selection

      Thomson: Lead Screws Q&A — Application Considerations describes sliding-contact heat and wear and the relationship between load and speed. Its discussion also distinguishes the generic lead screw from the ACME form. The absence of radial wedging does not remove contact pressure on the working flank.

    51. Engineering Fundamentals/Power Transmission/Screw Threads

      Addendum 51. The exact standard entries used here

      NBS Circular 479, Unified Screw Thread Standards, tables 4 and 6, prints the designation entries 1/4, 20, UNC-1A and 1/4, 28, UNF-1A. The examples above omit the class suffix to teach size and pitch. This historical public standard verifies those combinations; it is not a source of current production acceptance limits. The current Unified inch thread standard is ASME B1.1-2024.

      NAAMS Metric Fastener Standards, archived sheet F–2.1, dated 05/29/15, lists M6 x1.0 under screw size and M6 x 1.0 under nominal thread diameter and pitch. Only that designation is used here. ISO 261 identifies the general-purpose metric M-thread family; its catalog entry is not being used as a dimension table.

    52. Engineering Fundamentals/Power Transmission/Screw Threads

      Addendum 52. Direction reference

      IIT Kharagpur: Friction in Screws, opening page, defines right-handed advance using clockwise rotation away from the person turning the screw. This observer convention avoids ambiguous arrows.

    53. Engineering Fundamentals/Power Transmission/Lead Screws

      Addendum 53. Check the definition, not just the label on a catalog

      Thomson: Screw Pitch and Lead defines lead as nut travel per screw revolution and states the pitch-times-starts relationship. A supplier may list lead directly. Do not multiply a value already labelled lead by the number of starts a second time.

      Back to reference 53

    54. Engineering Fundamentals/Power Transmission/Lead Screws

      Addendum 54. Derive the 2π from equal power, or one revolution of work

      Ideally, power in equals power out: Tω = Fv. With n in rpm, ω = 2πn/60 rad/s and v = nL/60. Cancel n/60 at nonzero steady speed to get F = 2πT/L. Equivalently, one revolution puts in work 2πT and moves the load through L, doing work FL.

      With losses, Fv = ηTω. The motion ratio stays fixed, so the reduction appears in force. See Power and Efficiency. At zero speed both powers are zero; this derivation does not predict breakaway torque or static holding capacity. Lowering a load that drives the screw requires a different friction analysis.

      IIT Kharagpur: Power Screw Drives and Their Efficiency, section 6.1.2, relates output work, input work and friction. The calculator uses a given efficiency, not a friction coefficient or a thread-strength model.

      Back to reference 54

    55. Engineering Fundamentals/Power Transmission/Backlash and Lost Motion

      Addendum 55. Where the definition comes from

      Modern Machine Shop's column Eliminate Backlash From Machining Centers (Mike Lynch, 2000) defines backlash as “any non-movement that occurs during axis reversals.” This page uses the CourseWiki definition on Screw Threads: clearance that must be taken up after reversing before the load moves. In a real drive, elastic deflection can add lost motion as well; the lab below leaves it out.

      Back to reference 55

    56. Engineering Fundamentals/Power Transmission/Backlash and Lost Motion

      Addendum 56. A readout that measures the slide, and when the clearance still matters

      The MIT 2.670 milling machine notes (section “Using the Micrometer Dials”) also point out that a digital readout measures the bed position directly, so its reading is not thrown off by backlash. The clearance is still in the drive. A force that pushes the carriage along the screw can move it across the clearance without the handwheel turning; Climb and Conventional Milling explains when a cutting force does that.

      Back to reference 56

    57. Engineering Fundamentals/Power Transmission/Bearing Types and Loads

      Addendum 57. Manufacturer reading for bearing selection

      Use the exact product's current catalog to check its load, speed and lubrication limits. These references introduce the design choices.

      • NSK: Introduction to Bearings identifies rings, elements and cage.
      • NSK: Roller Bearings compares line and point contact.
      • Kingsbury: Hydrodynamic Bearings describes oil-film support and high-speed applications.
      • igus: self-lubricating plain bearings describes embedded solid lubricants.
      • SKF: Rolling Bearings, bearing type and arrangement, for product-specific selection.

      Back to reference 57

    58. Engineering Fundamentals/Power Transmission/Shaft Support and Axial Adjustment

      Addendum 58. Why two locating supports can create unwanted load

      A warming shaft wants to lengthen. If a housing prevents that length change, elastic deformation creates axial reactions. These can consume clearance, increase friction and cause heating. Actual force depends on shaft, bearing and housing stiffness, temperatures and initial clearance. A floating seat also has friction; “radial only” describes its intended support duty, not literally zero incidental axial force.

      Back to reference 58

    59. Engineering Fundamentals/Power Transmission/Shaft Support and Axial Adjustment

      Addendum 59. Position preload versus spring preload

      Position preload sets the bearing rings at a fixed relative distance, for example with shims. Compared with that arrangement, a spring allows more axial movement under an added load. The spring can maintain preload as dimensions change, but the shaft position changes more under load.

      Back to reference 59

    60. Engineering Fundamentals/Power Transmission/Shaft Support and Axial Adjustment

      Addendum 60. Manufacturer reading and open material questions

      Further reading: SKF Railway Technical Handbook, bearing installation, describes both internal displacement and ring-seat sliding. NSK: Preload shows position adjustment using shims. Smalley: Bearing Preload covers wave springs. SPIROL: Precision Shims lists both stainless steel and brass among available materials.

      No manufacturer restriction confining brass shims to a nonrotating ring was verified. Material and mounting instructions must come from the actual assembly documentation.

      Back to reference 60

    61. Engineering Fundamentals/Power Transmission/Linear Bearing Guides

      Addendum 61. Manufacturer reading and the rotary-motion qualification

      THK: Assembling the Linear Bushing includes the heading “Rotational Use Not Allowed.” This is why unkeyed geometry must not be taught as permission to run a ball bushing as a rotary bearing. HIWIN: Linear Guideways identifies MGN as its narrow miniature block and describes moment resistance. Bishop-Wisecarver: Guide Wheel Technical Data shows a three-wheel carriage and discusses wheel orientation.

      Back to reference 61

    62. Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Quantities/Current, Voltage, and Resistance

      Addendum 62. Why voltage and resistance are called derived units

      Of the four units above, only the ampere is a base unit — one of the seven that the rest of SI is built from. The others are derived: their definitions are ratios of units already defined. NIST expresses the volt as W/A and the ohm as V/A, and traces both back to base units as m2·kg·s−3·A−1 and m2·kg·s−3·A−2.

      That is why unit cancellation works on electrical problems exactly as it does on mechanical ones — the electrical units are made of metres, kilograms, seconds, and amperes underneath. The technique on Dimensional Analysis does not need a separate electrical version.

      Back to reference 62

    63. Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Quantities/Current, Voltage, and Resistance

      Addendum 63. The dropped voltage does not disappear

      The power lost in the cord is P = I2R = (10 A)2 × 0.1588 Ω = 15.9 W. That power becomes heat in the conductor, spread along its whole length.

      Notice the squared current. Doubling the load to 20 A does not double the loss, it quadruples it, to about 64 W. This is why the drop that is harmless on a light load becomes a real problem on a heavy one, and why the length and gauge of a cord matter more the more current the tool draws. The condition and routing of the cord itself are covered on Electrical Safety.

      Back to reference 63

    64. Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Quantities/Current, Voltage, and Resistance

      Addendum 64. Where these values were checked

      NIST SP 811, Chapter 4, Table 3, gives: volt V, expressed as W/A, base units m2·kg·s−3·A−1; ohm Ω, expressed as V/A, base units m2·kg·s−3·A−2; coulomb C, base units s·A; watt W, expressed as J/s; pascal Pa, expressed as N/m2; and farad F, expressed as C/V.

      The ampere is listed as one of the seven SI base units, with symbol A, by both BIPM and NIST. The rule that a unit symbol takes a capital first letter when the unit is named after a person is NIST SP 811, Chapter 6.

      Back to reference 64

    65. Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems/AC and DC

      Addendum 65. Why use RMS instead of the average voltage?

      A symmetrical sine wave averages to zero over a whole cycle, yet it still heats a resistor. RMS is the DC voltage that would produce the same average heating in that resistance. Square the instantaneous voltage, average those squares over a cycle, then take the square root. The square-root-of-two conversion applies to a sine wave; do not apply it to an arbitrary inverter waveform.

      Back to reference 65

    66. Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems/AC and DC

      Addendum 66. Why RMS answers the heating question

      Analog Devices' RMS explanation shows why ordinary signed or absolute averages do not predict heating for arbitrary waveforms. Its power note distinguishes average power from the RMS value of a power waveform: RMS voltage or current can calculate meaningful average power in the stated load. This classroom explorer uses a purely resistive fixed load; it does not model impedance, power factor, temperature, a meter's coupling mode, or an actual circuit.

      Back to reference 66

    67. Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems/AC and DC

      Addendum 67. A comparison with the same power and the same line

      In an ideal DC or unity-power-factor comparison, transmitting 8,000 W at 400 V requires 20 A. At 4,000 V it requires 2 A. If the complete line resistance is 0.5 Ω, the losses are 200 W and 2 W. Ten times the voltage gives one hundredth the resistive loss. This simplified comparison omits converter losses and voltage regulation; it is not a design for a real transmission line. For AC loads with a phase shift, see Power and Efficiency.

      The historical advantage belongs to the equipment available at the time. Modern converters also make high-voltage DC transmission practical.

      Back to reference 67

    68. Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems/Wire and Wire Gauge

      Addendum 68. Why a long wire can matter even below its current limit

      A wire can stay within its temperature limit yet drop too much voltage for its load. Length increases resistance, and both voltage drop and heating follow from that resistance. The worked cord example in Current, Voltage, and Resistance shows the calculation.

      Back to reference 68

    69. Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems/Wire and Wire Gauge

      Addendum 69. Definitions used to calculate every result

      For AWG number n, diameter d = 0.127 × 92(36 − n)/39 mm. Convert d to meters, then A = πd²/4 in m². Using annealed-copper resistivity ρ = 1.724 × 10−8 Ω·m at 20 °C, R = ρL/A. One foot is exactly 0.3048 m.

      With one-way run ℓ, L = 2ℓ and Rloop = ρ(2ℓ)/A. Vdrop = IRloop; percent drop = 100Vdrop/Vsource; Vload = Vsource − Vdrop; wire loss P = I²Rloop. A two-wire single-phase resistive approximation uses the same return path, but this model does not include AC effects.

      Back to reference 69

    70. Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems/Series and Parallel Circuits

      Addendum 70. Why the parallel formula uses reciprocals

      Each branch draws the supply voltage divided by its resistance. Add those branch currents, then divide by the common voltage. The result is a sum of 1/R terms. This reciprocal of resistance is called conductance: parallel branches add ways for current to flow.

      Back to reference 70

    71. Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems/Measuring Electric Circuits

      Addendum 71. Real meters change the circuit a little

      An ideal voltmeter draws no current. A real one has high but finite input resistance. An ideal ammeter drops no voltage. A real one has some resistance and a voltage drop, sometimes called burden voltage. The practice problems use ideal meters unless stated otherwise.

      Back to reference 71

    72. Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems/Reading Electrical Connections

      Addendum 72. Check the node count terminal by terminal

      The four separate conductor groups are B1+ to S1; the other side of S1 to R1; the other side of R1 to D1 anode; and D1 cathode to B1−. Closing an ideal S1 merges the first two groups into one, leaving three nodes. None of the component bodies is an extra node.

      Back to reference 72

    73. Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems/Electric Motor Principles

      Addendum 73. Where the alignment picture needs care

      This is a first picture, not a description of every motor's internal timing. A synchronous motor can rotate at the same speed as the stator field while keeping an angular offset that produces torque. An induction rotor runs slower than the field during normal motoring; that relative motion induces rotor current. A stepper can deliberately stop and hold a commanded position.

      Back to reference 73

    74. Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems/Electric Motor Principles

      Addendum 74. Sources for the torque formula and the commutator

      OpenStax, University Physics Volume 2, section 11.5, Force and Torque on a Current Loop, derives the torque on a rectangular loop in a uniform field (equations 11.19 to 11.22). It defines the magnetic moment of an N-turn loop as N·I·A along the loop's normal and describes brushes and a commutator reversing the current. HyperPhysics (Georgia State University), Commutator and Brushes on DC Motor, describes a split-ring device called a commutator that reverses the current as the coil passes the plane perpendicular to the field. Its Torque on a Current Loop page gives the same torque in terms of the magnetic moment.

      Back to reference 74

    75. Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems/Electric Motor Types

      Addendum 75. Why alternating current alone is not the full explanation

      A single winding supplied by single-phase AC makes a field that pulses back and forth; that alone does not establish a starting direction. Single-phase induction motors use an additional starting arrangement. The rotating field, rotor current, and relative speed explain rotation more clearly than saying the rotor field simply opposes the stator field.

      Back to reference 75

    76. Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems/DC Motor Torque, Speed, and Power

      Addendum 76. Manufacturer basis for the straight line

      maxon's Motor Data and Operating Ranges, p. 10, states: Enhancing the load torque leads to a linear reduction of the speed. It identifies no-load speed and stall torque as the endpoints and specifies fixed applied voltage.

      Back to reference 76

    77. Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems/DC Motor Torque, Speed, and Power

      Addendum 77. Derive the halfway result from the straight line

      Put x = n/n0. Then T = Ts(1 − x), so P = Tsω0x(1 − x). Since x(1 − x) = 1/4 − (x − 1/2)2, the largest value is 1/4 at x = 1/2. Thus peak power = Tsω0/4, at half no-load speed and half stall torque. The two endpoint maxima cannot occur at the same time.

      Back to reference 77

    78. Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems/DC Motor Torque, Speed, and Power

      Addendum 78. Manufacturer check on peak power

      Portescap's Brush DC Motor Basics, p. 1, point 4, places maximum mechanical power at half the stall torque. On the linear curve, this also means half no-load speed, as derived above.

      Back to reference 78

    79. Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems/DC Motor Torque, Speed, and Power

      Addendum 79. Manufacturer basis for the efficiency comparison

      Portescap's Brush DC Motor Basics, p. 1, point 3, states: The maximum efficiency is obtained at high speed. Its accompanying torque plot places the efficiency peak below the torque of peak power; the descending speed line therefore puts it at higher speed.

      Back to reference 79

    80. Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems/DC Motor Torque, Speed, and Power

      Addendum 80. Source and the standstill boundary

      The running conversion follows maxon's gear conversion note: motor speed equals reduction multiplied by load speed, while motor torque equals load torque divided by reduction and gear efficiency. The note also requires checking actual gear torque and speed limits. A separate maxon standstill note explains that power efficiency is undefined when both input and output power are zero. This lesson therefore treats stall as a boundary; it does not calculate blocked-state efficiency or a permissible output torque.

      Back to reference 80

    81. Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems/Microcontroller Basics

      Addendum 81. Pull-up resistance and current

      The Uno's internal pull-up is approximately 20–50 kΩ, not a fixed 10 kΩ. Arduino's Uno R3 documentation specifies “20-50k ohm.” At nominal 5 V, a closed switch carries about 0.10–0.25 mA through that resistor, using I = V/R. See Current, Voltage, and Resistance.

      Back to reference 81

    82. Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems/Digital and Analog Signals

      Addendum 82. Phototransistor circuits can measure light or switch at a threshold

      Vishay's Ambient Light Sensors — Circuit and Window Design shows both light-meter circuits and light-switch circuits. The phototransistor current changes with illumination; the surrounding circuit determines whether the output preserves a range or switches between logic states.

      Back to reference 82

    83. Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems/Digital and Analog Signals

      Addendum 83. Why an ultrasonic measurement can be digital

      The HC-SR04 manufacturer datasheet, hosted by SparkFun describes an Echo pulse whose width represents the range. Digital describes the two voltage states; the information can be carried by their timing. A single digitalRead tells you the current state, not the pulse duration.

      Back to reference 83

    84. Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems/Analog-to-Digital Conversion

      Addendum 84. Arduino's resolution and timing figures

      The official analogRead reference source gives “5 volts / 1024 units” and “about 100 microseconds (0.0001 s)”. That is roughly 10,000 reads per second on ATmega-based boards using the usual API, not an absolute ADC hardware limit or a guaranteed loop rate. Computation, communication and delays take additional time. The published analogRead reference is the learner's API lookup.

      Back to reference 84

    85. Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems/Analog-to-Digital Conversion

      Addendum 85. Why dividing by 1023 answers a different question

      There are 1024 codes but only 1023 intervals between code labels 0 and 1023. Multiplying by 5/1023 stretches those endpoints to exactly 0 and 5 V; that is endpoint scaling, not the nominal ADC step. The explorer and practice consistently use 1024. Real converters have transition offsets, noise and reference error; their exact thresholds are not predicted by this classroom bin model. A code cannot recover the original voltage exactly.

      Back to reference 85

    86. Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems/Analog-to-Digital Conversion

      Addendum 86. Quantize first or average first?

      ADC conversion floors each individual ideal sample into a bin. Averaging the reconstructed lower edges therefore need not equal converting the analog sample mean. For a 25% raw 0–5 V sequence with one HIGH and three LOW samples, the analog sample mean is 1.25 V; the lower-edge reconstructions average 4.9951171875/4 = 1.248779296875 V. Neither operation recovers information between sample instants.

      Back to reference 86

    87. Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems/Pulse-Width Modulation

      Addendum 87. Official frequency table and timer limitations

      The Uno R3 row of Arduino's analogWrite reference source states “490 Hz (pins 5 and 6: 980 Hz)”. See also the published analogWrite reference. A frequency near 31 kHz requires changing timer configuration; it is not the stock setting. analogWrite sets duty, not frequency. Arduino's Secrets of Arduino PWM explains prescalers and timer modes. Changing timers can also affect other functions and libraries.

      Back to reference 87

    88. Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems/Pulse-Width Modulation

      Addendum 88. Why more samples can still give the wrong mean

      If the sample clock repeatedly lands at the same PWM phase, every point can read HIGH or every point can read LOW even though the full-cycle time mean is 1.25 V. A sample-and-hold output keeps the most recent point value between samples; holding is not averaging. A carefully spaced finite set can match the cycle mean, but a higher rate or larger count alone does not guarantee an unbiased result. This bounded comparison does not claim reconstruction of an unbandlimited switching edge from a Nyquist test.

      Back to reference 88

    89. Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems/Pulse-Width Modulation

      Addendum 89. What the smoothed trace calculates

      During each constant input interval, V(t) = Vtarget + (Vstart − Vtarget)e−t/τ. The model solves for a repeating steady state, then draws the charging and discharging curves. It omits startup, output resistance, component tolerances and loading. At 0% or 100%, the settled output is simply 0 V or 5 V.

      Back to reference 89

    90. Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems/Electrical Generation

      Addendum 90. How rotation produces electricity

      Relative motion between a magnetic field and conductors induces a voltage. With a closed circuit, current flows and the shaft must supply work against the electrical load. Motor action and generator action reverse the direction of energy conversion; see Electric Motor Principles. Actual machines and controls determine how they can operate in either direction.

      Back to reference 90

    91. Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems/Battery Chemistries

      Addendum 91. Why a remote-control recommendation needs more than a chemistry name

      A low average load makes charge retention important, but it does not by itself select NiCd over NiMH. Compare the actual cells' self-discharge, usable capacity, voltage and charging requirements. A low-self-discharge NiMH cell behaves differently from an older conventional NiMH cell.

      Back to reference 91

    92. Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems/Battery Chemistries

      Addendum 92. Scope of this short chronology

      This overview uses the historical sequence in the course generation-and-storage notes, with dates rounded to eras. Invention, patent and market introduction are different milestones; the dates are not intended as a priority claim. The development of lithium-ion was a multi-researcher effort, not solely the work of the company that first sold it.

      Back to reference 92

    93. Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems/Battery Capacity and Packs

      Addendum 93. Why the battery estimate uses an approximate sign

      Wh = Ah × V is exact for constant voltage. A real cell's voltage changes during discharge, so nominal voltage gives an energy estimate. Usable charge also changes with load, temperature, age and the cutoff voltage. These calculations assume the stated capacity is available.

      Back to reference 93

    94. Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems/Soldering Equipment and Setup

      Addendum 94. What the iron's “sweet spot” means

      Use the broad, clean, solder-coated working face of the tip against both parts. Do not interpret “side of the iron” as the barrel or an uncoated surface. The useful contact area, not the sharpest point or the highest temperature setting, delivers heat into the joint. A tiny point can be hot and still transfer heat poorly.

      Back to reference 94

    95. Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems/Soldering Equipment and Setup

      Addendum 95. Why the battery rule stays absolute

      Heat applied to a cell can damage its seals and internal parts. Lithium cells in particular can fail dangerously if damaged. Use the intended battery holder or connector instead of applying a soldering iron to a battery.

      Back to reference 95

    96. Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems/Soldering Equipment and Setup

      Addendum 96. Further reading on flux fume

      The UK Health and Safety Executive's guidance for solderers describes rosin-based flux fume and recommends extraction and keeping your head out of the plume.

      Back to reference 96

    97. Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems/Soldering Equipment and Setup

      Addendum 97. Why tinning helps heat transfer

      A hot tip oxidizes. Oxide interferes with wetting, while a solder coating protects the working face and helps make thermal contact with the joint. Tinning the tip is the time to feed solder onto the tip. Making a joint is different: feed solder into the heated joint.

      See HAKKO's tip-life guidance for the construction of plated tips and the effects of oxidation.

      Back to reference 97

    98. Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems/Making and Inspecting Solder Joints

      Addendum 98. A one-second count is a rhythm, not a temperature test

      “Apply iron, one-second count, apply solder” reminds you to heat before feeding. The actual time depends on the joint, tip, alloy, and component limits. Look for solder flowing onto both surfaces. If it will not flow, stop and check cleanliness, flux, contact, and tool settings rather than holding the iron there indefinitely.

      Back to reference 98

    99. Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems/Making and Inspecting Solder Joints

      Addendum 99. Why lead-free solder may look different

      Kester's soldering FAQ, under lead-free joint appearance, explains that tin-silver-copper joints can have a dull surface without being poor joints. Judge the connection, not shine alone.

      Back to reference 99

    100. Engineering Fundamentals/Electrical Systems/Soldering Wire Splices and Through-Hole PCBs

      Addendum 100. When pre-tinning helps

      Some wires and terminals are pre-tinned: a small amount of solder wets the surface before final assembly. This can help the final joint flow, but too much solder makes a wire end stiff and bulky. Follow the connection's assembly method and still heat both parts when making the final bond.

      Back to reference 100
